Anthropic's shares have dropped back towards their initial price after a soaring first day on the stock market, as a wider tech sell-off deepens.
The fall in tech stocks continued to weigh on markets through Friday, with the S&P 500 down about 2.8% and the Dow Jones Industrial Average down more than 1% by mid-afternoon.
Both US indexes touched correction territory, a point where they are trading at 10% or more down from a recent high.
The tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite Index also fell more than 4% by afternoon trading as shares in major tech companies continued to fall.
The speed at which AI investment has been growing - with more than $1 trillion spent in the last year alone by a small handful of major tech companies - has led to ongoing concerns of a financial bubble. Questions are being raised over whether those investments will pay off, and when.
Despite a positive first day of trading, Anthropic's shares fell on Friday, dropping at one point by more than 12% to about $85, close to its initial public offering (IPO) price of $83.
The artificial intelligence (AI) company's introduction to the Nasdaq stock exchange on Thursday was a crucial test for the industry and was largely seen as a success, with trading starting at $111.50.
The maker of the Claude chatbot raised a record $81bn in its initial public offering (IPO), but its share price moved significantly in the first day of trading.
The shares peaked at $115 on Thursday, before easing to end the day up 17% at $97.17.
Analysts said volatility was to be expected in the first days or even weeks of Anthropic's trading, as the company was the first frontier AI firm to go public so had no direct peers.
Some have also noted the similarities with Elon Musk's SpaceX, which at the time of its debut in June was the largest IPO on record. Shares in the rocket and AI company experienced large swings in its first few weeks of trading.
Most tech companies see their shares fall after hitting the stock market, often after reporting quarterly results for the first time.
But many, including Meta, Amazon and Google, have gone on to become the largest and most profitable corporations in the world.
Ed Moya, a strategist at market intelligence firm AlphaSense, said Anthropic's blockbuster IPO did not appear to have restored confidence in the broader AI market.
While AI demand was still very strong, Moya told the BBC that investors were trying to answer the question of how much were they willing to pay for that growth.
"As we've gone through the past past few weeks, it seems that there's been more risks that have surfaced," he said.
"Right now you're starting to see Wall Street is trying to shift from rewarding growth at any price, to demanding stronger cash flow and a clearer path to profitability."
Shares in some of the largest US tech companies also fell on Friday as the market sell off continued.
Nvidia shares had plunged by more than 11% by the afternoon, while Musk's firms SpaceX and Tesla had both fallen by more than 6%.
Meta was down more than 5% and Amazon was down more than 3.5%, while Apple and Alphabet experienced smaller falls.
Europe's main stock markets - which contain fewer tech stocks - also took a hit.
Germany's Dax index closed down 2.6%, France's CAC 40 was down 1.9% and the UK's FTSE 100 ended trading 1% lower.
Earlier on Friday, tech-heavy Asian markets saw steep falls.
South Korea's Kospi and Japan's Nikkei 225 indexes closed down about 5%, with shares in memory chip makers Sk Hynix, Kioxia and Tokyo Electron, and other tech firms such as Samsung Electronics, seeing losses.
Taiwan's stock market dropped about 6% on Friday, taking the weekly fall to more than 17% and what was reported to be its biggest weekly fall since 1990.

French authorities are investigating disgraced actor GÃ©rard Depardieu and the author Michel Houellebecq over "allegations of a sexual nature", a source with knowledge of the investigation says.
The confirmation comes after reports in French media that the two were accused of being involved in a "gang rape" on the set of the film Thalasso in 2018 by an actress.

French law stipulates as of 2025 that all sexual acts performed without consent constitute rape.
The film's director, Guillaume Nicloux, has been accused of being complicit because he was said to have filmed the incident, Mediapart and AFP report. The BBC has contacted his agent and the Paris prosecutor's office for comment.

The site published production documents showing footage of the scene had been destroyed.

New guide lays out how Army installations can coordinate with local agencies before disaster strikes
The handbook was released after the Army’s second Defense Critical Infrastructure summit.
The Army relies on local fuel, water, electricity and more to keep its installations going and deploy troops in the face of enemy attacks and natural disasters alike, so the service is urging its 288 camps, posts, and stations to lay that coordination groundwork now, before the balloon goes up.
The service released its Defense Critical Infrastructure community coordination guide Thursday, after its second DCI summit.
“It's a good reminder that readiness is not confined to a motor pool, a runway, or a headquarters building, and it really depends on the civilian and military systems that connect our forces to the nation: power, communication, transportation networks, fuel, water, and ports, just to name a few,” Brandon Pugh, chief of staff to the acting Army secretary, told reporters.
The guide suggests ways that Army installation officials can coordinate with local governments, utilities, and other services to keep communication open in case of disaster.
To that end, the Army has held two DCI summits this year, the first in May at Fort Bragg, North Carolina, and the second at Joint Base Lewis-McChord, Washington, on Thursday.
“All of our installations are critically dependent on local partners, local agencies for a range of things, whether that is water and wastewater, electric, natural gas supply, but we are currently not necessarily islands, and we are tied in very tightly with the community,” said Jordan Gillis, the Army’s civilian head of installations, energy and environment. “And so, events like this are the perfect opportunity for us to sync face to face with the local partners, so that in any kind of crisis, we've already got those relationships, and we've established at least a baseline understanding of the things that we each need to do to keep critical missions going.”
The first meeting, at Fort Bragg, was more of a national-level focus, Pugh said, while the JBLM summit focused on the particulars of the base’s Pacific Northwest location.
“The electricity that powers our operation centers, the water that sustains our barracks and families, the networks that carry our communications and the state highways, rail corridors, and deep-water terminals at the Port of Tacoma that move our brigades and units are shared community lifelines,” Lt. Gen. Matthew McFarlane, who commands JBLM and the corps that oversees the Army’s infantry divisions in Hawaii, Alaska, Washington, and Colorado. “When an adversary or natural disaster disrupts a municipal power grid, a water system, or a fiber trunk, the mission feels it immediately.”
Representatives from Joint Interagency Task Force 401, the Army-led Defense Department effort to field counter-unmanned aerial systems throughout DoD and domestic security agencies.
“We have prioritized the protection of critical installations and power projection capabilities, including the first ever fielding of counter-UAS equipment through the Domestic Shield program, right here at Joint Base Lewis-McChord,” Sgt. Maj. Kellen Rowley, JIATF 401’s senior enlisted adviser, told reporters.
Drone attacks are a specific focus for DCI and JIATF 401, as well as DoD’s new FORTRESS America domestic security program.
“There needs to be a training ecosystem that exists between our state, local, territorial, and tribal law enforcement partners and our military members who can, at short notice, execute battle drills to kind of rehearse what it's going to take to effectively counter UAS,” Rowley said.

A 15-year-old Ghanaian boy who was killed in the US last month was remembered as a hard-working student with dreams of becoming a doctor, as his father, New York City's mayor and civil rights leaders gave eulogies during his funeral on Friday.
Javits Frimpong was shot and killed while walking to school in the Bronx. His death has sparked outrage in both Ghana and the US, and reignited debates about gun violence in America.
"Javits deserved so much better and so do every single one of you," Mayor Zohran Mamdani said. "Though he was only a New Yorker for a short time, New York City will forever be proud to call Javits one of our own."
Frimpong moved to the US about a year before the shooting.
"I worked hard to bring you from Ghana to America because I wanted you to have opportunities, a better future, and a chance to achieve everything that you dreamed of," his father, Thomas Frimpong, said.
His mother was granted an emergency visa from Ghana to mourn her son at Friday's funeral service, following Mamdani's lobbying of President Donald Trump earlier this month.
Frimpong was chased down and shot on 29 October. He was taken to a local hospital, where he was pronounced dead.
Police have said three teenage boys were involved in the shooting. A 17-year-old has been arrested and charged with murder, and will be tried as an adult. Police are still searching for the other two.
"Gun violence is never the answer," Ben Crump, an attorney representing the family, said at the funeral as he vowed to seek justice for Frimpong.
Ghana's government has condemned the killing and said it would follow the case closely to ensure justice was achieved.
It has urged US authorities to conduct a thorough investigation and said it was ready to provide legal and consular support to ensure the perpetrators were brought to justice.

A federal judge sentenced an Indian man to 235 months, more than 19 years, in an attempted plot to kill a leading Sikh political figure in the US.
Nikhil Gupta, an Indian national, pleaded guilty to murder-for-hire, conspiracy to commit murder-for-hire, and conspiracy to commit money laundering in February. On Friday, the judge said he likely will be deported or removed after his sentence.
US prosecutors alleged Gupta was directed by an Indian government official to kill Gurpatwant Singh Pannun, a leading figure of the Khalistan movement, which advocates for an independent homeland for Sikhs.
India has denied involvement. Its government has accused Pannun of being a terrorist, which he denies.
Pannun, an American citizen, is the spokesman for US-based Sikh separatist group Sikhs for Justice (SFJ), banned in India since 2019.
He previously told the BBC that "Nikhil Gupta's guilty plea was judicial confirmation that India's Modi government orchestrated a structured murder-for-hire assassination plot on American soil".
India has opposed the Khalistan movement, and its political parties also remain opposed to the matter. Sikhs are a religious minority that make up about 2% of India's population. Some groups have long called for a separate homeland for Sikhs.
Prosecutors alleged that in May 2023, Gupta was recruited by Vikash Yadav, an Indian intelligence officer, to carry out an assassination of Pannun.
Yadav allegedly provided Gupta with personal information about Pannun, including his address in New York and information about his daily activities, prosecutors said.
At his handler's direction, Gupta contacted someone to facilitate the assassination, but that person was actually a US government informant, prosecutors said. The informant introduced Gupta to a "hitman", who was actually an undercover officer with the Drug Enforcement Agency.
Gupta was arrested in June 2023 at an airport in Prague, Czech Republic and extradited to the US. He has been held at a jail in New York pending his sentencing Friday at a Manhattan court.
"He thought that from outside this country he could kill someone in it without consequence, simply for exercising their American right to free speech," then-US attorney Jay Clayton said in a statement, after announcing Gupta's guilty plea.
Following Gupta's arrest, a spokesperson for India's Ministry of External Affairs said that Yadav is no longer employed, external by the Indian government.
The country also set up an inquiry committee to address security concerns raised by the US, the spokesperson said.
Narinder Singh Randhawa, a Sikh separatist and successor of Hardeep Singh Nijjar as temple leader in Surrey, British Columbia, told the BBC the sentencing marks the "first time we see justice" against what he calls historic and systemic persecution of Sikhs by the Indian government in India and abroad.
Inderjeet Gosal, another Sikh separatist advocate based in Ontario, called the sentencing "a big community event".
"It's for all the community to finally witness someone getting caught red-handed."
India crushed a violent armed Sikh insurgency in the 1980s and 1990s aimed at demanding the creation of Khalistan. The movement has little support in India now although some in the Sikh diaspora continue to advocate for Khalistan.
Pannun is facing serious charges, including in connection with terrorism, in India, but he denies the allegations, saying he is an activist who just believes in Khalistan.
In a victim impact statement to the court, Pannun said the foiled assassination attempt has not deterred his activism.
"I am entirely willing to take India's bullets if that is the price required to achieve freedom," he wrote.
Gupta's case placed increased scrutiny on a separate incident, involving the 2023 murder of a Sikh separatist leader in British Columbia, which led to increased tensions between India and Canada.
In September 2023, then-Canadian Prime Minister Justin Trudeau said there were "credible allegations potentially linking" India to the murder of Hardeep Singh Nijjar, another advocate for the creation of Khalistan and an associate of Pannun's.
Nijjar was shot and killed by two assailants outside a Sikh temple in British Columbia. India also has denied involvement in his death.
The day after Niijar's murder, US prosecutors allege that Gupta told the undercover officer Nijjar "was also the target" and "we have so many targets."

e301ea5e4b05.text: By — Hannah Fingerhut, Associated Press Hannah Fingerhut, Associated Press By — Susan Montoya Bryan, Associated Press Susan Montoya Bryan, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/nation/court-grants-request-to-prevent-military-from-detonating-bomb-making-chemicals-in-iowa Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Court grants request to prevent military from detonating bomb-making chemicals in Iowa Nation Nov 20, 2026 2:27 PM EST DES MOINES, Iowa (AP) — A federal appeals court has granted a request by environmentalists to put on hold a permit that cleared the way for the U.S. Army to detonate several tons of bomb-making chemicals in Iowa. The ruling came late Thursday, putting in jeopardy the military's plans to deal with dozens of barrels of lead azide pending further direction by the court. READ MORE: Iowans brace for lead dust cloud as Army plans to detonate 5 tons of bomb-making chemicals "The Army can't detonate under the permit while the permit is stayed," said Thien Chau, an attorney with Earthjustice, which filed a petition on behalf of Iowa groups calling for a review of the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency permit. The 8th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals had yet to put out a schedule Friday for when it will issue a ruling on the groups' emergency motion or even if there will be a hearing. Chau said attorneys expect the court will try to decide before Monday's planned operation. The Army did not immediately return messages seeking comment on how the court action would affect its plans. The Army has said the chemicals are unstable, and the risk of an uncontrolled explosion is growing, particularly as temperatures drop. The detonation was initially planned for Friday, but the Army announced Thursday that it would push the operation back to Monday following an outpouring of public concern about the potential health and environmental consequences. "This will delay the detonation until the latest possible moment prior to a forecasted temperature drop, which would risk further destabilization of the material," Acting Army Secretary Adam Telle had announced in a post on X. The Army, the EPA and the federal Department of Health and Human Services followed up Friday with a joint statement saying they were working together to ensure the detonation is conducted in the safest way possible. "Officials have been meticulously planning for this event since March, and all agencies involved are prepared to take the most extreme mitigation measures available to ensure there is no risk to the public and any disruptions are minimized," the statement read. An inspection earlier this year at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant determined that the lead azide, which is used in munitions production, had started to degrade. The crystallization of the material created an unstable and dangerous situation, prompting the Army to assemble experts in munitions chemistry, engineering and environmental safety to come up with a plan. Grow your mind Subscribe to our Science Newsletter to explore the wide worlds of science, health and technology. Enter your email address Subscribe Form error message goes here. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. According to EPA documents, alternatives such as neutralizing and decomposing the drums' contents with other chemicals were considered. But officials said handling the drums would increase the probability of an accidental, fatal detonation. The environmental groups disagreed, arguing in their petition that other alternatives were not fully considered. They also criticized officials for not sharing more information with the public. The Army detailed its plans during a public meeting in Middletown in October, but a public advisory Sunday was the first time other communities — some as far away as 100 miles (160 kilometers) — became aware of the potential impact. Nearly 400 people live in Middletown — about 160 miles (257 kilometers) southeast of Des Moines — but thousands more in surrounding areas could be affected by detonated material that could disperse in the air and land on the ground. Some schools and businesses had planned to close, as the Army recommended that people stay indoors, bring their pets and livestock inside and keep their windows and doors closed. Officials also urged residents in the path of the predicted plume to clean cars, windowsills and outdoor surfaces afterward. "The detonation will result in an air plume with some lead-containing particles which will disperse in the air and deposit on the ground," an advisory stated. "Lead is toxic to humans and animals." Lucy Giehl, her husband and two dogs live about 4 miles (6.4 kilometers) north of the ammunition plant. She said during an interview Thursday that she didn't know if she needed to wear gloves to wipe down surfaces or to keep her dogs from drinking water in their pond. "There's just so many details that I feel like haven't been addressed with the public." Montoya Bryan reported from Albuquerque, New Mexico. A free press is a cornerstone of a healthy democracy. 1de069dddb7d.text: President Trump on Friday said he would block U.S. companies from building data centers overseas or impose a "tremendous tax" on them if they do. Why it matters: Trump's push to keep AI infrastructure in the country comes just weeks after data center expansion became a midterm-election flashpoint , as voters raised concerns about the environmental and financial impacts they pose. What they're saying: Trump acknowledged that the announcement may come as a surprise, saying he had not yet discussed it with his own officials. "They're making so much money they don't know what to do with it," he said of the data centers being built across the country. Trump also claimed data center expansion would help lower Americans' costs and taxes. He also encouraged Americans to negotiate deals with companies proposing data centers in their communities. "They have plenty of money," he said. "Take it." Reality check: It's unclear how Trump would implement the proposed tax, since Congress has the Constitutional authority to impose federal taxes. Trump did not specify whether he would seek congressional approval or use existing executive powers to penalize companies that attempt to build data centers globally. Thought bubble from Axios' Ina Fried : Even companies that build data centers in the U.S. often need to have them in other places in order to have reliability, low latency and comply with various laws that require data to be processed in a specific region or country. Friction point: Trump's remarks followed a trilateral summit with China's Xi Jinping and Russia's Vladimir Putin, but seemed torn between praising Xi and warning about the threats China poses to the U.S. "We're not allowing data centers to go into other countries because China will take all of them, and we're not allowing that to happen," Trump said Friday. Yes, but: Trump also said Xi respected and congratulated the U.S. on its achievements in what he calls "super intelligence." Go deeper: Voters deliver "AI earthquake," rebuking tech and billionaires Editor's note: This is a breaking news story and will be updated.

c4a363783a71.text: By — Bill Barrow, Associated Press Bill Barrow, Associated Press By — Ben Finley, Associated Press Ben Finley, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/trump-defends-calling-putin-a-friend-saying-they-have-a-very-good-personal-relationship Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter WATCH: After calling Putin his friend, Trump 'can't speak to' whether Putin is a friend to America Politics Updated on Nov 20, 2026 2:53 PM EST — Published on Nov 20, 2026 2:09 PM EST WASHINGTON (AP) — President Donald Trump doubled down Friday on his description of Vladimir Putin as a friend but said he "can't speak" to whether the Russian president is a friend to the U.S. Watch the video in the player above. Trump also insisted during a White House news conference that Putin wants peace with Ukraine, despite Russia's continued aggression after invading more than four years ago. Asked about the most recent attacks — hours after Putin met with Trump in China — Trump suggested that Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy and Putin share equal responsibility for the ongoing conflict. "He'd love to end the war," the U.S. president said of his Russian counterpart. But, "you have two guys that don't know how to end it. We're trying to help them. You have two people that hate each other, Zelensky and Putin. They don't know how to end it. They want to end it. They're both stuck in it." Educate your inbox Subscribe to Here’s the Deal, our politics newsletter for analysis you won’t find anywhere else. Enter your email address Subscribe Form error message goes here. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. During a wide-ranging news conference, Trump praised both Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping after returning from China, where he participated in bilateral and trilateral meetings with his fellow heads of state. Trump raised eyebrows on the trip with his warm welcome and repeated references to Putin as his "friend." He made no effort in the White House briefing room to walk back the comments. And he noticeably sidestepped a specific question about whether he views Putin as a friend to the United States. "I can't speak to America," Trump said, without expounding. He shifted immediately to his "very good" personal relationship with Putin and repeated longstanding grievances over the extended federal probe that concluded that Russian agents sought to influence U.S. voters in the 2016 presidential election on Trump's behalf. "I consider him to be somebody that I have a very good relationship (with)," Trump said. "It's actually very good." "I've been dealing with Putin" since "the fake Russia, Russia, Russia hoax," as Trump calls the Department of Justice investigation. "It was a hoax made up by the Democrats" and "probably helped me win," Trump said. Trump insisted his relationships with the other world leaders is key to an eventual peace. "You know, you're very lucky to have somebody that has a relationship with the heads of the most powerful countries," he said. Secretary of State Marco Rubio, who stood on stage during Trump's news conference and made brief remarks, echoed the president's sentiments, pushing back against criticisms that Trump was embracing autocratic leaders as trusted allies. "I want everybody to understand the relationships between heads of state are invaluable," said Rubio, who traveled with Trump to Asia. "It sets the tone for the entire relationship. It sets the tone for our trade negotiators. It sets the tone for our diplomats." Barrow reported from Atlanta. A free press is a cornerstone of a healthy democracy. 8b96bab42047.text: A second federal judge will block construction on President Trump 's embattled arch set to be erected near Arlington National Cemetery , multiple outlets reported Friday. Why it matters: It represents yet another barrier to the multi-year project to build a 250-foot arch that challengers said would obstruct the line of sight between the Lincoln Memorial and Arlington National Cemetery. Driving the news: U.S. District Judge Leonie Brinkema's preliminary injunction will indefinitely block the project, which she reportedly called a "rushed job" from the bench Friday. Zoom out: Brinkema's rebuke comes after D.C.-based District Judge Tanya Chutkan on Wednesday extended her separate order blocking construction on the arch for two weeks. Chutkan, who is overseeing consolidated challenges from military veterans and from the District of Columbia and Virginia, issued her initial temporary restraining order earlier this month. That order prohibited construction, excavation, land disturbance, utility installation and road closures related to the arch, Axios D.C.'s Mimi Montgomery reported. What they're saying: "The judiciary should not be abused to politicize a structure designed to unite our nation," White House spokesman Davis Ingle said in a statement. "We will continue making the case for this beautiful and fitting monument and are confident we will be fully vindicated as this litigation proceeds." The National Park Service did not immediately respond to Axios' request for comment. State of play: The legal hurdles came after the National Capital Planning Commission , which is stacked with Trump loyalists, gave its final approval for the project. Challengers, however, have argued the project requires congressional approval — and as Chutkan noted , "Congress has not enacted any statute authorizing construction of the Arch." Between the lines: The arch is one prime example of the president's quest to remake the nation's capital as he sees fit, from a sprawling White House ballroom to a community golf course . The NPS has backed Trump's arch, despite noting it "would alter several historic views." The FAA deemed the arch, which would sit near Ronald Reagan National Airport, safe for air travel, but said it should have "a non-standard eternal flame on top" and "floodlight projectors pointed" toward it. What we're watching: A Justice Department spokesperson said they would appeal the decision "immediately." Go deeper: The next two months are pivotal for Trump's D.C. projects

In a historic first, the Department of Interior has leased more than 31 million acres of Pacific waters to a deep-sea mining company seeking to exploit mineral-rich deposits from the ocean floor off American Samoa.
“This is the first time that a lease has been issued for deep-sea mining in U.S. waters,” said Arlo Hemphill, U.S. project lead against deep-sea mining for Greenpeace USA.
Deep-sea mining is a highly contested, emerging industry that aims to extract rock-like deposits on the seabed called polymetallic nodules, formed over millions of years. They contain cobalt, copper, manganese and nickel—so-called “critical minerals” used in batteries, electronics and other devices that have historically been mined on land. To date, no commercial deep-sea mining operations have begun anywhere in the world.
Scientists, environmentalists and Indigenous peoples with strong cultural connections to the ocean aim to stop the industry from moving forward at all.
“Once mining strips away habitat that took millions of years to form, no amount of money can bring it back,” said Hemphill in a statement. “Congress should press the administration to suspend these leases before work begins.”
The lease sale took place Thursday, during a live auction held at the Ventura County Fire Department in Thousand Oaks, California, as Hemphill and dozens of other activists from American Samoa and across the Pacific rallied, prayed and sang outside in protest.
“This is not just seabed on a map. This is our home, our livelihoods, our identity, and our responsibility to protect,” said Sabrina Suluai-Mahuka, founder of Finafinau, American Samoa’s youth and environment nonprofit, who traveled from American Samoa to protest the auction. “Ocean rights are human rights, and our home is not for sale,” she said in a statement.
Representatives from just two companies attended the auction, including Adepth Minerals Inc., from Norway, and Wetstone U.S. Ventures, a New York-based offshore critical minerals exploration and deep-sea mining company.
Ultimately, Wetstone bid $6 million on two areas marked for mineral exploration that lie adjacent to the Rose Atoll Marine National Monument, a marine protected area established by President George W. Bush in 2009 to protect more than 10,000 square miles of ocean from commercial fishing and other forms of extraction.
The bid made Wetstone the provisional winner of the auction, according to a spokesperson from the Marine Minerals Administration. The new office was established earlier this year within the Department of Interior to help promote the Trump administration’s agenda to secure critical minerals.
“A dependable critical minerals supply chain is essential to American manufacturing and the technologies that power our economy and national defense,” said Secretary of the Interior Doug Burgum, in a statement about Thursday’s auction. “Today’s sale opens a path to learn more about the resources off the coast of American Samoa and assess whether they could contribute to a more reliable domestic supply.”
The areas offered for leasing will be open for exploration activities, which include mapping and surveying the seabed to locate mineral rich deposits. Actual mining would require further federal approvals. But Hemphill and others warn that exploration in itself is a dangerous step towards paving the way for an industry that could threaten ocean ecosystems and the people that depend on them.
“The industry will push to move from surveys to exploration to extraction, putting profits ahead of marine life and trampling the culture, livelihood and objections of communities that have said no again and again,” Hemphill said.
Ever since the proposed lease sale was announced earlier this year, many American Samoan leaders and communities have voiced their concerns. Several lawsuits were filed against the Trump Administration to stop it from happening.
Just a few days before the lease sale, a federal judge in Hawaiʻi ruled the Marine Minerals Administration had violated the Endangered Species Act by approving the lease sale without taking into account the potential impacts of exploration and mining on endangered species.
The areas leased are home to several dozen endangered species including the blue whale, fin whale, sei whale and sperm whale, as well as the leatherback sea turtle, oceanic whitetip shark and giant manta ray.
Many of these species are already threatened by climate change, which is altering their sources of prey and migration patterns. More than 1000 marine science and policy experts from 75 countries say deep-sea mining could further add to the stress these marine animals are facing.
“In deciding to move forward with today’s scheduled sale, the Trump administration has performed a renegade, unlawful act,” said Chris Eaton, attorney at Earthjustice, an environmental nonprofit that represented American Samoan and Hawaiian plaintiffs in the lawsuit. “We will use the full extent of the law to vigorously push for the leases to be voided,” he said in a statement Thursday.

These days, Jessica Yih spends a lot of time talking to women about testosterone. Interest is “coming from all directions,” says the University of California, Irvine Health urologist. A major source: women who hope testosterone can boost the female libido. Only about a decade ago, women looking for libido treatments had few medical options — even though women of all ages struggle with low sexual desire.
Some non-hormonal treatments are now available, but the U.S. Food and Drug Administration has yet to approve a female testosterone product, despite years of research suggesting it can boost sexual function and desire among postmenopausal women. Female testosterone products are approved in countries including the United Kingdom and Australia.
Not many studies have looked at testosterone’s effects on libido in premenopausal women, but preliminary data in that area are also promising, according to a 2026 research review in The Journal of Sexual Medicine that Yih coauthored. “I have seen it change people’s lives,” Yih says. The hormone seems to make the female brain more receptive to sexual stimuli; it also promotes physical effects that enhance sexual pleasure, such as increased blood flow to the genitals. Right now, American women interested in these potential benefits have to look for them off-label. But that may change. In September, the FDA held a public meeting on testosterone use among menopausal women, “with the goal of informing future research and potential drug development in this area,” says Kaveeta Vasisht, the FDA’s associate commissioner for women’s health.
The hormone has a rocky regulatory past. In 2004, an FDA advisory panel unanimously voted against approving a testosterone patch for women, citing a lack of safety data. There are still outstanding questions on that front, Yih says—like how, if at all, long-term use affects risk of conditions such as breast cancer and heart disease. Then, in 2011, a pair of Phase III trials found that testosterone therapy didn’t significantly outperform a placebo — a benchmark the FDA looks for when deciding whether to approve a new drug. That’s not to say testosterone didn’t work, says Tami Rowen, an ob-gyn at UC San Francisco. Rather, it seemed that hype about the hormone was so strong that study participants went in with sky-high expectations, leading even the placebo group to report benefits. The treatment was a “victim of its own success,” Rowen says.
Interest hasn’t let up, though. By one estimate, the U.S. female prescription rate for all uses rose from 0.4 out of every 1,000 women in 2018, to 1.8 out of every 1,000 women in 2026. That’s an increase of nearly 400 percent. With so much buzz, the potential placebo effect remains “the biggest problem with testosterone right now,” Rowen says.
Another outstanding question, Yih says, is whether using testosterone long-term increases the risk of breast cancer and heart disease.
Women seeking a libido boost do have non-hormonal options. In 2015, the FDA approved Addyi, the first treatment for low libido in premenopausal women. The drug seemingly raises levels of neurotransmitters that promote sexual desire while tamping down those that block it. A competitor, Vyleesi, hit shelves in 2019. Then, last year, regulators expanded Addyi’s use to postmenopausal women younger than 65. An international group of experts, including Rowen, issued recommendations for treating low female libido in 2025 in Sexual Medicine Reviews. Psychological therapies and Addyi are backed by the strongest evidence, the group found.
Rowen currently has her eye on in-development products including Lybrido. The drug, which is slated to enter a Phase III clinical trial in Europe, aims to rev sex drive in the brain and enhance physical arousal. The demand for new treatments is there, Rowen says. “Women deserve better than placebo.”

cc00b186248b.text: By — Dave Collins, Associated Press Dave Collins, Associated Press By — Kathy McCormack, Associated Press Kathy McCormack, Associated Press By — John Raby, Associated Press John Raby, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/nation/northeastern-florida-now-under-flood-threats-from-heavy-rain-that-has-devastated-coastal-communities Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Northeastern Florida now under flood threats from heavy rain that has devastated coastal communities Nation Nov 20, 2026 1:46 PM EST Heavy rains that left large swaths of Florida's Atlantic coast under water and led to dozens of rescues moved further north on Friday as forecasters warned flooding threats could stretch into next week when a major river is expected to crest well above record levels. The National Weather Service posted flood warnings and watches stretching around 200 miles (320 kilometers) from just south of Melbourne to the Jacksonville area. Additional rainfall of 2 to 6 inches (5 to 15 centimeters) was expected through Saturday, while some areas could see an extra 8 to 10 inches (20 to 25 centimeters). WATCH: How a super El Niño is fueling extreme weather patterns "Severe, widespread flash flooding is expected," the weather service said in a Friday morning forecast. "In addition, areas that normally do not experience flash flooding will flood. Furthermore, lives and property (are) in great danger." The St. Johns River, Florida's longest, rose above a record level Thursday near Cocoa that was set in 1953. The river is forecast to stay at least 2 feet (61 centimeters) above flood stage through early next week, the weather service said. Also Friday, a nontropical low-pressure system was expected to form and could become a subtropical or tropical storm along the southeastern U.S. coast, the National Hurricane Center in Miami said. The southeast and mid-Atlantic coasts should expect strong winds, dangerous surf and coastal flooding into early next week ahead of the Thanksgiving holiday. Parts of Florida's east coast have been deluged with rainfall totaling more than 17 inches (43 centimeters) in some spots since Tuesday, according to preliminary totals by the weather service. That's in addition to heavy rains that fell earlier this month. Several places have already seen their wettest November on record. The storms shifted north to the Space Coast on Thursday, sending rivers over their banks and prompting water rescues of people and horses during what is supposed to be Florida's dry season that runs from October to May. "Never seen such a thing like this in Florida," said Jazmin Foster, whose Melbourne home was inundated with water for the second time in two weeks. In Brevard County on Thursday, people with trailers braved knee-deep water to rescue dozens of horses and other animals at the Blue Lake Equestrian Center, an animal hospice and boarding facility in Cocoa. The animals were taken to a dry pasture elsewhere. First responders conducted nearly 100 high-water rescues across the county, and those numbers continued to climb, Sheriff Wayne Ivey said. The city of Palm Bay conducted mandatory evacuations for some residents of a mobile home community. Shelters were opened for residents forced from their homes. Nearly 200 Florida National Guard personnel with 50 high-water vehicles have been deployed to help up and down the coast, the Division of Emergency Management said. Other responding agencies included about 235 officers with the Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission. This week's storms have been fueled by persistent high pressure over Virginia and a low-pressure system and an associated stationary front in the Gulf, which together have pushed a steady onshore flow across the Florida Peninsula. They're an offshoot of El Niño, the natural warming of the Pacific near the equator that warps weather patterns worldwide. Forecasters said El Niño conditions are expected to persist through the spring, meaning the soggy extreme weather in Florida and California will likely continue through the winter. The California coast, from the Los Angeles to San Francisco areas, was also swamped with flooding in many areas this week, leaving neighborhoods under water and forcing some drivers to abandon stalled vehicles in floodwaters. A long stretch of the coastal Highway 1 was closed south of the Monterey Peninsula due to rock and mud slides. Associated Press writers Amy Taxin in Santa Ana, California, and Jessica Hill in Las Vegas contributed to this report. A free press is a cornerstone of a healthy democracy. The Jensen Huang scandal is turning into a prediction-market bonanza for some traders.
There are more than 90 separate bets on Polymarket and Kalshi relating to the outcome of various elements of the Huang story and investigations.
âWill Jensen Huang be arrestedâ currently has $153,000 of trading volume on Polymarket. More than 13,000 people have bet on Kalshi on whether President Donald Trump will pardon Huang. And nearly a million people have bet on if, or when, Huang will testify in front of Congress.
Some people have cashed in by making big trades right before new developments. A user named paule334 made their first Polymarket trade ever on Nov. 10, betting that Jensen Huang would resign, and continued trading until the morning of Nov. 11, the day The New York Times broke the story of Huangâs second affair.
The user made about $38,000. Others made windfalls by betting quickly after news breaks. Bertapotamous, another user, made nearly $100,000 on the same trade in the late afternoon of Nov. 11, minutes after The Wall Street Journal reported Huang was set to resign.

OpenAI put a new rule in place that gives the company more control over how much of the world â including China â can access its AI models.
Gateways and routers that provide third-party access to OpenAIâs tech now need the companyâs review and approval.
Such gateways, the most prominent of which is OpenRouter, have become increasingly popular with developers and companies seeking access to a wide range of AI models: Instead of individual contracts with each lab, one account with a router can let you access hundreds of models from the US, Europe, and China.
Beyond the technical details, the move has implications in the global AI race. US security agencies and companies, including Anthropic, have accused Chinese AI labs of distilling, or copying, American frontier models by routing requests through intermediaries that resell access to their models, which obscures the identity of the end user.
Those cases largely involved gray-market resellers, known in China as âtransfer stations,â but OpenAIâs new rule extends its oversight to any service standing between it and the people using its models.

2f78c477f8b8.text: Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) is warning House Republicans that their jobs aren't over yet after so many skipped town this week that GOP leaders had to call it quits. Why it matters: Republicans still have a month-plus left in the majority, but Johnson is struggling to get enough members to show up to make last-minute headway on the GOP's legislative agenda. GOP leaders were forced to cut the week short after 14 Republicans missed votes, leaving Johnson without the headcount needed to advance party-line legislation. Eleven of those 14 won't be returning next Congress. Driving the news: "To state the obvious, barring any serious medical issue, we need every Republican to be here to faithfully complete our full two-year term," Johnson wrote in a Friday letter to his colleagues . "The Twentieth Amendment to the U.S. Constitution specifies that our clock doesn't run out until noon on January 3rd," he added. Zoom in: The outgoing speaker pointed to government funding, the annual defense authorization bill and permitting reform as priorities for the final weeks of the Republican majority. He also said he wants to pass "every meaningful Republican bill that can garner 218 votes" and force Democrats to take politically difficult votes. "LET'S SCORE EVERY POINT WE CAN AND LEAVE IT ALL ON THE FIELD!" Johnson wrote.

244193f4f19c.text:
The tech industry has enough of a public image problem with its warnings about AI leading to human extinction, and it risks further alienating people outside of Silicon Valley if it starts popularizing âthe handover.â
The handover is the period in which AI becomes so intelligent that it no longer makes sense for humans to make any decisions. Sam Altman brought the idea up on stage with me this week at Silicon Valley & The World, and he believes AI companies should do everything possible to avoid it. In a âpositiveâ scenario, the handover turns humans into pets of AI overlords (Altman referenced Labradors): Humans have everything they need, from food to entertainment, and donât need to work much.
The dystopian idea is mostly a product of the Silicon Valley echo chamber, where those inside AI companies see advanced models in their raw forms, doing both scary things like breaking into the internet and amazing things like solving the worldâs most difficult math theorems. Thereâs no evidence weâre on the verge of a handover or anything remotely like it, so tech leaders would be wise to find a more optimistic talking point.

96b6523ee6e5.text: By — Deepti Hajela, Associated Press Deepti Hajela, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/nation/travelers-concerns-spike-as-thanksgiving-nears-and-tech-hiccups-grow-but-few-are-dissuaded Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Travelers' concerns spike as Thanksgiving nears and tech hiccups grow, but few are dissuaded Nation Nov 20, 2026 12:58 PM EST NEW YORK (AP) — At this point, it's practically as much of a Thanksgiving tradition as turkey and stuffing — crowded airports, long lines, jam-packed flights, the ever-present worry about delays and cancellations and extra expenses. And for 2026's busy holiday travel week, which effectively begins Friday, there's another ingredient now: new concerns about the possibility of disruption and chaos when it comes to air-travel infrastructure in the wake of a rare nationwide ground stop last week — the longest since 9/11 — and a separate airline outage a few days later. Not to mention other, non-air-travel outages and tech problems that are causing nails to be bitten and hair to be pulled across the nation. READ MORE: White House taps Kirsten Davies as cyber chief after outages rattle Americans The thought of the potential travel problems is enough to make Tracey Evers feel iffy about whether she should continue with her plans to fly to the Caribbean this weekend to see her mother for the upcoming week or not, because she has things to take care of and getting stuck away from home would be a hassle. She's pretty sure she's not the only one. "For a lot of people, especially as they're paying attention and because it's in the news where they're tying together all of the IT-based infrastructure challenges we're having ... I think more and more people are now getting anxious," said Evers, of Raleigh, North Carolina, an executive in the energy industry whose work requires frequent travel. It's an anxiety fueled by the past 10 days' tech failures across industries and government — for airlines and in other sectors. But it's a familiar one, too. Americans are no strangers to complaining about flying. They have been doing so in different ways for decades as air travel grew into a staple of American life. And it's one they're likely going to find a way to deal with for as long as it remains so, as seen in examples like the resurgence of air travel following the COVID pandemic. But, just like bad weather, it irritates many Americans while dissuading comparatively few. "For the most part, air travel still remains strong," said Dan Bubb, a professor at the University of Nevada, Las Vegas who teaches commercial aviation history. People "might be unhappy. They might grumble, but they are still going to do it." Air travel is vital — and taken for granted In some ways, the country's aviation system could be considered a victim of its own success. The notion of human beings willing themselves into the air in a metal machine — once an unfathomable miracle, then a romantic adventure — is now, for many, often little more than a high-altitude commute. "Air travel now is indispensable for a modern economy ... and frankly, it is taken for granted," said Bob van der Linden, acting chair of the aeronautics department at the National Air and Space Museum. "You've got all these airlines out there. People want to fly. They want to go to new places," he said. "But that means more people are flying — more people flying, more congestion; more congestion, more inconvenience. It's a commodity. There's nothing romantic about it anymore. But in a way, that's a clear sign of its success — that you're in a bus." At this point, as a traveler, Michelle Jolene says she's used to the delays, the cancellations, the rerouting of flights. So while she's not thrilled at the idea of adding infrastructure issues to the list of potential problems, she's not rattled by it. READ MORE: Are tech disruptions and and outages the new normal? "I literally haven't had a normal flight in so long and I fly a lot. So I'm like, just, okay, here's another thing," said Jolene, who lives in Miami. She did think it would make some people reluctant to get on a plane, "the people who fly maybe once a year for their holiday." And instead of flying this year, they'll drive to "Disney or the beaches in North Carolina or something," she said. "But those of us who have to fly to work and to live our lives, there's just not much choice. What are you going to do?" The expense can be as much of an obstacle as the delays If anything, a more disruptive aspect to flying than the potential for delays might be the cost — another anxiety trigger for many that can't just be stuffed into the overhead compartment. Roundtrip domestic tickets for Thanksgiving and Christmas travel are up 31% and 23% from the same time last year, according to estimates from the travel-booking company Hopper. For travelers, that means dealing with the highest holiday airfares in a decade. Some of increases to fares and fees are linked to higher jet fuel costs tied to the war in Iran. In September, airfares were up 22% from a year earlier, according to the Consumer Price Index. It led Jolene, 50, to find a creative way to get her daughter's flight home to Miami for Thanksgiving: toilet paper. She saw a promotion on American Airlines' online shopping portal earlier this year that awarded 10 miles for every dollar spent. She bought 10 boxes of 48 rolls, earning her about 8,500 miles — which was enough to cover the entire flight from Washington, D.C., where her daughter attends college. The upfront cost was worth it, she said, because it's a product she would have bought anyway and one that doesn't go bad. She's keeping the rolls in her garage "The funny part," she said, "is we have to buy toilet paper anyway." AP Airlines and Travel Writer Rio Yamat in Las Vegas contributed to this story. Andy Burnham said the UK will discuss possible options for even closer ties with the EU, after agreeing a deal covering British food exports, emissions trading and a youth experience scheme.
The prime minister said it was a "good day" for Britain and Europe, adding the Treasury believes the deal could boost the UK economy by up to Â£17bn a year.
European Council President AntÃ³nio Costa said the EU remains "open to have the closest possible relationship" with the UK.
Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch said the deal "isn't fair" - and Reform's Nigel Farage called it a "betrayal of the British people".
Legislation to implement the deal is expected to be introduced in the UK Parliament next week.
Burnham arrived in Brussels to finalise the latest stage of the government's post-Brexit "reset" of relations with the EU, which originally began under former prime minister Sir Keir Starmer.
The agreements announced on Friday included scrapping most of the checks on British food exports, in return for the UK following some EU regulations, from 2028.
The UK government believes the changes will cut costs for businesses and could bring prices down for shoppers, while critics argue the change will make the UK a "rule taker" from Brussels rather than a rule maker.
The new youth experience scheme will allow up to 100,000 18 to 31 year olds from the EU to travel, work and study in the UK for up to three years. The same number of young Britons will be allowed into Europe.
The two sides want to ensure that opportunities under the annual scheme will be available to young people by no later than January 2030.
A further six months is available to discuss a deal on tuition fees, which could prove to be a potential stumbling block.
There have been calls from the European side for fees to be reduced for EU students at British universities. The joint statement says any agreement would also be for UK students in the EU.
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said she is "confident" a solution will be found, with Burnham adding: "Me too."
On immigration, the UK and EU have committed to working closely to tackle migrant smuggling and human trafficking. They also expect their law enforcement agencies to share more data.
Burnham said "significant progress" has been made to help "disrupt the gangs who are making those dangerous crossings across the English Channel".
The UK-EU statement also said talks on linking the EU and UK emissions trading systems have concluded and they aim to apply the agreement from 2028.
'Brainstorming process'
Burnham argued that polling suggests the UK public "want closer ties" with the EU and the deal "delivers that".
He added: "Beyond that we do need to consider what is the right long-term relationship. Incremental steps only take us so far."
The prime minister said his government will publish a 10-year plan next month, adding it will set out its ambitions for reindustrialisation, growth in "all parts of Britain" and opportunities for young people.
Burnham said these ambitions are "connected to our long-term relationship with our nearest partner".
He said over the coming months before the next UK-EU summit both sides will "seek to conduct an informal brainstorming process" to look at what those options are.
Burnham added: "What we are announcing today is probably the limit of what we can achieve in this Parliament, given what needs to be done to implement it.
"But we want to inform the Parliament after this one, so that decisions can be taken about that long-term relationship."
Labour's 2024 general election manifesto pledged there would be "no return to the single market, the customs union, or freedom of movement", and Burnham has committed to this.
The prime minister said the "British people will be the boss of what happens next", with the next election needing to be held by August 2029.
Von der Leyen, who said the summit was a "turning point" for the EU-UK relationship, said "we are open for brainstorming".
'Endless betrayal'
Badenoch said the deal was not fair because UK farmers would now have to follow rules made by Brussels and more young people will come to the UK to "compete with our young people who are struggling to get jobs".
Badenoch was also asked about the Treasury's analysis, which Burnham said suggested the deal "will add up to 0.5%" to UK gross domestic product and he described it as a "Â£17bn boost to the British economy".
She claimed Burnham has "plucked that figure out of the air" and "the only modelling I've seen that even talks about that figure says it's actually 0.0%".
Farage said Friday was a "very good day for the EU", adding: "A good day to try and humiliate the one member state that actually had the courage to say, 'We don't need to be part of you, we can govern our own country'."
In a social media post, Farage, who was a leading figure in the 2016 campaign to get Britain out of the EU, added: "Like every prime minister before him, Burnham is a total fraud. Only Reform will stop the endless betrayal of the British people."
Liberal Democrat leader Sir Ed Davey said there needed to be more than "tweaks" to the UK's relationship to the EU.
"A youth mobility scheme is a big step forward, but it's nowhere near enough. We need a whole new deal that actually works for Britain, and fast."

In parts of California, public officials are going door-to-door, warning residents to get ready. The state has strategically stockpiled sandbags, pumps and generators. Debris has been fished out to clear storm drains, seepage blankets shore up aging levees and dams, and wire mesh cages hold back precariously placed boulders.
What is expected to be the strongest El Niño on record is already pounding the state with giant waves. The fury of this year’s El Niño is being unleashed around the globe as well, from inundating Florida with floods to exacerbating drought in the Amazon. And much more is still to come, forecasts show, with the peak of the climate phenomenon expected to arrive between November 2026 and January 2027.
Californians know all too well the threat. El Niño has historically brought relentless rainfall to the state, flooding cities and triggering landslides.
State officials learned a lot about preparedness and emergency water management from previous El Niños — particularly the strong event that spanned the winter of 1997–1998. But this year’s event is likely to be even more challenging, a “Super” El Niño superimposed on the backdrop of global climate change.
Climate change has made water management in California more complicated than it was just 30 years ago — as it has elsewhere around the world, says environmental scientist Letitia Grenier, the director of water policy at the Public Policy Institute of California, a nonprofit, nonpartisan think tank based in San Francisco.
In 1997, California’s overall climate was much drier; El Niño brought a big, long rainy season that spanned the state, Grenier says. But now, “it’s just so humid. The air is warmer, so it can hold more water.”
That waterlogged atmosphere means that even without El Niño, there’s been less of a distinct rainy season in California, and more rapid flip-flop between intense episodes of rain dumped on the ground followed by periods of heat and dryness. “It’s these strange, erratic patterns that we’ve never seen before,” she says. And the state is bracing for how the Super El Niño will clash with this new climate normal.
A climate event becomes a household name
1997 was the year that the term “El Niño” shot to global fame. It was the most powerful El Niño in recorded history, and the first to be scientifically monitored in real time, continuously tracked by satellites and breathlessly reported on by news outlets. El Niño’s rise to household name status was even cemented in pop culture by an appearance on Saturday Night Live, in a classic sketch by comedian Chris Farley.
But the event was no laughing matter. It caused global devastation during its brief reign. El Niño events form as westward-blowing trade winds over the eastern tropical Pacific Ocean weaken, allowing warm water to accumulate at the surface. Those waters can then release massive amounts of heat to the atmosphere, altering the position of the Pacific jet stream and helping to disrupt global weather patterns.
In 1997–1998, global temperatures spiked by 1.5 degrees Celsius on average. Along with the torrential rains in California, the event brought brutal drought to Southeast Asia and deadly summer floods to central Europe and Peru. Record-breaking floods also hit East Africa, which in turn triggered a surge in mosquito-borne Rift Valley fever. The oceans were so warm that 16 percent of the world’s reefs died.
In all, the El Niño–related weather extremes were linked to more than 22,000 fatalities around the world, including nearly 200 in the United States, and an estimated $5.7 trillion in global economic losses.
Not every El Niño is equally intense, or impacts weather in quite the same way. “There’s a lot of variability event to event,” says Washington, D.C.–based climate scientist Tom Di Liberto, of the nonprofit climate news organization Climate Central.
But there is a general overall pattern to how El Niño tends to affect weather around the planet, Di Liberto says. For example, there tend to be more tropical cyclones in the Pacific Ocean, and fewer in the Atlantic — a pattern also observed in 2026.
El Niño also tends to flatten and accelerate the Pacific jet stream, shifting its flow southward, says Mike Anderson, California’s state climatologist for the Department of Water Resources, who is based in Sacramento. And that has historically meant that a conveyor belt of back-to-back moisture-loaded storms is set on a collision course with the U.S. West Coast.
Swell season
The El Niño rapidly strengthened during the summer of 2026. As westerly trade winds weakened, warm waters accumulated in the eastern tropical Pacific Ocean, raising both ocean temperatures and the sea level height (shown in this animation). Red and white colors indicate the highest sea level. Beginning in April and intensifying through November, the El Niño event generated Kelvin waves, massive swells that sweep eastward along the equator toward the Americas.
Humans bear the cost
The 1997–1998 El Niño revealed just how devastating that pattern could be in California.
As much as 30 centimeters inundated parts of the state during the month of February 1998 alone. Storm winds and high surf pounded the coast, while rivers swelled and overtopped their banks. Flooding from the “Groundhog Day Storm” destroyed some 1,700 homes in Bay Area cities Palo Alto and Menlo Park. On February 6 near Rio Nido, about 100 kilometers from San Francisco, a forested hillside suddenly crumbled, sending a wall of mud rushing down the mountain. It destroyed about 30 homes.
Landslides also threatened homes and lives in Southern California.
On February 23, then 25-year-old Jenifer Segraves and her fiancé Glenn Flook were living in an apartment on Laguna Canyon Road, in the city of Laguna Beach. The heavy rains had saturated the neighborhood’s steep hillsides, making the terrain unstable.

d6d8ae85385c.text: By — Anthony Izaguirre, Associated Press Anthony Izaguirre, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/nation/mamdani-sets-plan-to-close-nycs-notorious-rikers-island-jail-by-2032 Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Mamdani sets plan to close NYC's notorious Rikers Island jail by 2032 Nation Nov 20, 2026 12:31 PM EST NEW YORK (AP) — New York City's Rikers Island jail complex would close by 2032 under a sweeping plan announced Friday by Mayor Zohran Mamdani, whose strategy for finally shuttering the notorious facility hinges on substantially reducing the number of people kept behind bars. READ MORE: Mamdani hits 100 days as mayor of New York City The mayor, a Democrat, unveiled the plan as the city is all but certain to blow past a legal requirement to close Rikers and replace it with four smaller, more modern jails by 2027. For years, Rikers Island has stood as a symbol of dysfunction, with the network of jails so plagued by violence and overcrowding that a federal judge, citing " abnormal and unacceptable " conditions, appointed an outside manager to restore order and implement reforms. Mamdani has been a vocal proponent of closing Rikers, though the longstanding plan to build new jails has met fierce pushback, including from his predecessor, former Mayor Eric Adams, who opposed federal oversight and borough jails. At a celebratory news conference at City Hall, Mamdani said the extended timeline was needed because of resistance from the previous administration, calling Rikers "a place we have long turned our eyes away from rather than confront head on." "The call to close Rikers has echoed across our city for decades. Work has begun to do so, then stopped, then started once again. What will make this chapter different is our commitment to see it through," he said. The plan centers on a goal of lowering the city's inmate population from the around 6,700 people currently housed at Rikers to a little over 4,000. The Mamdani administration is proposing a new slate of diversion and supervised release programs, expanding housing and social services to prevent recidivism, along with restoring an online bail payment system and reducing case delays so people spend less time behind bars. "Our nation has a very real mass incarceration problem," the mayor said. "We are making a conscious decision to advance a new model of a criminal legal system in our city, one that takes on that problem head on." Instead of housing prisoners at Rikers — an island in the East River near LaGuardia Airport — the city will shift people to jails in the Bronx, Queens, Brooklyn and Manhattan, as well as a handful of medical facilities for people who need healthcare or psychiatric treatment. The city also plans to reduce the number of beds for women, diverting them into community-based programs. The borough jails are expected to open in Brooklyn in 2029; the Bronx and Queens in 2031; and then Manhattan in 2032, according to City Hall. The new deadlines require approval from the New York City Council. Julie Menin, speaker of the City Council, praised the mayor's plan at the news conference, saying that after years of delay "we are finally getting back on track." The City Council voted to close the jail complex in 2019 and replace it with newer jails located in the city's boroughs by 2027. At the time, city officials had also called for shrinking the jail population to accommodate the closure, but ran into opposition from critics who argued doing so would mean more violent criminals on city streets. WATCH: Why Grand Theft Auto VI's release is a major cultural moment The game, which launched on Thursday, has hit $2.36 billion in revenue with approximately 24.6 million units sold, according to Sensor Tower, which is a market research firm that tracks mobile apps, digital advertising and consumer behavior online. Earlier this month, the PlayStation blog said that "GTA VI" was the most preordered game in the history of its namesake store. Due to the demand, PlayStation said that it was teaming with Rockstar Games to allow players to start preloading the game nine days early, so that they'd be ready to play on launch day. "GTA VI" is the latest installment in the hyperviolent, open-world video game series that has skewered American culture with fictionalized versions of New York and Los Angeles and is now returning to its sun-baked version of Miami — Vice City. It's the first new "GTA" game in 13 years, with the story of "GTA VI" centered on a couple trying to improve their circumstances through crime. Early reviews for the game have noted that it has a depth of relationship building that goes beyond the violent stickups and bank robberies. The "Grand Theft Auto" franchise has sold more than 470 million units globally, according to publisher Take-Two Interactive. "Grand Theft Auto V," released in 2013, accounts for more than 230 million of those sales and generated $1 billion in retail sales in just three days. Watch the news conference in the player above. While Russia and the U.S. lead the world by each possessing thousands of nuclear weapons, China is rapidly expanding its nuclear arsenal. In its annual review of China's military buildup, the Pentagon said China's stockpile of nuclear warheads remained in the low 600s through 2024, but the country was on track to have more than 1,000 warheads by 2030. "They'll catch us within 10 years," Trump said of China's nuclear buildup during a news conference at the White House. "They're going at it hot and heavy, but they have a lot." WATCH: Inside the historic summit between Trump, Xi and Putin Trump's public remarks were his first since his controversial summit with Xi and Putin, leaders of countries long considered U.S. rivals, in the southern Chinese city of Shenzhen on Thursday. Secretary of State Marco Rubio, who spoke to reporters alongside Trump on Friday, said it was imperative for the three nuclear powers to talk. "These three countries possess the overwhelming majority of nuclear weapons on this planet," Rubio said. "The idea that these three leaders should not engage on a regular basis is not just absurd, it's dangerous." After the trilateral meeting, the leaders issued a joint statement, saying they "affirmed that a nuclear war cannot be won and must never be fought" and "will conduct a dialogue on reducing nuclear risks and preventing the proliferation of nuclear weapons." Prior to the meeting, observers had doubted if China would agree to nuclear talks. With a much smaller nuclear arsenal, Beijing had resisted joining nuclear arms control talks with the U.S. and Russia. -- Didi Tang, Associated Press A free press is a cornerstone of a healthy democracy. 4e446c5d7711.text:
Ashleyâs view
Earlier this week at Semaforâs inaugural Silicon Valley & the World conference in Palo Alto, I interviewed Senator Mark Kelly, an Arizona Democrat with some 2028 presidential buzz. At one point during our conversation, as he beamed in virtually from Washington, he described one particular data center project in New Mexico as being the size of âa thousand football fields.â
A participant in the front row rolled their eyes and shook their head, clearly exasperated at the comment. As the interview continued, the audience laughed when Kelly joked about President Donald Trump threatening to jail him, stared blankly when he spoke about regulating AI, and perked up when he talked about how Washington is thinking about investigating the controversy surrounding ousted Nvidia leader Jensen Huang.
Toward the end of the interview, Kelly made the 1,000 football field comment again, in the context of data center projects needing to be built thoughtfully â with guardrails and input from the local community. The same audience member that rolled their eyes raised their hands in disbelief. After the interview, I fact checked the claim that a data center project could be quite so large. According to a report in the investigative outlet Searchlight New Mexico, the projectâs acreage is indeed equivalent to about 1,000 football fields.
The exchange was a perfect encapsulation of the dynamic between Silicon Valley and the rest of the United States right now: Those building the AI-powered future are well aware that not everyone is bought in on their vision. That was abundantly clear after the midterm elections, in which more than 40 ballot measures seeking limits on data center growth passed across the country, and candidates who embraced pro-AI regulation messaging handily won in competitive districts.
But the post-midterms soul-searching only goes so far, at least at the Rosewood Sand Hill, nestled among top venture capital firms dotting Menlo Park. From my permanent perch in Washington, I know that Silicon Valley knows they have a problem. But theyâre squinting at it, red-teaming it and trying to invent their way out of it. Itâs reminiscent of how Big Tech companies viewed the lawsuits, Capitol Hill investigations, and Justice Department antitrust cases that piled up as anti-tech sentiment grew in the last decade: Expensive, and a hindrance to all-out growth; but ultimately, the cost of doing business.
Tech executives are looking to keep building and growing, even as the financing gets more precarious and the infrastructure as well as the regulations that control it get harder to navigate. For many in Silicon Valley, AI anxiety and disdain can be explained away as a marketing problem, an education problem, or a location problem. For these innovators, it is not, however, a sign to stop.
This attitude from AI and tech companies is not new. But the raging anti-AI public sentiment, considerably more intense than the tech anxiety of past years, is. And governors and state lawmakers across the country are ready to pounce (some are already pouncing). So while newly empowered Democrats on Capitol Hill may not ever manage to pass significant AI regulation in the new Congress, and companies will surely find ways to appease Washington, tech leaders should perhaps take complaints about the scale of AI growth, including data center projects matching the size of 1,000 football fields â more seriously.
Room for Disagreement
Tech executives may face a hostile environment in Congress and in most of the states, but theyâve still got a powerful ally in the White House. Trump this week warned that ârobustâ regulation of AI could âstifleâ development. âWe wonât allow that to happen, frankly,â he said at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in China.
