Police departments are reminding Americans that street racing, auto theft and gun violence are still crimes in real life, as excitement over Grand Theft Auto 6, a game following the lives of career criminals, reaches a fever pitch in the US.
"Play the game. Don't play yourself," Atlanta police warned in a social media post, while Denver authorities said that "running from police is still illegal".
Over 20 million units of the game have been purchased worldwide since its release this week, making GTA 6 likely the biggest entertainment launch in history.
The game, known for its freedom of play, ranging from buying a cheeseburger to firing a grenade launcher, is set in a Florida-inspired state.
"Assaulting someone for extra points, it's not worth it," an officer from the San Antonio Police Department, in Texas, said in a video.
Since Rockstar Games' 1997 inaugural release in the Grand Theft Auto series, the game has been both celebrated and condemned for its depictions of violence and its invitation to players to virtually participate.
It allows players to do everything from selling drugs to soliciting prostitutes and shooting law enforcement officers.
GTA 6's release in the US on Thursday ended a 13-year break in the series, unleashing a surge of fan enthusiasm and also concern among police departments.
"We need to talk," the San Juan Police Department, also in Texas, said in a video published on Instagram the same day the game launched in the US.
"We know you're excited and we know you've been waiting a long time, but what happens in GTA 6 stays in GTA 6."
In Arizona, the Pima County Sheriff's Office told GTA 6 fans in a Facebook post: "Real-life laws don't come with cheat codes, respawns, or mission restarts."
Law enforcement officials weren't the only ones worried, with one pundit on Fox News wondering if the game might "destigmatise crime". Rosanna Scotto also raised the question of whether it made young people "more inclined to use guns at an earlier age now because of these kind of video games".
Research on the relationship between video game violence and its effects on players is mixed.
The American Psychological Association (APA) issued a resolution, external in 2020 that said "violence is a complex social problem that likely stems from many factors".
"Attributing violence to violent video gaming is not scientifically sound and draws attention away from other factors," the APA said.
But the APA also said research showed an association between violent video games and increased aggressive behaviour and decreased moral judgement.
Despite concerns, the release of GTA 6 has had a meteoric landing, topping $2.36bn (Â£1.8bn) in first-day sales, and generating news headlines over the surge in people skipping school and work in order to play.

1b5350b7fff8.text: By — Mike Corder, Associated Press Mike Corder, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/myanmar-is-the-first-state-found-responsible-for-genocide-heres-how-the-icj-ruled-in-other-cases Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Myanmar is the first state found responsible for genocide. Here's how the ICJ ruled in other cases World Nov 20, 2026 11:03 AM EST THE HAGUE, Netherlands (AP) — The United Nations' top court has for the first time ruled that a nation committed what legal scholars call the crime of crimes, finding that Myanmar committed genocide in a brutal 2017 military crackdown against the Rohingya minority. The International Court of Justice has been asked to reach that conclusion before, but never found enough evidence to make the determination of a state-sponsored genocide like the one targeting the Rohingya. WATCH: International Court of Justice finds Myanmar guilty of genocide against Rohingya The World Court has more cases on its docket dealing with alleged breaches of the 1948 Genocide Convention, including a politically charged case about Israel's actions in Gaza. 1. Bosnia-Serbia: The Srebrenica genocide What happened: The Srebrenica massacre was a peak in the violence of Bosnia's 1992-95 war, which came after the breakup of Yugoslavia unleashed nationalist passions and territorial ambitions across the region. On July 11, 1995, Serbs overran Srebrenica, at the time a U.N.-protected safe area. They separated at least 8,000 Bosniak men and boys from their wives, mothers and sisters and slaughtered them. Those who tried to escape were chased through the woods and over the mountains around town. How the court ruled: The court, basing itself in part on verdicts at a United Nations war crimes tribunal, said in a 2007 ruling that the Srebrenica killings amounted to genocide. However, it did not find Serbia responsible. It did find Serbia had violated its obligation to prevent genocide. That obligation is enshrined in the 1948 Genocide Convention. 2. Croatia-Serbia: Attacks on Croatian regions What happened: In another war that erupted out of the messy breakup of Yugoslavia, Serb forces attacked several regions of neighboring Croatia, killing and wounding Croat citizens. Croatia accused Serbia of controlling forces responsible for attacks from 1991-95 that Zagreb said amounted to genocide. How the court ruled: In a 2015 decision, the court said that it found genocidal acts, but it said it did not establish genocidal intent. Under the Genocide Convention, intent to destroy a group, in whole or in part, is necessary for a finding of genocide. 3. South Africa-Israel: The Gaza conflict What happened: Israel launched a devastating military campaign in Gaza following Hamas' Oct. 7, 2023, attack, when militants stormed through Israeli communities, killing some 1,200 people and taking around 250 people hostage. WATCH: UN's highest court hears request from South Africa on Israel's offensive in Rafah The Israeli campaign has laid waste to much of the Gaza Strip and killed more than 74,000 people, according to Gaza's health ministry, which does not distinguish between civilians and militants. South Africa has accused Israel of breaching the genocide convention during its offensive, a claim Israel vehemently denies. At public hearings, Israel insisted that its war in Gaza was a legitimate defense of its people and that it was Hamas militants who were guilty of genocide. How the court ruled: In a 2024 interim ruling, the court ordered Israel to do all it can to prevent death, destruction and any acts of genocide in Gaza. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said the fact that the court was willing to discuss the genocide charges was a "mark of shame that will not be erased for generations." There has been no ruling yet on the merits of the case and won't be for years. Israel has until May 2029 to file written arguments and only then can the court schedule public hearings. A final ruling could only come months or years after hearings. Professor Janina Dill, an Oxford University expert on international law and the use of force, said in a statement that the Myanmar ruling "is very instructive of how the Court approaches some of the crucial questions that it faces in other pending genocide cases, including the polarising case of South Africa versus Israel." She said the 9-6 majority in the Myanmar genocide and a number of separate and dissenting opinions from judges "highlight the lingering doctrinal complexities." 4. Ukraine-Russia: Moscow's war on Ukraine What happened: Russia invaded Ukraine in February 2022, after earlier illegally annexing the Crimea peninsula. Shortly after the invasion, Ukraine filed a case accusing Russia of fabricating genocide claims against Ukraine to justify the attack. Kyiv argues that those claims amount to a breach of the Genocide Convention. How the court ruled: The court has already thrown out much of the case. Judges said they have jurisdiction to rule on a request by Ukraine for a declaration that Kyiv is not responsible for genocide, but not on other aspects of the case. Like the South Africa-Israel case, this is at an early stage of proceedings and no final decision on the merits is expected for years. A free press is a cornerstone of a healthy democracy. Catherine Zeta-Jones's daughter has said her parents warned her people might have "preconceived notions" about her embarking on an acting career, as she shared her views on the "nepo baby" label.
Carys Douglas, 23, made her stage debut this year, playing the lead role of Nina in Anton Chekhov's The Seagull in Brooklyn, New York.
Zeta-Jones, who is married to Michael Douglas, son of Hollywood star Kirk, previously said the "nepo baby" term was "horrific". It refers to children of famous parents perceived to have achieved riches and success off their parents' backs.
But the young actor said her parents taught her to build her "own identity" and she has learned how to deal with the "pressure".
During an interview with Elle Spain, Carys Douglas said her parents "do not hide" from her that people would have preconceived ideas about her.
"They taught me that building my own identity depended on me and no one else. It was my responsibility, and it still is.
"As time has gone on, I've come to understand that there are different ways to deal with that kind of pressure," she said.
Her father, star of hit 1980s films such as Wall Street and Fatal Attraction, recently stated that he is not a fan of the "nepo baby" label, calling it an "unfortunate title".
"I guess you could say that about any business. The same thing with Hollywood royalty. My father's father was a junkman," Douglas, 82, said, referring to Kirk, who was considered a Hollywood Golden Age icon.
Zeta-Jones, 57, from Mumbles, Swansea, also criticised the phrase, saying it was "horrible because these kids didn't ask to be born into this, they're finding their own way in life".
"You have to go with your dreams, your passion," Zeta-Jones said.
She added: "But they love it, and they're good. Otherwise, Michael and I would be the first to go, 'you know what? Maybe law school looks really good'."
Zeta-Jones' big break came when she landed a West End role in 42nd Street in 1987, before she became a household name in the UK in 1991 after starring in the ITV hit The Darling Buds Of May.
She has since become a global superstar, with roles in The Mask Of Zorro, Entrapment, Traffic and 2002's adaptation of Chicago, for which she won an Oscar for Best Supporting Actress.
The couple's children, Dylan and Carys, have both followed in their footsteps into acting.
Michael Douglas said his children have been performing "since they were in kindergarten".
"Every play, every show, summer theater camps, graduating... I mean, they've done so much work. It's unbelievable," he said.
Douglas and Zeta-Jones' children predominantly grew up in the US, but the family regularly travels to Wales, a place they are fond of.
Speaking to British Vogue last November, Carys Douglas said her summers were spent reading on her grandmother's sofa and travelling around the Gower Peninsula in Swansea.
"I feel so lucky that this is where I'm from," she told the magazine, reflecting on the "weird but magical places" scattered across the peninsula.
"Those beaches are some of the most beautiful in the world," she said.
"The Gower Peninsula is breathtaking."
She also spoke about her "theatrical" family's traditions, recalling how "there'd be lots of little competitions for singing and pantomime shows all summer".
"It's true, the Welsh love to sing," she added.

New rules on what Airbnb hosts can reasonably ask guests to do have come into force.
Hosts should now not normally ask guests to wash up, for example, but can appeal to Airbnb if they have a compelling reason.
Some guests have found lists of house rules laborious to complete, with one telling the BBC "it was not relaxing at all".
But some hosts have said that the costs of paying for extra cleaning may have to be passed on to customers.
The new Airbnb rules, announced last month, allow hosts to choose from seven standard house rules, which include determining how many people can stay overnight, and whether or not pets or smoking are allowed.
Hosts can then set additional rules, but guests shouldn't be asked to do the washing up, remove sheets from beds, take rubbish out or avoid using utilities.
Airbnb has begun reviewing listings and will be sending emails to hosts, external "who need to take action" it said.
Hosts can appeal to Airbnb to argue an additional house rule is necessary, and ask Airbnb to approve it.
If the house rule is not approved and the host keeps it anyway, Airbnb will flag this to guests on the host's listing page with a message such as "includes cleaning tasks".
Airbnb said chores can make customers hesitate about booking through the platform, arguing that making house rules "clearer" would increase the number of clients.
But some hosts have said they may have to pass the extra cleaning costs on to guests.
Lisa Clewes, who runs a Welsh holiday let, told the BBC she was "horrified" at the state her guests left the house after a dinner party.
There were broken glasses, drinks cans on the floor, pans full of food on the table and fish guts left in the garden.
Clewes said it typically takes cleaners four hours to turn around her three-bedroom property.
She said guests leaving more mess could mean hiring extra cleaners and increasing costs â expenses that may ultimately be passed on to her customers.
Edinburgh-based holiday home owner Fiona Venter told the BBC that Airbnb's new rules were "nonsense" and would not accept bookings if guests refuse to take their rubbish away.
Talking about a time when she was worried she might get a mice infestation after six bags of rubbish were left in her cottage, she said: "I would rather have my house still standing."
But Fiona said increased cleaning costs due to the rule change would be unfair to those who do clean up after themselves: "Why should they pay extra for the guests that choose to abuse a cottage?"
The changes have come as a relief to guests like Jessica Newhook, who says she has been faced with lengthy checkout lists, often on top of hefty cleaning fees.
She booked an Airbnb in Florida for a family reunion of 11 guests and says they had to "leave the property move-in ready for the cleaners", despite paying a $250 (Â£187) cleaning fee.
"We had rules about everything and it was not relaxing at all," she said.
The new rules have added to growing frustration among owners following increases in Airbnb's commission rates last year.
Many are investing in their own websites and social media to attract direct bookings and avoid platform fees.
Not all hosts are concerned about the changes, however.
Matt Porsz, who hosts and manages other Airbnb properties full-time, told the BBC previously the review system encourages both hosts and guests to behave reasonably.
Additional reporting from George Baylis

e1b8db06b8a4.text: A federal judge said Thursday that Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins' overtly Christian messages to department employees went "too far" and put enough pressure on staff to raise a First Amendment violation. The big picture: The Supreme Court has repeatedly weighed the boundaries of the Establishment Clause . While the judge said Rollins could express her religious beliefs with interested colleagues, she concluded the department-wide messages overstepped those boundaries by amounting to coercion. But a USDA spokesperson slammed the decision as "a completely unprecedented attempt to muzzle a Cabinet Secretary" in a statement to Axios. Catch up quick: The complaint from a federal employees union and individual staffers alleged Rollins sent "increasingly proselytizing communications to the entire USDA workforce," including an Easter email where she celebrated "the greatest story ever told, the foundation of our faith, and the abiding hope of all mankind." The USDA employees who sued, who came from varied religious — and nonreligious — backgrounds, reported that the messages made them feel pressured to share Rollins' beliefs. What's inside: District Judge Trina Thompson ordered Rollins to "recognize certain boundaries when disseminating messages which convey religious content." She determined the messages overstepped and suggested "acquiescence that amounts to coercive pressure." "After reviewing and weighing the Establishment Clause jurisprudence, the Court finds that Secretary Rollins appears to exploit her position of authority to convey a religious message beyond mere holiday wishes and amounting to coercion," Thompson wrote. She said she was not trying to regulate Rollins' own religiosity; rather, she directed Rollins to follow her own department memorandum on religious expression rights, which states employees can't "use official authority to pressure subordinates." The other side: The administration argued that the employees lacked jurisdiction and that the secretary's messages fell "within this Nation's deeply rooted history and tradition of religious invocations in official discourse, including on holidays." Members of the Trump administration frequently discuss their Christian faith, though the president himself has had a complicated relationship with Christians despite the evangelical MAGA base helping him reach the White House. The DOJ did not immediately respond to Axios' request for comment. What we're watching: A USDA spokesperson said the department "is evaluating all options including a prompt appeal." Grow your mind Subscribe to our Science Newsletter to explore the wide worlds of science, health and technology. Enter your email address Subscribe Form error message goes here. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. The repercussions from the Iran war will "leave lasting marks" on the world's energy sector, said the Paris-based IEA, founded after the 1973-74 oil crisis. Energy-hungry nations will prioritize the security and affordability of their electricity, the report said, which will benefit renewable technologies, like solar energy, and other alternatives, like nuclear power. But it also reinforces the case to keep coal as a backup for times of crisis. This is especially true in coal-rich Asia, which went into energy triage when the Iran war cut off the Strait of Hormuz, a narrow passageway where about a fifth of the world's traded oil flowed. The report looks "past the current turmoil to explore the range of energy futures that could emerge from today's upheaval," said IEA Executive Director Fatih Birol, who warned that "the longer the crisis lasts, the deeper the effects will be." "I don't see any credible pathway for the energy world to return to the way it was before," he said. READ MORE: Iran widens Gulf attacks by targeting U.S. air base in Kuwait and sites in Bahrain The annual United Nations climate talks in Turkey, known as COP31, are in their final week. Before these negotiations, the U.N. announced the world is dangerously close to missing its goal of limiting global warming to 1.5 degrees Celsius (2.7 degrees Fahrenheit) above pre-industrial temperatures. Electrification — the process of powering homes, cars and industries with electricity — and moving away from planet-warming fossil fuels are major issues at COP31. "For the first time, we are actually seeing the policies used to respond to energy security concerns being very strongly aligned with policies needed for energy transitions," said IEA Director of Sustainability Laura Cozzi in an interview with The Associated Press. "This is a unique convergence that sees electrification at the heart of crisis response." Flagship report projects energy future The IEA is the world's leading intergovernmental energy organization, with more than 30 member countries. Its flagship report this year analyzes government and private data to project various future scenarios based on whether countries stick with current policies or drastically shift because of ongoing crises. There is a clear before and after the Iran war for the energy sector, experts said. In March, the IEA coordinated the emergency release of 400 million barrels of crude oil stocks to stabilize global markets. "When we look at how energy crises change the world over the long term, governments are only just beginning to get their head around just how much things will change," said Dave Jones, co-founder of the think tank Ember. Conflicts, trade tensions, climate risks and cyberattacks are increasing the number of possible energy futures, and the IEA said the "drive to diversify" fuel supplies will reshape the energy trade. "The world will not look the same after this crisis, but how we will look exactly, this still depends, and we will see in the next few months," Cozzi said. The IEA projects the Middle East will still be the world's largest oil exporter, but nations will likely reduce dependence on the Strait of Hormuz. The IEA projects the amount of oil passing the strait could go from 20 million barrels per day before the Iran war, to 8.5 million barrels in 2030, and even under 2 million barrels by 2035. While fossil fuels still dominate energy mixes, the IEA said solar and nuclear power are the "biggest beneficiaries" of governments prioritizing domestic energy sources. "This crisis has exposed the price of fossil fuel dependence," said Mohamed Adow, director of Power Shift Africa. "It's crazy that a conflict thousands of miles away can send energy bills soaring at home." READ MORE: UN chief says 'immediate and drastic' emissions cuts needed to avert climate change catastrophe Energy security concerns, however, may lead nations to rely on coal as a fallback option. Michelle Manook of FutureCoal, an industry-backed group formerly known as the World Coal Association, said "for coal-rich economies, domestic coal remains an important energy security asset." "We see coal has a momentum," said the IEA's Birol. "We will see if it is long-lived or not." Climate talks eye electrification COP31 follows a year rattled by the Iran war, as well as several climate-induced disasters, like Europe's deadly heat waves and Nepal's devastating flooding. Global warming is adding pressure to rising electricity demand. In what the IEA called a "striking milestone," energy demand for cooling overtook energy demand for heating for the first time this year. Cozzi said this is "the beginning of the trend that will last for the next decade and beyond." India, the world's most populous nation, will account for more energy demand growth over the next decade than anywhere else in the world. China, already one of the world's most electrified economies, may see electrification grow from 32% last year to 43% by 2035, the highest among major economies. What we know about the latest Russian missile strikes on Ukraine
Russia targeted bridges in Kyiv and railway stations overnight in a major attack launched days after Ukraine badly damaged the strategically important Crimean Bridge.
Ballistic missiles hit key crossings in the capital during a nationwide assault which Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said was "one of the most massive strikes" of the war so far and left at least nine dead.
Russian President Vladimir Putin had threatened to retaliate for the attack on the Crimean Bridge, which the Kremlin built to link Russia and the occupied peninsula.
The latest Russian strikes coincided with a flurry of talks around the war, and came as the Kremlin pushed back against a US claim that Russia could be open to Western-backed security guarantees for Ukraine.
The BBC's Sarah Rainsford is in Kyiv after the night of strikes.

3fe0b06613b5.text: By — Nicholas Riccardi, Associated Press Nicholas Riccardi, Associated Press By — Becky Bohrer, Associated Press Becky Bohrer, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/trump-administration-moves-to-have-lawsuit-dismissed-in-challenge-to-alaskas-u-s-senate-race Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Trump administration moves to have lawsuit dismissed in challenge to Alaska's U.S. Senate race Politics Nov 20, 2026 9:22 AM EST JUNEAU, Alaska (AP) — The Trump administration on Thursday moved to effectively drop its lawsuit that sought to block the certification of Democrat Mary Peltola's victory in Alaska's U.S. Senate race, ending a much-criticized gambit by the president to prevent one of his political rivals from taking office. Stand with free and independent journalism. Join Press Pass from PBS News The legal challenge centered around the presence on the ballot of a second candidate with the same name as the incumbent, Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan. The Alaska Supreme Court already ruled that the second Sullivan's candidacy is legal and that he could be on the ballot. Attorneys for the state, which is currently controlled by Republicans, also objected to the administration's move, calling it legally "meritless" and filing papers to help get the initial case dismissed. The administration moved Thursday to have an appeals court declare its case moot, two days after the race was decided. In their filing, Justice Department attorneys urged the 9th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals to overturn the lower court's dismissal of the case to erase the loss, but then dismiss the case anyway. They said the court "should hold that this case is moot, vacate the underlying order, and remand for dismissal on that ground." That decision comes after Peltola won an outright majority in the race to become Democrats' 56th senator, the ninth Senate pickup for the party in its midterm blowout. Peltola won by more votes than were taken by the other candidate, Dan J. Sullivan. READ MORE: Alaska voters reject ballot measure seeking to repeal open primaries and ranked voting system In a statement responding to the filing, Peltola said it was time to move on: "Now that the election is over and the voters sent a very clear message about the direction they want our state to go in, I'm eager to move forward and get to work on behalf of all Alaskans." Messages seeking comment also were left with Sen. Sullivan's campaign and the Alaska Department of Law. The Department of Justice filed the lawsuit at President Donald Trump's direction, saying that a Peltola win should not be certified until an investigation can determine if voters were confused. The administration never explained how such an investigation could take place given the secrecy of the ballot. Educate your inbox Subscribe to Here’s the Deal, our politics newsletter for analysis you won’t find anywhere else. Enter your email address Subscribe Form error message goes here. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. The case was filed before The New York Times reported on texts and other documents that appeared to show Peltola's campaign was involved in recruiting the retired schoolteacher from the tiny fishing community of Petersburg. He was listed as Daniel J. Sullivan Jr. on the ballot, with no party preference, to distinguish him from the senator, who was identified as a Republican and the incumbent. Dan J. Sullivan has long insisted he ran on his own and Peltola has denied any involvement. Trump also has demanded that Peltola be prosecuted for the scheme, and federal investigators swarmed into Alaska before Election Day. Tricks involving decoy candidates such as the second Sullivan have been a staple of U.S. politics for decades, and Trump's allies have also used them, though occasionally the schemes do lead to criminal charges. It was at least the second time since the Nov. 3 election that the Department of Justice has acted to dismiss one of its high-profile lawsuits interfering in states' handling of their elections. Just days after the election that saw Democrats flip control of Congress and peel off big wins in races for governor and state legislatures, the Justice Department moved to drop a lawsuit seeking to prevent California officials from counting roughly 20,000 ballots. The Trump administration alleged the ballots belonged to suspected noncitizens, but election officials questioned the validity of the data and said the government's list contained many U.S. citizens. Riccardi reported from Denver. A free press is a cornerstone of a healthy democracy. Support trusted journalism and civil dialogue. Senegalâs president enacted this yearâs revised budget by decree on Thursday after it was rejected by parliament. Bassirou Diomaye Faye took the step a day after lawmakers voted down the first part of next yearâs spending plan, widening a rift with the president that threatens to delay a new IMF loan.
The proposed $12.3 billion budget for 2027 trims spending as the government tries to meet the lenderâs conditions. Ousmane Sonko, the parliament speaker and a former ally of the president, opposes the governmentâs plans to cut expenditure and restructure foreign debt. Faye could again use his powers to enact next yearâs budget by decree once parliamentâs deadline expires in December, though some analysts expect him to dissolve the chamber first and call a parliamentary election for early next year.
Final approval of the $2.2 billion IMF deal, agreed in principle in September, would help Senegal regain access to international debt markets, where some of its bonds traded below half their face value on Thursday. The new program would replace one that was frozen after billions of dollars in unreported government debt surfaced in 2024.

The military lacks an ‘overarching plan’ to improve munition stockpiles—partly because it’s no one’s job
Pentagon officials largely concurred with GAO’s recommendations.
The Defense Department has no “overarching plan” to identify, achieve, or measure its progress toward long-term munition production goals, according to a Government Accountability Office study released on Thursday, which said the military was too reactive to global events and unprepared to forecast its own needs.
The GAO cited—among other issues—a lack of centralized authority over weapons inventories, which have been depleted by the Iran war and are vital to U.S. plans for a potential conflict with China.
At the center of the problem lies a discrepancy between what the military can buy and what it actually needs, which the GAO said could even result in munition investments that exceed the Pentagon’s requirements.
“While DOD is taking steps to focus on munitions shortages, it is not positioned to address these gaps,” the report’s authors wrote. “DOD does not have an overarching plan or designated and empowered leadership to improve munition inventories and meet its munitions requirements. By not identifying long-term goals, strategies to achieve them, and metrics to gauge progress, DOD cannot be sure that its actions will address its munition shortfalls. ”
Top administration officials, including Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, have denied that the U.S. has a shortage in munitions, despite reports and independent analyses showing the Iran conflict has alarmingly drained key weapons, especially for highly-sought Patriot interceptors that can take more than two years to make.
But in its response to the GAO study, Pentagon officials concurred with the recommendation that the military needed to develop a long-term plan to improve its munition production.
“We agree with the need for an overarching framework that better integrates munition requirements, inventory levels, production, resources, and long-term objectives,” wrote David Cadman, the Pentagon’s acting deputy for acquisitions, who added that the department “already executes many elements” of the GAO’s recommendation.
The GAO study did not explore the inventories of specific munitions, but examined the processes by which an expansive list of weapons — from artillery shells to Tomahawk missiles — are tracked, forecast and generally addressed by the Pentagon.
“The important thing is that [the study] is not about current shortages,” Mark Cancian, a senior adviser with the Center for Strategic and International Studies who has written extensively on munitions policy. “It's about the future and deciding long-term inventories, production, and munitions mixes.”
Defense officials have emphasized the need for a “high-low” mix of munitions—that is, a balance between high-tech, hard-to-make weapons and cheaper ones. The Iran war illustrated the U.S. military’s reliance on expensive interceptors, which were heavily expended to shoot down cheap Shahed drones that only cost tens of thousands of dollars.
“When you have an exquisite capacity, and you are starting to expend an exquisite capacity to knock down non-exquisite capabilities that are rapidly replenished, it is an economical game that we're not going to win,” said Wayne Sanders, a defense analyst with Bloomberg Intelligence. “This is starting to turn into one of those revolutions in military affairs to say we have to change our doctrine as well as we change our production capacity in the U.S.”
In an email to Defense One on Friday, the GAO’s director for defense capabilities, Diana Moldafsky, noted that the Pentagon had identified shortfalls before the conflict with Iran, but said that the war “made addressing those shortages more urgent.”
“Our key point is that meeting DOD's munitions requirements will be challenging,” Moldafsky said. “A department-wide plan would help the department direct its resources towards its most critical munitions needs.”
Cancian said that Russia’s 2022 full-scale invasion of Ukraine, and the consequent transfer of Patriots and other weapons to Kyiv, introduced concerns about the defense industrial base and its ability to respond to munition needs around the world.
Meanwhile, the Pentagon has inked billions of dollars in multi-year “framework agreements” with top defense companies over the last year to help increase high-tech munition production, which require funding from Congress to come to fruition. The Trump administration also invoked the Defense Production Act earlier this year in an attempt to bolster munition supply chains.
A Pentagon spokesperson declined to address the GAO study directly, or even to be quoted by name. But they said the military is “fully equipped to strike at the time and place of the President’s choosing…while preserving a deep, ready stockpile to defend our people and interests.”
Part of the problem is that no one authority is really in charge of keeping arsenals topped off and ready, the report found.
The GAO identified several Pentagon offices and working groups, including individual service entities, responsible for managing munition inventories, but no one dedicated authority “that empowers the leadership to make decisions that improve munitions inventories department-wide and hold them accountable for the outcomes achieved, such as improving munitions inventory levels.”
The study also said that the services maintain separate tools to track munition inventories, which then feed into a Pentagon system known as the Munitions Readiness Initiative. But researchers said the DOD has limited oversight over that tracking platform and hasn’t regularly reconciled it with service-level numbers.

Every morning for a month, Mildred Juarez woke up at five to be the first person in the showers at the immigration centre in Texas where she was being detained. Her friends had paid her bail, and she wanted to look presentable when she was finally released.
But every day, she was told her bond had not been paid.
Juarez was confused. Her friends had wired $2,600 (Â£1,970) to a bond company, Libre Immigration Services (LIS), that had been recommended by her lawyer. LIS said it would begin "the process of paying her immigration bond". But the next day came, and the day after that, with no release.
What she didn't know was that LIS was owned by a convicted fraudster, who had acquired the assets of another bail company co-founded by two men who also had fraud convictions. These two men were fined $811m in 2024 for scamming their clients.
Their firm, Libre By Nexus, which was at one point the largest immigration bail company in America, had appeared to shut down after federal regulators caught up with them.
But public records and BBC interviews with clients and former employees reveal a tangle of interconnected operations continued - along with the flow of cash - while leaving immigrants stuck in detention centres.
Since President Donald Trump has returned to office after promising an immigration crackdown, Immigrations and Customs Enforcement (ICE) has made over 1.2m arrests, and fast-tracked deportations. The administration has tried unsuccessfully to make it illegal to give migrants bail but the sharp increase in detentions has increased demand for bond companies to secure bail and their release.
Conditions in these centres can be poor. Held in custody, away from family, often scared to speak out, many have faced health problems and endured inadequate food or treatment, according to immigrant advocates and reports by the US government.
In the detention centre where Juarez was locked up, she and about 100 other detainees slept in bunks laid out in rows in a cacophonous room. The lights were left on all night and guards routinely woke everyone up for roll call. According to Castro and advocacy groups, detainees who caused trouble were put in "the hold" - solitary confinement.
The White House and officials from Homeland Security did not respond to the BBC's request for comment.
For Juarez, the wait to be bailed out of detention seemed interminable.
In an email to the BBC, a spokesperson for LIS said Juarez "misunderstands" their services - that they are not bondsmen themselves, but they connect detained individuals to those who are licensed bondsmen. They said another company ultimately decided not to work with her.
An email sent by LIS, and reviewed by the BBC, said that the company had paid a cash bond to ICE on behalf of Juarez. The message was forwarded to Juarez as proof of payment a few days before her release.
But it was another bail agent, who was not affiliated with LIS, that got her out of detention - after her friends raised even more money to hire another company.
"I was losing it inside there," Juarez recalled, using an expletive.
"I lost everything. When I was released I had nightmares I was back inside."
Libre Immigration Services never paid back her deposit, despite sending messages promising a refund. A spokesperson told the BBC that they would refund Juarez's bail amount once her friend verified their details.
Ankle monitors and debt
It is notoriously difficult for migrants like Juarez to make bail, which can be upwards of $7,000.
Once charged with illegal entry, a judge may grant bail, which allows the migrant to live freely while their case is heard, a process which can take years. Once a person's court case is completed, the bond amount is returned.
Bail agents, who are licensed to provide a down payment on bail and vouch that if the accused does not show up for court they will pay the rest, can help people get out of detention sooner. But many won't help migrants because they view them as too much of a flight risk. A 2024 government report found that a third of migrants not already in custody did not show up for court.
Libre by Nexus, also known as Nexus, was willing to take that risk.
Founded in 2013, its co-founders Michael Donovan and Richard Moore had served prison time in the 1990s and early 2000s for a string of fraud and forgery convictions.
Through his attorney, Donovan declined to comment. Moore did not respond to the BBC's request for comment.
Although people with felony convictions are barred from holding a bond licence in many states, Nexus operated as a kind of middleman between immigrant clients and licensed bondsmen.
Holed up in detention in Louisiana after crossing the border, Rosa Murillo heard about Libre by Nexus from another inmate, and the 18-year-old Honduran's mother called them to arrange her $7,000 bail.
A Nexus employee picked her up and took her to a hotel room where she was told she would have to pay $420 a month and wear a GPS ankle monitor until her case was completed.
Federal regulators accused Nexus of implying, in their contracts, that the GPS bracelets were court-mandated, when they were actually the private company's requirement.
Murillo got a job as a waitress and tried to hide the ankle bracelet for fear that people might think she was a violent criminal.
Over the course of a decade, Libre by Nexus enabled more than 20,000 migrants like Murillo to be released on bail - and took in more than $230m in revenue, court documents show.
But the ankle bracelets were a constant source of annoyance for Nexus clients released from detention, according to two former employees who spoke to the BBC.
A former Nexus co-owner, Evan Ajin, told the BBC that the company stopped requiring released detainees to wear ankle bracelets in 2018.
But Mark Supetran, who was based in the Philippines and worked for the company for a few months in 2022, says the bracelets were still in use when he worked for the company.

US President Donald Trump has said air traffic control systems that manage flights across the country are "ancient" and is pushing Congress to fund costly upgrades.
Trump called the systems "obsolete", saying they were at least "55 years old" and noted some towers were not in good shape structurally.
"It's very safe. But it's safe for a different reason because we do it very slowly," he said. "In other words, we travel slower. That's why you have lots of waits at the airport."
His remarks came a week after a historic ground stop halted flights across the US for hours - the longest such event since the terror attacks on 11 September 2001.
Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) officials said the agency planned on Friday to share more information about what led to the four-hour ground stop on 13 November.
Top aviation officials within the Trump administration have previously said the cause was related to old equipment overloading, as well as updates to systems.
At a press briefing, Trump responded to some concerns about whether the ground stop issue was at all linked to other tech outages in the same week.
"They're all separate events," he said. "You know we have thousands of companies that are upgrading right now, and when they upgrade, bad things happen."
US Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy has explained a government contractor was upgrading an aviation telecommunications network, swapping out copper lines for fibre and installing a router, which directs traffic across the network.
The switch led the router to start flooding others in the air traffic control system, sending 1,000 connection attempts every four to five seconds. It is unclear whether the root cause of the issue was the wire replacement or a fault with the router.
As a result, 17 out of 22 air route traffic control centres in the US experienced issues with voice and ground communications. It took the aviation authority 45 minutes to identify where the problem was because maintenance is logged manually on paper.
More than 15,000 flights in the US were delayed or cancelled the day of the outage, according to data from flight tracking sites, affecting an estimated 1.5mn passengers.
Ripple effects from the incident caused issues for days, with thousands more flights being cancelled or delayed over the weekend.
In some cases, passengers were left stuck inside planes on the tarmac, unable to take off or return to gates.
The ground stop also had a knock-on effect on schedules around the world, with some flights out of the UK and Europe cancelled.
Since the outage, transportation leaders have repeatedly pressed Congress for billions in funding to upgrade US systems and warned that without an overhaul outages like this would continue.
Trump on Friday weighed in and backed members of his administration, who are asking for $50bn (Â£38bn) to rebuild air traffic control systems. He said the transportation department had been allotted $12bn (Â£9bn), which is not enough for such a large undertaking.
"I said, 'Sean, let's not spend money to patch up all over the place because when we get the new system, everything's going to be torn out, so let's not spend the 12. Spend as little as you can to keep it going,'" Trump said he told Duffy, the transportation secretary.
He reiterated accusations that Congress - which is currently controlled by the Republican party - was blocking the funds.
"We need to have new air traffic control, and to do that we have to get the money now," Trump said.
"Congress has been very bad on it, but if there's any silver lining to what happened last week, it's that Congress seems to be very receptive now to giving us the money."

Europeans, with Ukraine’s help, brace for more Russian attacks
Meanwhile, Trump greets Putin as “my friend” and downplays Russian missiles in Poland.
IZMIR, Turkey—Vladimir Putin would “love to end the war,” as Donald Trump asserted on Friday, but European NATO members and Ukrainians are working to make sure Russia’s invasion of Ukraine doesn’t end on Moscow’s terms.
In several meetings this week, officials described plans to support their beleaguered European neighbor—and to draw upon the experience to modernize allied militaries and erect new defenses against Russian aggression.
In Berlin on Thursday, the leaders of Germany, France, and Britain reaffirmed NATO’s pledge to provide 70 billion euros’ worth of military equipment, assistance, and training to Ukraine this year—and at least that much in 2027. The European Union has also promised to lend the war-wracked country 60 billion euros for defense and 30 billion for budget support through the next year.
Meanwhile, NATO and Ukrainian officials, along with European arms makers, used an alliance technology conference here to deepen their ties.
Multiple reports suggest Trump is unhappy with the European leaders’ plans to keep funding Ukraine. On Thursday, he phoned them from Air Force One and reportedly questioned their plans to spend more billions. At least one source described the call as a “tirade,” although a U.S. official said that the suggestion that Trump had told leaders to stop funding Ukraine was “not accurate.”
On Thursday, Trump downplayed Russian drone and missile incursions into NATO countries.
“Putin has been landing drones in Poland and a couple of little missiles, by mistake,” he said, hours after warmly greeting the Russian leader as ‘my friend’ and hours before two more Russian missiles and a suspected drone came down in Poland on Friday.
European and NATO officials see the defense of Ukraine as directly tied to their own defense. They see Putin as undeterred in his ambitions to control Ukraine and already waging an unconventional war against them.
“We understand that we are under a very specific kind of a war, which Russia initiated against us, and that we are in phase zero of this war,” Paweł Ksawery Zalewski, secretary of state at Poland’s Ministry of National Defence, said in September. So these acts of incursions of drones of, you know, sabotage and others prepare or can prepare for further operations.”
At this week’s NATO Edge conference here, French Adm. Pierre Vandier described Russian “cyber attacks against our infrastructure, challenging the cohesion of our society.” Vandier, who serves as NATO’s Supreme Allied Commander Transformation, said the attacks seemed to be intended to intimidate European allies.
“I think much of the activity that we're seeing is related to Russian ambitions to discourage us from helping Ukraine, so it's putting us on the string,” he said.
Indeed, Russia’s hybrid attacks are meant to undermine NATO more broadly, said Alik Kasman, chief strategy officer at the Peace Through Strength Institute, a Washington think tank.
“This is how they discredit NATO, and this is one of their objectives too,” Kasman said in a recent interview. “They're going to fly a drone here and there, pretend it's not them, pretend it wasn't intentional, and they're going to see how NATO countries respond, or rather, do not respond.”Vandier said alliance members are responding by spending more on intelligence, surveillance, and reconnaissance to spot incoming drones and missiles.
They are also enlisting civilian institutions to help prepare for and respond to such attac, and are working to figure out how best to“coordinate the military response and the civilian arm,” he said.
Learning from Ukraine’s experience is essential as well, Vandier said.In September, UK defense companies became the first foreign firms allowed to access Avengers Labs, a Ukrainian Defense Ministry platform for training AI models on data collected directly from the battlefield.
Even as the Trump administration lowers sanctions on Russia and Trump calls Putin “my friend,” U.S. envoys are reportedly floating a proposal to add Ukraine to NATO, according to the Wall Street Journal. That would be an outcome Putin has consistently opposed, and it comes with a condition—Ukraine would cede territory to Moscow—that Kyiv has consistently rejected.
Still, French President Emmanuel Macron backed reopening the membership question.
“Faced with the maximalist nature of the Russian position, I believe we need to reopen the question of Ukraine's accession to NATO,” Macron said in Berlin on Thursday, adding that now is not the time to reduce support for Kyiv. “Everyone who has the capacity to provide the means to defend and protect Ukrainian citizens must do so now,” he said.
On Friday, Russian Deputy Foreign Minister Sergei Ryabkov called any prospect of Ukraine joining NATO “unacceptable to us.”

The party that has dominated South Africa for more than 30 years is in a race against time to secure power-sharing deals in most of the country's cities after a massive drop in its support in this month's local elections.
The African National Congress (ANC) suffered its worstâ¯result since it came to power in 1994 when South Africa transitioned from the racist apartheid system to democracy.
It won a majority in just one of the country's nine provinces, Limpopo, down from six in the last elections. It won the most votes in just two of the country's eight cities, compared with six in 2021.
At the national level, the ANC is sharing power with its long-time rival, the Democratic Alliance (DA), but while there is still no official announcement, it appears that ANC party officials do not want to replicate this at the local level.
Parties have until 27 November to negotiate and form local governments.
What happened in the local election?
While the ANC saw a massive decline in its support, it still got more votes than any other party, 31%, down from the 46% in the last local election.
But in the country's economic powerhouse, Gauteng province, which includes Johannesburg and Pretoria, the picture is different. The pro-business DA got the most votes in both cities, as well as the province's other main region, Ekurhuleni.
Nationally, the party got 25% of the vote, up from 22% five years ago.
It also retained its majority in its power base of Cape Town, and got the most votes in Nelson Mandela Bay, where Gqeberha (Port Elizabeth) is located.
The left-leaning uMkhonto weSizwe (MK) Party, led by former President Jacob Zuma, came third, with 10% of the vote. This is a repeat of its performance in the 2024 national election, when it came in third and became the official opposition after the DA joined the coalition government.
It emerged as the biggest party in KwaZulu-Natal province, which includes the port city of Durban, securing 34% of the vote. However, this leaves it reliant on agreeing a coalition with other parties.
The only party to secure an overall majority in a city was the DA in Cape Town.
Why is the ANC apparently choosing smaller parties over the DA?
The DA and ANC have had an uneasy alliance since they entered a coalition, along with eight other political parties, in 2024.
The two, long-standing rivals due to their opposing policies, were forced into an agreement after the ANC lost its parliamentary majority for the first time since the end of apartheid. This became known as the Government of National Unity (GNU).
Despite this, the two parties have continued to disagree on key issues, and both sides have threatened to rip up their power-sharing deal.
Ahead of the local elections, analysts predicted that the two parties could team up at municipal level, mirroring the national arrangement.
The ANC seems to have rejected this, with state broadcaster SABC reporting that most of the party's top leaders see an agreement with the DA as a last resort.
Instead, the party has been courting smaller parties to try and form councils in South Africa's cities.
In Gauteng, numerous reports point to an arrangement between the party and the anti-immigrant ActionSA, which emerged as the third largest party in the province with 17%, leaving it as a potential kingmaker.
The DA has also been trying to reach arrangements with smaller parties, and the ANC, but looks set to assume the opposition benches at least in Gauteng.
ActionSA is unlikely to work with the DA as they cannot agree on the mayoral candidates in Johannesburg and Pretoria.
Does this signal a breakdown in the relationship between the ANC and DA nationally?
It's too early to tell. Neither the ANC nor DA have spoken publicly about the future of their arrangement on a national level amid the ongoing coalition talks but the ANC's reluctance to partner with the DA in key cities points to continued strain between the two.
While the GNU has remained intact since it was formed in 2024, there have been those in the ANC who have been angered by what they view as the DA's dual role as opposition and partner in the coalition government and have pushed for the arrangement to end.
A party insider told the Daily Maverick on Sunday that a nationwide agreement to work with the DA at municipal level "was overwhelmingly rejected" at a meeting held by ANC members.
While some experts predict that the DA may have to consider its position in the coalition government given the ANC's stance, political analyst Andre Duvenhage told the BBC there was a possibility that "a lot of asymmetrical coalitions" could emerge - parties working together in one area and being in opposition elsewhere.
Another political analyst, Sandile Swana, said that any party wanting to leave the GNU over the failure to secure deals locally would be "[shooting] yourself in the foot".
Would coalition governments improve services?
This is what voters want.
The decline in the ANC's support was seen as being mainly due to high levels of corruption and a loss of confidence in its ability to provide basic services, such as electricity, water and rubbish collection.
While some attribute the increase backing for the DA to its record of competent management in municipalities under its control, some have accused it of neglecting poorer areas and townships.
But the experience of coalition governments over the past 10 years does not inspire much confidence that things will improve.
Half of the country's cities have been governed through power-sharing agreements since 2016 and these types of arrangements have often been viewed as unstable and chaotic.
As agreements collapse and new ones are forged, the delivery of basic services has often been affected.
This has been particularly evident in Gauteng, where governance in all three cities has come under scrutiny in recent years partly because of unstable governments.

Lederer, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/rights-groups-urge-sanctions-after-icj-finds-myanmar-guilty-of-genocide-against-rohingya Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Rights groups urge sanctions after ICJ finds Myanmar guilty of genocide against Rohingya World Nov 20, 2026 7:28 PM EST UNITED NATIONS (AP) — Rights groups are calling for military and economic sanctions against Myanmar after the United Nations' highest court, in the first ruling of its kind, determined that its government committed genocide against the Rohingya minority in a brutal 2017 military operation. WATCH: International Court of Justice finds Myanmar guilty of genocide against Rohingya The International Court of Justice has no power to enforce Thursday's ruling, which orders Myanmar's military-supported government to allow those who fled the violence to return home safely, to pay reparations to the Rohingya Muslims and prosecute those suspected of having committed genocide. Myanmar's government has denied committing genocide, claiming it acted against insurgents, and is considered unlikely to fulfill any of the court's demands. President Min Aung Hlaing, the former military leader, was in charge of the 2017 operation. The court said evidence showed Myanmar forces killed about 100,000 Rohingya. Khine Khine Soe, the president's spokeswoman, noted the International Court of Justice decision handed down Thursday had been the result of a nine-to-six vote of the judges. "Not all 15 judges agreed with the decision," she told reporters in the capital Naypyitaw. "So it was not a decision made unanimously. I would say that it was unfair." While the World Court's rulings are final and legally binding, it has no recourse beyond reporting noncompliance to the U.N. Security Council. UN Security Council has the power to impose sanctions The Security Council scheduled closed consultations on the ruling next Wednesday and a private meeting on Dec. 7 at the request of the United Kingdom, which expelled Myanmar's defense attache after Thursday's ruling. But Daniel Forti, the International Crisis Group's head of U.N. affairs, said it's unlikely there will be any immediate action from the 15-member Security Council, which could impose sanctions on Myanmar. He said any action would likely be blocked by China and Russia, both permanent members with veto power. "China has discouraged the Security Council from acting on the Myanmar file since 2021, as it is reluctant to cede any influence in its own backyard," Forti told The Associated Press. "The ICJ ruling will not alter China's calculations, and it is hard to imagine that either Beijing or Moscow would support any potential Security Council resolution that attempts to enforce the court's recommendations." READ MORE: Myanmar is the first state found responsible for genocide. Here's how the ICJ ruled in other cases Forti said Gambia, which launched the court proceedings, may eventually pursue a resolution in the 193-member General Assembly calling on Myanmar to comply with the ICJ's demands, even though its actions are not legally binding, unlike those of the Security Council. General Assembly President Khalilur Rahman plans to hold "an informal dialogue" with the U.N.'s 193 member nations on the ICJ ruling and remains open to other exchanges, assembly spokesperson Melissa Summers said. Rahman, who is also Bangladesh's foreign minister, went to Cox's Bazaar Friday and told a crowd of Rohingya "at this historic moment" that there must be action and pledged to be their voice in New York, she said. Justice for All, an American human rights organization that advocates for the rights of Muslim minorities, called on the Trump administration to support a General Assembly resolution demanding Myanmar's compliance with the judgment, and establishing international monitoring and follow-up. Rights groups call for targeting Myanmar's economy and military Justice for All, which has a task force of 38 U.S. and Canadian Muslim organizations that have advocated for Rohingya rights since 2017, argued that sanctions should target Myanmar's oil and gas sector and the networks that provide weapons and other support to its military. Amnesty International's Secretary General Agnes Callamard urged governments not to welcome the president "on the international stage, especially as grave violations continue unchecked inside Myanmar." "Instead, they should stop any transfer of all weapons, security and surveillance equipment, and military and security assistance to Myanmar," she said. "The U.N. Security Council should impose a global arms embargo and refer the entire situation in Myanmar to the International Criminal Court." That court, however, is under U.S. sanctions along with many of its judges and staff, so any action by the Security Council would face an almost certain U.S. veto. Prosecutors at the ICC requested an arrest warrant for Min Aung Hlaing in late 2024 alleging he was responsible for crimes against humanity against the Rohingya. There has been no public announcement on a decision by judges at the court who would have to issue a warrant. The court's Office of the Prosecutor said in an email response to questions from The Associated Press that the ICJ judgment "will not have any bearing on matters that are currently before the Judges of the ICC," and noted that the ICC deals with allegations of individual criminal responsibility of people, as opposed to state responsibility. No clear path for reparations for the Rohingya Human Rights Watch urged governments to step forward to help the Rohingya. "Concerned governments should strongly support the Rohingya and promote justice for atrocities, press Myanmar's junta to comply with the judgment, and ensure the safe and voluntary return of Rohingya refugees to Myanmar," Maria Elena Vignoli, the group's senior international justice

de0d3f2c230a.text: By — Jaimie Ding, Associated Press Jaimie Ding, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/nation/federal-jury-convicts-man-of-starting-deadly-2025-palisades-fire-in-los-angeles Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Federal jury convicts man of starting deadly 2025 Palisades Fire in Los Angeles Nation Nov 20, 2026 7:01 PM EST LOS ANGELES (AP) — The man accused of sparking last year's deadly Palisades Fire was found guilty of arson charges Friday after his first federal case earlier this year ended in a mistrial. READ MORE: Mistrial declared after jury deadlocks in arson trial over deadly 2025 Palisades Fire in Los Angeles Jurors convicted Jonathan Rinderknecht, 30, of lighting a fire on Jan. 1, 2025, that burned undetected deep in root systems before flaring back up Jan. 7, becoming one of the most destructive wildfires in California history. The Palisades Fire killed 12 people as it incinerated entire neighborhoods in Los Angeles and Malibu. Rinderknecht, with little apparent reaction, gave his attorneys hugs before leaving the courtroom. His father was present for the trial and as the verdict was read. Rinderknecht pleaded not guilty to federal charges of destruction of property by means of fire and arson. The scope of the first charge was narrowed to only include the Jan. 1 blaze, known as the Lachman Fire, and the second addresses the Palisades Fire. He was convicted on both charges. Prosecutors continued to pursue the case after Rinderknecht's first jury deadlocked 10 to 2 in favor of acquittal after a two-week trial in June. They dropped a third charge of timber set afire when they filed a new indictment for the retrial. During the second trial, prosecutors presented a more tightly organized case that presented digital forensic data, expert testimony and Rinderknecht's state of mind in the hours leading up to the fire. They did not focus as much on his resentment toward the rich and powerful to present the crime as arson motivated by "societal revenge" like they previously did. Prosecutors zeroed in on evidence placing him at the fire's origin area, such as photographs that showed his car parked at the base of a trail leading up to where the fire started and cellphone tower data pointing to his movement on the hill. Fire detection camera images showed the time window the blaze ignited, and experts eliminated any other source of ignition that night, including fireworks. They established that Rinderknecht was acting erratic and angry in the hours leading up to the fire through the testimony of Uber passengers and texts sent to his girlfriend at the time. "He was mad at everything, and frustrated," said Assistant U.S. Attorney Mark Williams. After the fire began, Rinderknecht called 911 more than a dozen times as he walked down the hill. Prosecutors presented the video he screen-recorded on his phone while calling. As he was calling, he asked ChatGPT: "Are you at fault if a fire is lit because of your cigarettes?" These were part of an alibi Rinderknecht was trying to create for himself, prosecutors said. They also presented extensive testimony on how fire investigators determined the Palisades Fire was a holdover fire from the initial blaze Rinderknecht sparked. Jurors were instructed not to consider the Los Angeles Fire Department's role in putting out the fire. Rinderknecht's defense attorney Steve Haney casted doubt on the government's case and said that their evidence proves nothing. Haney said the fire scene could have been compromised because the area was accessible to the public until the Palisades Fire started Jan. 7. "Six days of anyone and everyone walking across the spot the government now calls a crime scene," he said. The defense called their own expert witnesses, including a retired fire investigator for the U.S. Forest Service who argued the fire origin area was different from what the government concluded. Haney argued the government could not conclusively say there was no one else by the fire ignition point that night because of missing cell data records, and pointed to a neighbor's testimony that he saw a group of teenagers running away from the direction of the trailhead. He told jurors to disregard any evidence related to Rinderknecht's character, such as his angry text messages, because they were "evidence of the man, not evidence of the act." Finally, Haney presented an alternate explanation for what ignited the fire — fireworks. Multiple witnesses, including two neighbors and a local firefighter, all said they heard a loud bang or explosion from the direction of the hill the fire purportedly started on. In the thousands of images of the evening collected from cameras in the area, none showed fireworks in the sky above the hill where the fire started, prosecutors said. New York City's official overseeing the closure of the city's most notorious jail hopes a new plan from Mayor Zohran Mamdani will lead to "a moment of transformation" for how people are detained in the largest US city.
Mamdani on Friday unveiled a plan to close the Rikers Island complex by 2032, to build four new jails and drastically reduce the city's detainee population.
Plans to shutter the troubled facility date back to 2019, when the city council first voted to close it by this year. But plans have been delayed over the years in part due to the logistical difficulties over where to place inmates.
Dana Kaplan - who Mamdani appointed as the city's "Close Rikers Czar" told the BBC News channel on Friday that his latest proposal is not just about getting rid of a decrepit facility.
It is also a "generational opportunity" to "build a different type of detention system" and figure out how to detain people more appropriately, she said.
The Rikers Island jail complex is perched on a 413 acre (167 hectare) island between Queens and the Bronx, and has earned a variety of nicknames over the years because of its dilapidated conditions, including Gladiator School and Torture Island. The jail has housed a number of high-profile inmates awaiting trial, including Tupac Shakur, DMX and Harvey Weinstein.
It houses more than 6,500 inmates at a given time. Mamdani hopes to reduce that number to 4,100 - a goal that has been met with skepticism by the New York City correction officers' union.
"[B]uilding a new system that puts an arbitrary cap on the City's available jail beds is ill-conceived, irresponsible and jeopardizes the safety of all New Yorkers, including our Officers," NYC Correction Officers' Benevolent Association said in a statement. "The City cannot keep the jail population at around 4,100 without irresponsibly releasing individuals who committed violent felony charges."
Kaplan disagreed.
"It's actually possible to have fewer people in jail in New York City - and that is what we should be planning for," she said.
The jail complex has long faced backlash over staffing shortages, crumbling conditions and inmate deaths in the facility, including nine this year. Legislation required the jail to be shuttered by 2027, but Mamdani blamed lags under former Mayor Eric Adams' administration as well as the Covid pandemic for the delays.
Last year, under Adams, a federal judge removed Rikers from the city's control, appointing an independent outside official to make decisions concerning the facility.
In an 88-page report released on Friday, Mamdani said Rikers was a product of "deteriorating infrastructure" and that officials had a "moral imperative" to close it.
New York City Council must approve the updated timeline, with members, including the city's speaker, indicating they support the plan.
Mamdani's office said the city would open up four new jails - one in Brooklyn by 2029, two in the Bronx and Queens by 2031 and one in Manhattan by 2032.
The mayor's office argues the new, smaller facilities will provide inmates "access to daylight, fresh air and clean space" leading to better outcomes for detainees. The facilities will be easier for families to access as well, as travel to the remote Rikers can take hours.
Mamdani said his administration would work to reduce the number of people being held in jail across New York City, including by offering alternative programmes to detention for some awaiting trial, by making it easier for families to post bail online and by trying to speed up the pretrial legal process.
He also wants to open up hundreds of beds in therapeutic housing units for prisoners with serious mental health issues.
Kaplan said Mamdani's administration had already opened 100 therapeutic beds at Bellevue Hospital in Manhattan, moving 100 people off of Rikers Island.
The proposal involves a large investments: $146m (Â£111m) for mental health and substance use treatment and vocational and education programming inside and outside the jails.

0050bf5ce708.text: In a lengthy press conference, President Trump touted his recent trip to Asia and defended his relationship with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin. White House correspondent Liz Landers was in the briefing room as the president took questions from reporters. Amna Nawaz: In a lengthy press conference today, President Donald Trump touted his recent trip to Asia and defended his relationship with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin. Our White House correspondent, Liz Landers, was in the Briefing Room today as the president took questions from reporters. She joins me now. So, Liz, let's begin with that trilateral meeting in China the president just returned from. What did he have to say about that today? Liz Landers: Well, he just got back from Shenzhen late last night. He gave a glowing review of this trip that he took, in particular, that trilateral meeting between Russia, the U.S., and China. And he defended calling President Putin a friend. He was asked today, whether Putin is a friend of America, and he wouldn't really answer that part, saying, I don't know if he's a friend of the U.S., but said that we, Donald Trump and Putin, have a fantastic relationship. Secretary Rubio was also at the podium there today, and took some questions from reporters, and sort of defended what the president was talking about with this visit. Here's what he said. Marco Rubio: These three countries, the United States, Russia, and China, between these three countries possess the overwhelming majority of nuclear weapons on this planet. The idea that these three leaders should not engage on a regular basis is not just absurd. It's dangerous. And if these leaders can't get along and can't engage with one another and don't have a positive relationship, it is impossible to get anything good done for the country and the safety of the world. Liz Landers: So, Rubio there kind of prebutting some of this criticism or responding to some of this criticism that we have heard in Washington, in particular from Democrats, saying, why did President Trump invite Putin to this meeting and elevate Russia, which has a much smaller economy than the U.S. and China, and also is in the middle of this war with Ukraine? Another point that I just wanted to make, Amna, President Trump keeps saying that President Putin wants peace. He said that again today. But President Putin and Russia bombed Ukraine just this morning. Amna Nawaz: Meanwhile, the president also made some news when it comes to regulating AI data centers. What should we understand about that? Liz Landers: Yes, the president has been an ardent defender of data centers really since this has become a burgeoning policy and politics issue. Especially, it was in the midterms too. We heard that from voters. He made this announcement earlier today. President Donald Trump: We're not going to allow companies to build data centers in other countries. If they do that, they can, but we're going to put a tremendous tax on them if they do it. We want them to build it here. Liz Landers: The president has said repeatedly that many cities and states want to have these data centers, that they are a -- quote -- "tremendous asset." That was something that he reiterated again today. And he said that the U.S. needs to have these centers, these data centers here, to be competitive with China in this AI race. These data centers are a physical aspect of this race with AI, and he said that he wants them here instead of China. One of the things that I think came up today as well throughout this briefing, were questions that he was not really answering about Jensen Huang. And since this news has come out that he stepped down from Nvidia earlier this week, the administration has tried to be more aggressive about AI chips and regulation, and they put out this new policy on Monday clamping down on who can export chips across the world. Amna Nawaz: Meanwhile, Liz, as we have been reporting, the White House is also preparing for this change in Congress, right? In just a few short months, the president's going to have to work with Democratic majorities in both the House and the Senate. How did he address that today? Liz Landers: The president vacillates between saying that he wants to veto anything that comes across his desk, and then says that he wants to work with Democrats. Today, he said that he thinks that the incoming likely speaker, Hakeem Jeffries, is smart and that, if Democrats want to work with him, then he will be willing to do that. There were two areas, though, in particular, that he identified that he thinks there's some bipartisanship, health care and also immigration. He did not get into specifics on those policies at all. Amna Nawaz: We will wait and see. White House correspondent Liz Landers beginning our coverage. Liz, thank you. Liz Landers: Of course.

Amna Nawaz: We start the day's other headlines on Wall Street, where stocks tumbled to end the week, as worries about AI rattled the market. (BELL RINGING) Amna Nawaz: By the closing bell, all three major averages were deeply in the red, as investors weigh the health of the AI sector following Nvidia's leadership upheaval and Anthropic's record IPO. Looking at the numbers, the Dow Jones industrial average fell more than 900 points on the day. The Nasdaq dropped more than 5 percent, erasing all its gains for the year. The S&P 500 is now down more than 10 percent from its recent high, meaning it's now in what investors call correction territory. A second federal judge is blocking President Trump's Memorial Arch in Washington, D.C. The judge in Virginia called the project a rush job today, saying it lacks a legal basis. She put construction there on hold indefinitely, pending the outcome of legal challenges to the arch. Earlier this week, a separate judge extended a previous block for two more weeks. President Trump is trying to build a 250-foot Memorial Arch near Arlington National Cemetery, which has led to criticism from veterans groups and local environmentalists. In Iowa, a federal appeals court is blocking the U.S. Army from detonating several tons of bomb-making chemicals amid concerns over environmental and health risks. The controlled explosion has been scheduled for today, and was expected to send lead dust as far as 60 miles around the area. Acting Army Secretary Adam Telle had agreed to postpone the detonation until Monday. But he warned that a coming drop in temperatures could further destabilize the material. It's unclear whether the court will weigh in again before Monday. In Florida, heavy storms are moving north after drenching parts of the Atlantic coast. Torrential rains turned roads into waterways, with some areas already seeing their wettest November on record. The National Hurricane Center is warning of severe widespread flash flooding for parts of Eastern Florida and says the threat could carry into next week. In the meantime, across the country, in California, heavy flooding left some neighborhoods in Los Angeles underwater, as surging waters affected a large stretch of the California coast. In Poland, authorities say two Russian missiles and a suspected drone landed in Polish territory overnight. In Southeastern Poland, CCTV footage showed a large explosion and a bright flash. The crash site was around 20 miles from where European troops from 11 countries were taking part in rare military exercises to prepare for a potential postwar Ukraine mission. Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk called the incursions an intentional provocation and said Poland, which neighbors both Ukraine and Russia must be involved in future peace talks. Donald Tusk (through interpreter): It seems that we are dealing with an intentional provocation. It is no coincidence that these objects fell near the site where military exercises are taking place.
