Data: House historian, U.S. Senate ; Chart: Erin Davis/Axios Americans want change , and they're about to get it: A perfect storm of congressional retirements, primary upsets, gerrymandering, flipped seats and lawmakers who died in office has created the biggest freshman class in decades. Why it matters : Congress had a 14% approval rating (not a typo) when Gallup polled registered voters in October. That's its lowest pre-midterm number since 1974. The big picture: The Senate is on track for its biggest freshman class since 1946. In the House, it's shaping up to be the biggest since 1992. Zoom in: The turnover featured data points that would be stunning on their own, let alone together. 28 House lawmakers chose to run for their next elected office outside the House, Pew noted in September. Six lawmakers died in office this Congress, the most in nearly 20 years. Thirteen House and Senate incumbents lost primary races. The bottom line: Congress is saying goodbye to former House Majority Leader Steny Hoyer (D-Md.), Senate Minority Whip Dick Durbin (D-Ill.), former Senate GOP leader Mitch McConnell (R-Ky.) and former Speaker Nancy Pelosi (D-Calif.). They've been in Congress since 1981, 1983, 1985 and 1987, respectively.

e962c27d9d8b.text: After years of being overlooked by national Democrats, Black organizers are using stunning Southern election upsets in the pursuit of something more lasting: a new generation of candidates who can win and govern. Why it matters: Activists say the 2026 midterms proved Southern races long dismissed as unwinnable could flip with grassroots organizing and investment. Now they're building a multiracial, working-class political bench — from school boards to statehouses. Organizers want to turn Black political gains into a durable Southern coalition united by economic interests, not just opposition to Republicans. By the numbers: The midterm election results gave organizers fresh ammunition. Roughly nine in 10 Black voters backed Democratic House candidates nationally, according to the AP Voter Poll . Democrats flipped 10 South Carolina House seats, seven won by Black candidates, ending the GOP supermajority, the South Carolina Daily Gazette reports. State of play: The Working Families Party plans candidate recruitment events in Georgia, Tennessee, South Carolina and Mississippi in early 2027, targeting community organizers, teachers, young activists and other political outsiders. It plans training, digital outreach and spending to support dozens of Southern candidates. Its Southern Made initiative aims to recruit and train 1,000 working-class candidates by 2030. Zoom in: South Carolina illustrates the opportunity. WFP-backed Jumelle Brooks , a home health care provider, lost a 2024 House race by roughly 700 votes before winning this year by nearly 10 percentage points. Another WFP-backed Democrat, Sonja Ogletree Satani , won a Charleston-area rematch. What they're saying: "We are building concentrated governing power," Britney Whaley, WFP's Southeast regional director, tells Axios. Whaley wants clusters of allies in elected bodies who can pass legislation, not isolated progressives powerless to advance an agenda. "Black people across the country voted for historic change, and now it's time for systemic policy change," Kristin Powell of Black to the Future Action Fund said in a statement to Axios. Zoom out: The Southern breakthroughs extended well beyond statehouses. Mississippi: Scott Colom became the state's first Black senator elected since Reconstruction. South Carolina: Annie Andrews won a long-shot Senate race. Georgia: Keisha Lance Bottoms became the nation's first Black woman elected governor; Democrats flipped the state House . Texas: James Talarico became the first Democratic U.S. senator elected since 1988. Yes, but: The South remains deeply Republican, and organizers say Democrats left winnable races on the table. WFP-backed Angie Nixon lost in Florida by roughly three points; Justin J. Pearson lost Tennessee's 9th District by 2,539 votes . The WFP spent about $200,000 on each race and argues more national investment could have tipped them. That's unproven. The intrigue: Pre-election findings from the 2026 Black Census , a nationwide voluntary survey by the advocacy group Black Futures Lab, found 95% of respondents planned to vote — yet just 3% trusted Washington and 22% trusted Black elected officials. Economic anxiety runs deep, with 44% hoping to escape debt, 35% to earn more and 25% to find affordable housing. Southern organizers now face a test of turning votes into economic relief, though the survey isn't representative of all Black voters.

The Resistance, Part 3: A key ally to environmentalist Diane Wilson opposes a move by Texas regulators to issue Formosa Plastics Corp. a new permit without requiring the petrochemical giant to stop discharging plastic waste into Lavaca Bay.
Palm trees surrounded the meeting hall, near the edge of Lavaca Bay in a tiny Gulf Coast town, where about 100 people took their seats one evening last month for a discussion with state authorities.
A panel of technical experts from Texas’ environmental regulator had traveled 150 miles from the capital in Austin to talk about industrial wastewater discharges from the sprawling conglomeration of petrochemical infrastructure that loomed across the water, Formosa Plastics’ Point Comfort complex.
The regulator, the Texas Commission on Environmental Quality, had proposed a regular renewal of Formosa’s discharge permit, so agency representatives came to take questions and comments from the public.
A silver-haired former supervisor at Formosa, Ronnie Hamrick, stepped up to the microphone.
“Why are y’all sitting here saying that you’re going to renew their permit?” he asked indignantly. “You know what they’re doing!”
Hamrick, standing in a baseball cap, jeans and camouflage Crocs, had sacrificed mightily to make sure of it. He had gathered much of the evidence that convinced a federal judge, in 2019, that the Taiwanese plastics giant had chronically violated its wastewater permit for decades, releasing vast amounts of polyethylene pellets and PVC powder into Lavaca Bay.
Hamrick played a critical role in the landmark lawsuit led by one of the most acclaimed environmentalists in Texas, Diane Wilson, who continues to lead campaigns against petrochemical giants on this rural stretch of coastline.
The lawsuit against Formosa led to a $50 million settlement, the largest ever awarded in a citizen lawsuit under the Clean Water Act. In it, Formosa committed to zero discharge of powder or pellets from Point Comfort—the first prohibition on release of plastic material from any plastics manufacturing complex in the world.
But fighting against Formosa cost Hamrick most of his friends and family. It even got him kicked out of church.
Despite what he lost, Hamrick felt that achievement helped redeem him for the 25 years he spent at the plant, and made up for some of the damage he feels he suffered to his central nervous system as a result.
But since the settlement took effect in 2021, records showed, Formosa never stopped releasing plastic and had paid an additional $48 million in penalties into an environmental trust fund under the settlement as a result. Still, TCEQ declined to press the issue earlier this year when it issued its draft permit renewal for Formosa that did not include a ban on plastics discharge.
“They’re still doing it!” Hamrick told the panel of TCEQ staff in Port Lavaca. “We’ve got the proof!”
The meeting moderator interjected. Unless Hamrick had another question, she said, they’d move on to the next speaker. Hamrick tossed his hands up in exasperation and walked back to his seat.
Luke Metzger, executive director of Environment Texas, a nonprofit in Austin, took the microphone. TCEQ had included the zero discharge standard in earlier drafts of Formosa’s wastewater permits, he said. He had obtained documents through records requests showing the regulation in internal TCEQ documents in 2023 and 2025.
“There will be zero (0) discharge of Plastics from Formosa’s Point Comfort Plant,” said a recommendation issued by the TCEQ executive director in June 2025 for the 140-page wastewater permit. But the TCEQ’s final draft, released to the public in March 2026, didn’t include that language.
“Why the 180?” Metzger asked. “Y’all reversed your decision.”
“That provision in the earlier draft permits was more or less put in there as a placeholder,” replied the permit’s lead writer, Michael Sunderlin, a 34-year writer of industrial wastewater permits.
“Our management reviewed it and made a determination that we really could not be in a position to enforce that,” he said. “It also could set a dangerous precedent that we would have to start putting that in other permits.”
Almost a dozen enormous plastics manufacturers operate complexes along the Gulf Coast of Texas, and Formosa isn’t the only one that lets large volumes of plastic waste wash into the sea. Enacting a prohibition here could put the TCEQ under pressure to impose the same rule elsewhere.
Instead, Formosa’ permit would authorize 3,110 pounds per day of plastic particle discharge from its main wastewater outfall and “trace amounts” from the other eight, along with scores of other chemicals. (Although, if such discharges continued under a new permit, Formosa would still have to pay penalties into the trust fund under the lawsuit settlement).
“Steady and Persistent”
Hamrick, listening from the audience with folded arms, wondered how much these experts from Austin really knew about Formosa’s facility. Not many people knew it like he did.
Hamrick, a 1973 graduate of Port Lavaca High School, worked on a construction crew that built the first plants of the complex. Hamrick went to work there the day it opened, then spent two decades as a shift supervisor in a PVC unit of the complex’s vinyl chloride plant.
After he quit, in 2005, he joined the resistance that was led by Diane Wilson, the shrimper woman, an environmentalist and notorious local agitator. For three years, Hamrick had spent most of his days skipping and wading around the beaches and marshlands of the bay system, collecting plastic pellets and powder as evidence in support of Wilson’s 2019 landmark lawsuit against Formosa.
Hamrick got to know the outfalls where wastewater and stormwater runoff washed vast volumes of plastics out of Formosa while he volunteered with a small team of other former chemical plant workers.
“He was by far the most steady and persistent,” Wilson later said in an interview. “And he’s got pure hell for doing it.”

From our collaborating partner Living on Earth, public radio’s environmental news magazine, an interview by producer Aynsley O’Neill with Nathaniel Stinnett of the Environmental Voter Project.
With late word from Alaska, Democrats now have 56 seats in the US Senate. And while climate was not on the ballot directly, many campaigned on climate-adjacent issues like utility affordability and high gas prices.
In a September survey, the Environmental Voter Project found voters in battleground states want politicians to spend more time talking about climate change—not less. That challenges the wisdom of what’s been called “climate hushing,” or keeping climate out of political campaigns, and offers insight into how climate might play out in the 2028 presidential primaries.
Nathaniel Stinnett is the founder and executive director of the Environmental Voter Project. This interview has been edited for length and clarity.
AYNSLEY O’NEILL: Tell us a little bit about the organization that you founded, the Environmental Voter Project. What is your goal here?
NATHANIEL STINNETT: Our goal is to get millions of people who care deeply about climate and the environment who aren’t voting to start voting more often. At the end of the day, the only way we’re going to get good climate policy is if voters force politicians to lead on climate.
We’ve identified tens of millions of people who care deeply about climate and the environment who don’t vote, and they are disproportionately young. They’re disproportionately people of color, and they’re disproportionately lower income. I know that goes against many of the stereotypes that people have. I think a lot of people think of environmentalists as sort of driving around in a Prius wearing a fleece or something like that, but it’s not. We’re seeing that a Latina teenager living in Arizona is just as likely to care deeply about climate and the environment as some hipster living in Brooklyn is.
O’NEILL: In November’s midterms, I’m sure there were plenty of voters who wouldn’t necessarily rank the environment as their number one issue, but they probably cast their ballot with things like data center development and high gas prices in mind. Tell us more about how these issues manifested in this election.
STINNETT: You’re right. It isn’t like the words “climate change” were on everybody’s lips this year. They clearly weren’t. However, if you look at exit polling data, it is very clear that voters are extraordinarily concerned about gas and diesel prices. We saw that 87 percent of voters said that they were either very or somewhat concerned about the cost of gas and diesel. And obviously, if you transition away from fossil fuels, you’re not going to have those worries.
Similarly, 86 percent were very or somewhat concerned about the cost of utilities. Well over three-quarters of voters said that AI and data centers were a significant concern of theirs when they voted. So yeah, climate change wasn’t at the front of everybody’s mind, but these climate-aligned or climate-adjacent issues were.
O’NEILL: We’ll definitely give you some credit for getting some of those voters out to the polls. But if you had to guess, what all came together to get environmental voters so fired up for this particular midterms?
STINNETT: It was a perfect storm. Thank you for giving the Environmental Voter Project some credit, but the truth is, I don’t think anything was going to stop this historic wave election. I think a huge part of it was certainly anti-Donald Trump sentiment. Even in the reddest of red states, people were sick of the president. When you combine that with him not being on the ballot, so he couldn’t drive the people who love him to the polls, the haters still showed up. Boy, did it make it hard for any Republican who was running for office to keep their head above water. This was just a historic election.
O’NEILL: I want to talk about one of these major pieces of history in Texas, where Democrats had a very surprising series of victories for a very deep red state: James Talarico in the Senate, Gina Hinojosa in the governorship. To what extent would you say that environment was on the ballot in Texas, even if not explicitly?
STINNETT: We need to be very careful and honest about claiming that climate and the environment drove people to vote in any state this year. It was not a top voter priority. It was kind of in the middle of the pack. But what we do know is that voters in Texas are very concerned about climate and environmental issues, and the fact that Democrats swept every statewide office and won with such margins that many races were decided before the sun even rose on election day. James Talarico is a perfect example of this. He won his U.S. Senate race by so much that he amassed more early votes than his Republican opponent got in total votes. He won before election day even dawned.
This new crop of Democratic politicians, who are typically more likely to lead on climate and environmental issues anyway, are going to look at this data and see how many of their supporters care about climate and the environment. It’s a real opportunity for a state that is at the very center of how we make energy and electricity in the United States.

Negotiations at the COP31 UN climate summit in Turkey are in deadlock, having run through the night, as countries remain unable to agree on a new global climate deal.
In a late intervention on Friday, a group of countries led by France and Panama pushed back against the draft agreement which included no reference to reducing the world's demand for fossil fuels.
Separately, the Africa Group are fighting to get commitments on more money for adaptation, saying they did not come to the COP "to beg".
A new and potentially final agreement is expected to be published on Saturday.
Ministers from island states, Panama, and a strong contingent of EU nations which include Spain, France, Belgium, Sweden and Finland have said they are pushing to get a commitment to move away from oil, gas and coal back into the final agreement after fossil fuel producers led by Saudi pushed for its removal.
"It is not acceptable to have a COP or a cover decision that does not even mention fossil fuels and we simply will not put up with it," said Juan Carlos Navarro, Panama's minister for the environment.
His words were echoed by France's Minister of Ecological Transition Monique Barbut.
She took aim at several references in the text to carbon capture, use and storage - the technology that takes emissions when they are released and stores them underground - as a licence for other countries to keep burning oil and gas.
"We cannot be announcing to the world that we are now getting to 1.5 increase in the temperature and do business like nothing was happening," said France's Minister of Ecological Transition Monique Barbut.
For the first time at a COP the agreement - known officially as the Antalya Accords - acknowledges that the goal of keeping global temperature rise below 1.5C has been missed.
The world is entering a period called "overshoot".
Beyond this point scientists warn, external that millions more people will be exposed to sea level rise and extreme heat.
The BBC understands that a number of other EU nations were asked to join the rebellion but declined, considering it unhelpful to negotiations.
Although one lead negotiator said he sympathised: "How can you have a climate agreement with no mention of the cause."
But Chris Bowen, Australia's climate change and energy minister who is leading negotiations, pushed back.
He argued that this summit was about implementation, and should focus on the move towards clean energy sources.
Away from COP, renewable energy is growing at unprecedented rates. For the first time this year a modern renewable source - solar panels - contributed the largest share of global energy demand growth, outstripping oil and gas, external.
The International Energy Agency also warned this week that the longer disruption to fuel supplies through the Strait of Hormuz due to the Iran War, the stronger the incentive to switch to electricity powered by renewables.
Although this week US President Donald Trump, Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin agreed at a meeting in Shenzhen to increase oil production in the face of fuel supply disruption.
The 'worst' COP ever?
It is understood that one proposal is to keep fossil fuels off the table in exchange for Saudi Arabia and other petro-states signing up to a pledge for 35% of their energy consumption to come from electricity by 2035.
This does not solve one of the other key issues raised by developing nations - the lack of money.
Earlier versions of the text included an agreement to ramp up money for adaptation to $120bn by 2035 - that has now been removed.
"We did not come here to beg we came here to claim what is rightfully ours for our people who are suffering the brunt of anthropogenic activities of developed countries," said Zanetor Agyeman Rawlings, Ghana's Environment Minister and chair of the African Group of negotiators.
Climate activists and environmental groups, who are observers to these talks, have slammed negotiations.
"I can tell you without any doubt that this has been the worst COP ever," said Mohamed Adow of Powershift Africa.
These groups are normally highly critical of the process for not moving fast enough. But it seems that Turkey have been particularly unpopular as hosts after their lead negotiator walked out of some crucial negotiations leaving many countries feeling "disrespected" said one observer.

A deal agreed between the UK and the European Union on Friday will come into force regardless of whether the two sides can negotiate a separate tuition fees agreement, Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband has told the BBC.
The measures agreed in Brussels include scrapping most checks on British food exports in return for the UK following some EU regulations from 2028, and a new youth mobility scheme.
However, a proposal from the bloc to lower the level of tuition fees paid by EU students in the UK has not been agreed.
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said she was "confident" a solution would be found, with Prime Minister Andy Burnham adding "me too" during a press conference announcing the deal.
Meanwhile, asked in his interview with the BBC's Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg programme whether rejoining the EU would be looked at, Miliband said "all the options will be on the table".
It came after the prime minister said that he would discuss possible ideas for even closer ties with the bloc in the coming months.
UK and EU leaders have hailed the closer cooperation agreement, with Burnham calling the deal a "win-win" that could lower the cost of living and reduce red tape.
The prime minister said the Treasury believes the deal could boost the UK economy by up to Â£17bn a year.
EU sources had earlier suggested that the bloc might hold up applying the wider deal until it was agreed that EU students who wanted to study in the UK would pay the same fees as British students.
Miliband said it was "absolutely clear" the agreements on food exports, energy and youth mobility would apply, even though there has not been a deal on tuition fees.
"President von der Leyen... was very clear about this at the press conference we just had. She said there are those three agreements and then there's a separate piece of paper and a separate issue, which is looking at the issue of tuition," he said.
Asked again whether the agreements would definitely become law, the foreign secretary said: "Yes, absolutely."
"The dates are set out in 2028 when these things are coming in, we're introducing legislation in Parliament, so definitely."
Miliband said there would be "no cost" to the UK taxpayer for anything agreed at Friday's summit, adding that there would be no new contributions to the EU budget.
He said previously announced agreements on EU schemes like Erasmus+ were a "separate decision" and the summit "was not about cost to the taxpayer".
Speaking on Friday, Burnham argued that polling suggests the UK public "want closer ties" with the EU and the deal "delivers that".
Miliband told the BBC that "of course all the options will be on the table" when pressed on whether rejoining the bloc would be considered, adding that "we will look at the benefits and the costs of all the different options".
He said that while he accepted the result of the 2016 Brexit referendum, "the world has changed massively".
"Europe is changing too, so we've got to look at what that means. It's not about this parliament, we're respecting the red lines in this parliament," he added.
Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch said the deal was "not fair", arguing that UK farmers would have to follow rules set in Brussels and young people from the EU would "compete" with young Britons struggling to get jobs at home.
She also claimed Burnham had "plucked" the Â£17bn figure out of thin air, and said the only modelling she had seen of how the agreement could boost the economy put the figure at "0.0%".
Reform UK leader Nigel Farage said Friday marked a "betrayal of the British people" and a good day for the EU to "try and humiliate" the UK.
Farage, who was a leading figure in the 2016 campaign to get Britain out of the EU, wrote on social media: "Like every prime minister before him, Burnham is a total fraud."
Liberal Democrat leader Sir Ed Davey said there needed to be more than "tweaks" to the UK's relationship to the EU.
"A youth mobility scheme is a big step forward, but it's nowhere near enough. We need a whole new deal that actually works for Britain, and fast."
Speaking to BBC Radio 4's Today programme, the University of Manchester's vice chancellor Professor Duncan Ivison said closer UK-EU relations were a "good thing" but "the issue of tuition fees is something we do have to figure out because there is a cost".
He warned that EU students being allowed to pay domestic university fees would "take Â£500m, we estimate, out of the higher education sector at a time where there's a lot of pressure on the sector".
He added: "If EU students come and are paying domestic fees, it's not clear we'd be able to increase the number of places for EU students anyway."
Environment Secretary Dame Angela Eagle said the Treasury and Department for Education would work with universities to find a solution during negotiations.
She told BBC Breakfast: "I don't think anybody wants to do deals that negatively impact anything. We want win-win deals."

The FBI is investigating an apparent breach of its criminal information database, US media report citing two people briefed on the issue.
The National Crime Information Center (NCIC) database is used by federal and local law enforcement to share information on warrants and background checks. The BBC has contacted the FBI for comment.
This comes after string of tech outages which hit banking, air traffic control and other sectors in the US last week. Officials have said they were not caused by cyberattacks - but the blackouts have sparked scrutiny from lawmakers.
White House National Cyber Director Sean Cairncross was fired this week, with US President Donald Trump saying he was not good enough.
It would not be the first time hackers have targeted the FBI, the domestic intelligence and security service of the US.
In September, the FBI said it was investigating an apparent breach by a cyber-crime group ShinyHunters, which claimed it had stolen sensitive information on all bureau staff - around 38,000 people.
After that hack, one former FBI agent told the BBC he feared for the safety of current employees, whose personal information could soon become available online to criminals and hostile nation-state hackers.
In a separate development, NBC reported an apparent cyberattack against the US Department of Agriculture (USDA) .
Employees were informed on Thursday that its farm payment system had been targeted, NBC said.
The USDA has not publicly commented on the issue.

Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky has said Vladimir Putin is a "killer" in response to Donald Trump referring to the Russian leader as his "friend" in China this week.
Speaking to CNN, Zelensky said it was up to the US president "how to call Putin" but "for us, he is an enemy... for us, he's a killer".
Before Thursday's historic trilateral meeting with Chinese leader Xi Jinping and Putin, Trump called Putin his "friend" and said the two leaders have had a "great relationship for many years".
Russian attacks continued overnight, with two people killed, including a boy, and 52 injured in missile and drone strikes on Zelensky's hometown of Kryvyi Rih in the central Dnipropetrovsk region, officials said.
Ukraine's state emergency service DSNS said 11 people were also injured in the north-eastern Kharkiv region, and one person in Rivne, in the north-west.
On Friday, at least nine people were killed in Russian strikes targeting bridges in the capital Kyiv and railway stations in western Ukraine - with Zelensky calling the attack the "biggest this year" after an onslaught of 110 missiles, including 27 ballistic, and more than 400 drones.
The strikes came days after Ukraine had badly damaged the Crimean Bridge.
Hours after Friday's strikes on Ukraine, Trump told reporters at the White House that Putin would "love to end the war".
"They [Zelensky and Putin] both want to end it and it's a very good thing I have a relationship," he said on Friday.
Trump also doubled down on his description of the Russian leader as a friend but said he "can't speak" to whether Putin is a friend to the US.
However Zelensky said despite Trump's stance, he saw Putin as "a killer".
"I think mostly for the people in the world, he is a killer because he's killing - by the way- he's killing each day and night," he told CNN.
Zelensky also said speaking about Putin like he was a "friend" meant "he doesn't feel enough pressure".
The war of words came as neighbouring Poland said a Russian cruise missile was among three objects that violated its airspace in the south-east of the country early on Friday.
Polish Defence Minister WÅadysÅaw Kosiniak-Kamysz said the missile hit a rural area at Nowy Lipowiec about 50km (31 miles) from the Ukrainian border.
This was about 100km from where European troops - from 11 of the 36 member nations of the coalition of the willing - were completing a training exercise, Polish authorities said. Another cruise missile and a jet-powered drone were suspected to have hit two other locations, they added.
On Saturday, Polish Foreign Minister RadosÅaw Sikorski told the BBC the cruise missiles had guidance systems, so "it is very unlikely that they veered off course as a result of Ukrainian electronic warfare".
"This is a war in Europe that affects our security," he told Radio 4's Today programme, also referencing similar incidents in recent months across Europe.
Nobody was hurt and no damage has been reported, but Warsaw described the incident as a "provocation" from Moscow.
Nato Secretary General Mark Rutte condemned "grave violations of Polish airspace" and said the military alliance had scrambled its jets in response.
Russia has made no comment about the violations, which took place during Friday's massive attack on Ukraine.
Putin launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.

This year's Trafalgar Square Christmas tree has been cut down in a forest outside Oslo, ready to begin its journey to London.
The 21m (69ft) tree, nicknamed Jolly Cheery, is about 75 years old. It was felled on Friday by the Lord Mayor of Westminster, Karen Scarborough, and the Mayor of Oslo, Anne Lindboe.
Norway has sent a tree to the capital every year since 1947 as a thank you for Britain's support during World War Two, when King Haakon VII and the Norwegian government lived in exile in London.
Its lights will be switched on by the two mayors at a ceremony in the square on Thursday, 3 December.
Scarborough said: "It's my greatest honour to take part in this wonderful tradition for both the cities of Oslo and London.
"This tree is a powerful symbol of friendship and peace, reminding us to be there for one another during the festive period."
Scarborough thanked "the people of Oslo and Norway for this truly fabulous gift" and added: "With the care and dedication of the team, I'm sure it will look magnificent on Trafalgar Square."
Lindboe said: "Oslo has been sending a Christmas tree to London for almost eight decades, and every year we send a tree across the North Sea with the same message: we have not forgotten.
"The tradition has a powerful history, and its message remains just as relevant today.
"I hope Jolly Cheery spreads warmth and Christmas cheer to everyone who passes by, and reminds us how much it means to be there for one another, especially in difficult times."
For the second year running, the tree was chosen with the help of a social media poll.
Organisers said it would travel by road in Norway and England using only electric and biodiesel vehicles, cutting the journey's carbon footprint by 80%. It will cross the North Sea on a regular cargo ship from the port of Brevik.
Once in London, it will be decorated in the traditional Norwegian style, with 25m strings of festoon lighting fitted with energy-efficient bulbs.

A jury in Los Angeles has found a 30-year-old man guilty of starting one of the most destructive wildfires in California's history.
Jonathan Rinderknecht was convicted of arson after starting the fires that swept through Pacific Palisades and parts of Malibu in January last year, killing 12 people and destroying more than 6,800 buildings in the US state.
The conviction was handed down nearly five months after deadlocked jurors led to the judge declaring a mistrial.
Rinderknecht, who had pleaded not guilty, was convicted of two federal charges. He is due to be sentenced on 17 March when he faces between five and 20 years in prison on each charge.
Rinderknecht was found guilty of lighting a fire on 1 January last year which burned undetected deep in root systems before flaring back up six days later.
One of the charges was for starting the original brush fire, while the other centred on the damage caused when it reignited into a catastrophic blaze.
"We were determined to hold him accountable, and today's guilty verdict delivers a measure of justice for the families who lost loved ones and the thousands whose lives were upended," said Bill Essayli, who leads the US Attorney's Office for the Central District of California.
Rinderknecht is a Los Angeles resident and former ride-share delivery driver.
Defence attorney Steve Haney had argued at trial that prosecutors lacked sufficient physical evidence or records to prove their case.
Lawyers for the defendant said they were "disappointed" by the verdict but respected the jury's decision.
Los Angeles Mayor Karen Bass, who was widely criticised for her handling of the fires, said in a statement that "no verdict can bring back the lives lost or erase the pain families have endured".
"So many are still struggling to rebuild," she said. "For those still displaced, the devastation remains a daily reality."
Prosecutors had argued that Rinderknecht was driven by revenge, anger and loneliness because he had nowhere to go for the holiday.
They cited geolocation data from his iPhone, security camera footage that showed his car's location and witness testimony from passengers.
They alleged that Rinderknecht had a "deeply entrenched belief that the wealthy were destroying the world" and in turn purposely started the blaze in the affluent neighbourhood.
The fire was one of several that ignited back-to-back across the LA region in January, which in total left 31 people dead and destroyed 16,000 structures.

A Missouri judge on Friday approved a $7.25bn (Â£5.5bn) settlement stemming from lawsuits â alleging that Bayer's weedkiller Roundup causes cancer.
Judge Timothy Boyer said the settlement was "fair, reasonable, and adequate".
Bayer, the German bio-tech giant, had proposed paying the $7.25bn to definitively resolve a legal battle in the US.
The nationwide settlement will be paid to Roundup users who are already sick with non-Hodgkin lymphoma and those who fall ill in the future.
The company had already paid roughly $10bn to resolve litigation related to Roundup.
The settlements to participants range from $10,000 to $165,000, depending on how frequently they used the product, when they were diagnosed with the cancer and how severe their illness was.
Bayer will make annual payments into a fund for up to 21 years, providing as much as $7.25bn.
Some attorneys had objected to the settlement funds, arguing they were not enough, but the judge said he did not want to delay payouts to sick victims.
Bayer denies that its Roundup product causes cancer.
The settlement comes after the Supreme Court in June ruled in favour of Bayer, overturning a $1.25m settlement for a Missouri man who said Roundup and its ingredient glyphosate was to blame for his non-Hodgkin lymphoma.
The court ruled 7-2, saying Bayer cannot be sued in state courts because federal regulations do not mandate a cancer warning label.
The company has faced thousands of claims in US state and federal courts from people alleging they developed cancer after using the product.
Roundup was developed by Monsanto in the 1970s. Its active ingredient, glyphosate, was identified by the International Agency for Research on Cancer, a unit of the World Health Organization in 2015 as a probable human carcinogen.
Bayer and some other regulators, including the US Environmental Protection Agency, have disputed those findings.
But the issue has forced the company through years of costly litigation in the US, as juries in several states opt to award billions of dollars to users of the herbicide.

Nepal Prime Minister Balendra Shah's visit to India has raised hopes of a reset, marking the first high-level engagement between leaders of Nepal's new political generation and its giant neighbour.
It is Shah's first bilateral visit since his Rastriya Swatantra Party (RSP) swept to power in March, six months after a Gen Z uprising against corruption and nepotism toppled K P Sharma Oli's government.
The 36-year-old rapper-turned-politician arrives in Delhi on Sunday for a two-day visit, during which he will meet his Indian counterpart Narendra Modi and other senior officials.
The talks are expected to cover a broad range of issues, including economic and energy cooperation, the opening of new air corridors, and a reconstruction assistance package following the devastating flash floods that struck Nepal in August.
The disaster killed more than 1,450 in the Himalayan nation, while thousands remain missing and unaccounted for.
India and Nepal share close ethnic, cultural, religious and economic ties, with a largely open border stretching more than 1,750km (1,080 miles).
Wedged between India and China, Nepal is a strategic buffer and, analysts say, its stability has direct implications for India's security.
But over the decades the relationship has been strained by territorial disputes, allegations of political interference and resentment over what many in Nepal see as the dominant 'Big Brother' attitude of Delhi.
Nevertheless, analysts see Shah's visit as an opportunity for a reset.
"The new Nepali leadership says they do not have the political baggage of the past and they want to focus on development, diplomacy and economic partnership," Ranjit Rae, a former Indian ambassador to Nepal tells BBC.
"They seem to be more pragmatic, less ideological. I personally feel it's an optimistic moment," he adds.
Since Nepal abolished monarchy and became a democratic republic in 2008 three political parties dominated the governance.
Delhi has maintained close contacts with all of them â the Communist Party of Nepal (CPN â UML), the Nepali Congress and the Communist Party of Nepal (Maoist Centre).
Nepal's communist parties were seen as closer to India's rival China, owing to ideological ties, and often criticised Delhi over what they viewed as unequal bilateral agreements.
Due to Nepal's strategic location, both Delhi and Beijing compete for influence in Kathmandu, leading to accusations the two Asian giants are meddling in the internal affairs of Nepal.
But Nepal's ties with India extend beyond diplomacy and strategic interests.
The Hindu-majority nations share deep social ties, with families straddling the open border and communities interacting daily.
Bilateral trade exceeds $9bn, heavily skewed in India's favour - a longstanding source of resentment in Kathmandu. India is also Nepal's main supplier of petroleum products and several food items, and a key transit route for its trade with the rest of the world.
One key area of co-operation is hydropower. India has approved projects to import up to 1,200MW of electricity from Nepal and is looking to expand imports further.
"India has a huge demand for electricity and Nepal has the potential to generate due to its water resources and geography. It's not just bilateral, Nepal also exports electricity to Bangladesh via India," says Rae.
India has often been among the first countries to assist Nepal during major natural disasters, including the 2015 earthquake and the flash floods in August this year.
Despite the close links, Nepal and India have their differences.
In 2019, Nepal was furious after India published a map that included areas claimed by Kathmandu, in a western region close to the border with China, as part of its territory. That raised heightened awareness in Kathmandu about the region.
The diplomatic wrangle escalated after Nepal published its own map which included those disputed areas.
"I hope Nepal's prime minister raises the border issue with Delhi this time. There may not be a resolution immediately, but they should start negotiations to settle the issue," Kanak Mani Dixit, a veteran Nepali political analyst, told the BBC.
Nepal has also long urged India to open additional air entry routes, allowing large aircraft to fly in from the west to its new airports at Bhairahawa, near the Buddhist holy site of Lumbini, and Pokhara, a major tourist destination.
Access to Indian airspace would mean shorter flights at lower cost and, with more flights, the airports would become commercially viable.
Some in Nepal also believe that Delhi is wary of the fact that the Gautam Buddha international airport was constructed by China's Northwest Civil Aviation Airport and the airport in Pokhara was built with Chinese financial assistance.
Shah has yet to make any overtures to Beijing, but sent a 20-member delegation of party MPs to China for an 11-day visit from 15 November, ahead of his trip to India - seen as an effort to balance ties with Nepal's two powerful neighbours.
Shah had pledged not to travel abroad during his first year in office, but devastating flash floods in August have changed the calculus.
His government estimates reconstruction will cost nearly $5bn, while international aid pledged so far has fallen short of expectations.
But some observers in Nepal believe that Shah's preparations for the high-stake India visit have been less than thorough.
"Prime Minister Shah and his advisors are young and fresh, but they do lack experience. Repeatedly they have exhibited a lack of gravitas in governance, which would be essential for diplomacy with an overwhelmingly powerful neighbour," says Dixit.
Shah is already facing criticism over some of his government's recent decisions, including to remove police chief Dan Bahadur from his post after he allegedly refused to comply with directives from the Prime Minister's office.

Cooper, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/trump-auditions-potential-successors-as-rubio-and-vance-join-him-for-white-house-briefing Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Trump auditions potential successors as Rubio and Vance join him for White House briefing Politics Nov 21, 2026 12:32 PM EST Marco Rubio fidgeted and sighed. JD Vance smiled and furrowed his brow. For 90 minutes on Friday, the secretary of state and the vice president, both potential 2028 presidential contenders, stood nearly shoulder to shoulder in matching outfits, an arm's length from President Donald Trump as he spoke to reporters crowded into the White House press briefing room. WATCH: What Trump addressed during his lengthy White House news conference It was the latest episode in the public audition that the president and former reality television star has appeared to delight in arranging for his potential successors as he nears his last two years in office. In the same room months earlier, Rubio and Vance each took a turn defending the president and selling his agenda while filling in as White House press secretary. The president has also been known to quiz his public and private audiences on their opinions of the two men. Educate your inbox Subscribe to Here’s the Deal, our politics newsletter for analysis you won’t find anywhere else. Enter your email address Subscribe Form error message goes here. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. Vance and Rubio maintain that they're good friends and have both demurred about whether they'll seek the White House in the next presidential race. Rubio has said he won't run if Vance does. Even so, the race to succeed Trump as the GOP nominee is quietly heating up, with Vance and Rubio widely seen as some of the likeliest contenders. Rubio and Vance get a turn in the spotlight One by one, Trump called them to the lectern, turning his gaze from them to the audience as he surveyed how each of their remarks landed with the dozens of journalists in the room. Vance went first. He explained that it was in his job description to stay in Washington while Trump, Rubio and others were on the other side of the world for international summits in the Philippines and China. Vance said he had to "stay back and hold down the fort," like the movie "Home Alone," but "with better food and more gold" at the White House. "So, I missed you, sir," Vance said before shifting into lauding Trump's economic leadership. Trump said Vance's statement distancing himself from the war in Iran and blaming it for the GOP's midterm losses was "fine" and "accurate." Notably, Vance passed on an opportunity to say the Iran war was worth the political costs. WATCH: Trump hosts news conference after meeting with Xi, Putin "I think the president is the one who makes the decision, and the president has said he would do it again," Vance said. As Trump spoke, Vance laughed at his jokes but stood mostly still, hands clasped in front of himself with a serious expression on his face. Rubio, by contrast, fidgeted behind Trump, turning from side to side and adjusting his tie. At one point, he pulled a note out of his breast pocket to review it. When Rubio took the microphone, he spoke in his typical rapid-fire clip as he recapped Trump's Asia trip and forcefully defended Trump's decision to meet the authoritarian leaders of China and Russia. His tone suggested irritation at a question that nobody asked. "If these leaders can't get along and can't engage with one another and don't have a positive relationship, it is impossible to get anything good done for the country and the safety of the world," Rubio said. It was a show of symmetrical endurance It wasn't just a rhetorical showcase. It was also a display of stamina. When the president delivers the State of the Union address each winter, the House speaker and vice president flank him, their faces on camera the entire time. But at least they get to sit. On Friday, Vance and Rubio stood behind Trump for the entire hour-and-a-half he was in the briefing room, an appearance that lasted longer than nearly every State of the Union speech on record. There's no doubt they were both keenly aware that they were on camera the whole time. Both men wore navy blue suits with white shirts and red ties that created, intentionally or not, a symmetrical backdrop for the president, aside from Vance's advantage in height. The most obvious difference in their dress was the flag pins on their lapels; Rubio's was rectangular, just the stars and stripes, while Vance's pin had the flag swaying on a pole. Trump has declined to anoint a successor Even after the GOP was thrashed in midterm elections that were widely seen as a repudiation of Trump, the president continues to enjoy deep support from the Republican base. His endorsement is likely to carry considerable sway among 2028 primary voters. Trump has praised both men and suggested they might be running mates, declining to elevate one over the other. He again avoided the question on Friday, when a journalist asked which of them he thinks would make a better president. "Oh, let me give you the answer to that," Trump deadpanned. The reporter moved on to his next question. WATCH: After calling Putin his friend, Trump 'can't speak to' whether Putin is a friend to America At the end of the briefing, Trump called up his new chief of staff, Stephen Miller, who showered Trump in praise and ran through a laundry list of accomplishments. When he was done, the president threw a jab at Vance and Rubio. "We have breaking news — he was better than these two guys," Trump said. Turning to Miller, he joked: "Do you want to run for president?" Cooper reported from Phoenix. Associated Press reporters Darlene Superville, Bill Barrow and Ali Swenson contributed. c28bb0d61a90.text: By — Suzan Fraser, Associated Press Suzan Fraser, Associated Press By — Seth Borenstein, Associated Press Seth Borenstein, Associated Press By — Anton L. Delgado, Associated Press Anton L. Delgado, Associated Press By — Sibi Arasu, Associated Press Sibi Arasu, Associated Press By — Victoria Milko, Associated Press Victoria Milko, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/climate-talks-in-overtime-as-nations-wrestle-with-response-to-worsening-global-warming Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Climate talks in overtime as nations wrestle with response to worsening global warming World Nov 21, 2026 12:03 PM EST ANTALYA, Turkey (AP) — Work crews boxed up the venue for this year's United Nations climate talks in Turkey, as negotiators went into overtime on Saturday in an attempt to reach a final agreement on global warming. But hopes are slim that additional discussions will produce concrete plans to slash fossil fuel use. The added day of talks came as the two-week annual summit, or COP31, drew strong condemnation for failing to mention fossil fuels in a draft of the final agreement. The document is meant to address how the world will deal with climate change, which drives heat waves, floods and other disasters. To avert the most catastrophic effects of warming, experts said the world needs to urgently and drastically cut emissions from the use of coal, oil and gas. READ MORE: Activists, leaders criticize COP31 climate talks as fossil fuels go unmentioned in draft deal In a letter sent on Saturday to this year's co-hosts, Turkey and Australia, 100 civil society groups warned that they were "on course to preside over one of the most disappointing COPs" the U.N. has ever held. The letter stated there were only hours left "to save this COP from becoming a low point of three decades of climate negotiations." In the lead-up to these talks, the U.N. announced that the world will likely blow past the 2015 Paris Agreement goal of limiting warming to 1.5 degrees Celsius (2.7 degrees Fahrenheit) above pre-industrial temperatures. "No one knows what is happening behind closed doors, or what the outcome of COP31 will be," said Teresa Anderson, global lead on climate justice at ActionAid International. Climate talks enter overtime Inside an area of the COP31 venue known as the pavilions, where countries showcased innovations and hosted panels, workers were seen packing up electronics and boxing up belongings on Saturday. The hallways, previously bustling with tens of thousands of participants, stood largely empty, with only a handful of security guards seen taking photos by deserted pavilions. "COP31 is in a bleak overtime, with dwindling food and water, and no sign of any progress since the alarmingly underwhelming texts we saw earlier," said Rachel Cleetus of the Union of Concerned Scientists, who is at the venue in the Mediterranean coastal city of Antalya. Earlier during the summit, the nonprofit Climate Action Tracker warned that progress on slowing global warming has stalled for the past five years, even as disasters — including this year's heat waves in Europe and flooding in Nepal — become more deadly. READ MORE: UN chief says 'immediate and drastic' emissions cuts needed to avert climate change catastrophe Countries most vulnerable to climate change, including small island nations whose lands are battered by rising seas, also say wealthy nations that caused the climate crisis must contribute more to U.N. funds to help them recover from disasters and adapt to a warmer world. "Every year there seems to be a greater discontent, a mistrust and frustration for civil society, indigenous people and countries that are more climate vulnerable," said Tuvalu's Minister of Environment Maina Talia, during a Saturday press conference. "I am still holding the line, trying to be very optimistic until we see the text," he said. The United States, a major polluter and the world's largest economy, did not participate directly in this year's talks. The next climate summit will take place in Ethiopia's capital, Addis Ababa, in November 2027. Criticism of COP31 grows On Friday, a protester wearing a red noose around his neck and a vest emblazoned with the slogan "you are killing the future" interrupted official proceedings by clambering onto a table and shouting: "You take out fossil fuels. You killed 1.5. There is no money. Just kill me now. The Global South cannot wait." The Global South isn't a geographical term, but a reference to developing countries in general. As the protester was escorted out by security, he shouted: "You keep doing nothing at all. Nothing at all. Kill me now. Kill me now." READ MORE: At UN climate talks, 5 nations back plan to double rooftop solar panels by 2030 The demonstration interrupted Turkey's Minister of Environment and COP31 co-president Murat Kurum, who said "let's try to maintain the peace in the room" before continuing with his scheduled remarks. "Yesterday, of course, this place was buzzing and today it's nearly empty. But all the key negotiators are here, civil society is here, watching the negotiations," said Harjeet Singh, a strategic adviser to the Fossil Fuel Treaty Initiative, who has attended 18 climate summits. "We are still stuck with many, many disagreements and nobody knows how long this will go on," he said. Borenstein reported from Kensington, Maryland, Delgado from Bangkok, Arasu from Bengaluru, India, and Milko from Islamabad, Pakistan. Associated Press journalist Tammy Webber contributed from Fenton, Michigan. The Associated Press' climate and environmental coverage receives financial support from multiple private foundations. 8e31919b700f.text: President Trump said Saturday he'd gladly work with Democrats to cap interest and fees on credit cards , arguing that card companies simply make too much money now. Why it matters: Though some argue capping rates would save consumers billions of dollars a year, the banking industry is equally adamant that it would deny credit to millions of Americans by making lending too risky. Driving the news: Trump, in a Fox News interview Saturday morning, was asked whether a rate cap on cards was something on which he could find common ground with Democrats. Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.), poised to be the new chair of the Senate Banking Committee, is an outspoken advocate for such caps and has recently said she's ready to work with Trump to pass a bill. What they're saying: " I would do it. These credit card companies have made a lot — and the credit card fees that they charge. I'm all into it," Trump said . "I know that some people would say it's not free enterprise. But what's free enterprise when you're sitting home and you get a bill that some guy set up in an office on Park Avenue and they said 'let's charge a fee that's too high.' So I'm all for that," Trump said. "The credit card companies, they're getting too much. The fees are too high and the interests are too high." Context: The credit card industry argues that capping interest rates would reduce the revenue needed to cover losses when borrowers default, prompting lenders to reject more applicants. Reality check: This isn't the first time Trump has said he'd cap card rates. In January, he said on Truth Social he'd set a 10% cap for one year and any lender that didn't comply would face legal consequences. Nothing came of the threat, which credit unions claimed could deprive more than 47 million people of access to cards. Nonetheless, the mere idea was enough to send shares in major card issuers lower, and prompt a full-throated response from the industry. What to watch: As much as both Warren and Trump support the idea, it's not clear how much Democrats will want to prioritize it once they take control of Congress in January.

029f6d229e54.text: By — Ed White, Associated Press Ed White, Associated Press By — Russ Bynum, Associated Press Russ Bynum, Associated Press By — Kim Chandler, Associated Press Kim Chandler, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/nation/texas-says-an-execution-went-as-planned-a-witness-says-screams-showed-tremendous-distress Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Texas says an execution went as planned. A witness says screams showed 'tremendous distress' Nation Nov 21, 2026 11:46 AM EST A Texas official on Friday defended how the state carried out the execution of a 70-year-old man who loudly insisted he was in pain and pleaded, "Don't let me suffer like this," during a lethal injection that followed a struggle to find a suitable vein. Yet Reinaldo Dennes' spiritual adviser, who had his hand on Dennes' shoulder inside the death chamber in Huntsville, said he felt like he was holding a bucking bronco Thursday. WATCH: Christa Pike describes pain after botched execution "Twice he said, 'It's not working. It's not working. It's not going how it's supposed to go. This isn't right.' Those types of words kept coming," said the Rev. Jeff Hood, a death penalty opponent. Dennes was "clearly in tremendous distress," said Hood, who called it torture. It was the ninth execution this year in Texas, which has a long history of using the death penalty as punishment for murder. Executions across the U.S. have garnered more attention since Christa Pike survived two doses of pentobarbital in Tennessee in September. The drug didn't enter her bloodstream correctly. State says execution worked 'as planned' Amanda Hernandez, a spokesperson for the Texas Department of Criminal Justice, said initial attempts to place two IV lines into Dennes' hands and arms were unsuccessful. Dennes was strapped to the gurney at 6:04 p.m. Hernandez said an IV was successfully placed in the left side of his neck 16 minutes later at 6:20 p.m., followed by another line in his left foot at 6:38 p.m. Witnesses, including Hood and an Associated Press reporter, were escorted into the death chamber before Dennes began his final statement at 6:52 p.m. Lethal drugs began flowing less than a minute later, Hernandez said. Almost immediately, Dennes exclaimed: "The pain! Go! Go!" He uttered an expletive and implored "the father" to "take this pain." He subsequently shouted: "My right leg is killing me!" and described it as a cramp. After another profanity, he grunted, then said, "I don't think this is normal. Take me, father. Don't let me suffer like this. C'mon." READ MORE: Alabama executes man for 1991 killings in last of 3 U.S. executions carried out the same day The drugs were stopped at 7:07 p.m., and he was declared dead a minute later, slightly more than an hour after he was restrained in the death chamber, Hernandez said. "We feel that all of our processes and procedures were followed and that it was carried out as planned," she told the AP. Hernandez said she didn't know how many attempts were made to place IV lines. "It's not a race — it's not how quickly can we get this done," she said. "It's something you want to do correctly. There is no normal time limit. It's what it takes for it to be successfully done." In May, Tennessee called off the lethal injection of Tony Carruthers after failing for over an hour to establish an IV line. Idaho, in 2024, tried eight times to establish a line to execute Thomas Creech before stopping. Republican Gov. Brad Little subsequently signed a law making a firing squad the primary method of execution. Advocate says Dennes would not fake pain As for Dennes' claims of extreme pain, Hernandez said the state plans no additional inquiry. She said there were reasons to suspect he was exaggerating, adding that he complained even before the lethal drugs were given and grumbled about pain in a leg that didn't have an IV line. Hernandez said "it makes you wonder" if the high-profile Pike case has influenced death row inmates to act out. "They watch the news. He was aware of the other executions," Hernandez said. Dr. Paul Wax, executive director of the American College of Medical Toxicology, said he couldn't think of any reason why an injection of pentobarbital into the left foot or left side of the neck would cause pain in the right leg. Michael Graczyk, The AP reporter who attended the execution, said witnesses can't see when the drug starts to be administered. Dennes' foot was covered by a sheet, and the IV in the left side of his neck wasn't visible from their position. READ MORE: IV team warned Christa Pike's vein might have 'blown' during failed execution, court filing says It's not possible to definitively know what caused him to scream in pain. Hernandez said the lethal drugs had not passed their expiration date, though she didn't know the date. Hood, the spiritual adviser, said assertions that Dennes was faking pain were "disgusting." "We have heard them say repeatedly since last night that this was not botched. That is absolutely, unbelievably absurd," Hood said. Dale Baich, an Arizona lawyer who has represented death row inmates and witnessed 17 U.S. executions, said the latest Texas lethal injection raises concerns. "Calling a prisoner's screams an act is not a medical finding. It is an accusation, and the state should be required to produce evidence to support it," Baich said. Associated Press reporter Kate Brumback in Atlanta contributed to this story. A free press is a cornerstone of a healthy democracy. Support trusted journalism and civil dialogue. 0b73866b7c19.text: By — Kaitlyn Huamani, Associated Press Kaitlyn Huamani, Associated Press By — Christopher Rugaber, Associated Press Christopher Rugaber, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/bessent-says-no-further-restrictions-are-needed-for-nvidia-chip-exports-to-china Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Bessent says no further restrictions are needed for Nvidia chip exports to China Politics Nov 21, 2026 11:28 AM EST WASHINGTON (AP) — Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said Friday that no further restrictions on the sale of older Nvidia chips to China are needed following the Trump administration's move earlier this week to block China's remote access to the latest semiconductors. The ability of Chinese tech firms to access Nvidia's technology came under scrutiny after CEO Jensen Huang stepped down amid allegations of his affair with an executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore-based company that uses advanced chips to generate computing power that Chinese firms access remotely. "The proper chip restrictions are in place," Bessent said in an interview with CNBC after returning from a trip to Asia with President Donald Trump. "And the remote access has been curtailed." WATCH: Bessent accuses Lutnick of failing to prevent China from obtaining Nvidia chips Bessent's comments came a day after the House Foreign Affairs Committee released details of the Commerce Department's approval of the sales of more than 850,000 chips from Nvidia and its competitor AMD to Chinese companies. The Pentagon has identified some of those companies as having ties to the Chinese military. The report tracked applications from Nvidia to sell its H200 chips — one of its more powerful products, though not the most advanced — and AMD's applications to sell its roughly comparable MI325X chip to companies that are either located or headquartered in China, or entities with parent companies based in China. Educate your inbox Subscribe to Here’s the Deal, our politics newsletter for analysis you won’t find anywhere else. Enter your email address Subscribe Form error message goes here. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. The Commerce Department's Bureau of Industry and Security approved the export, re-export, or transfer of 879,868 of these chips to companies with Chinese ties across 21 license applications as of May 11, 2026, the report said. Nvidia and AMD had requested to sell a cumulative total of more than 3.4 million of the chips to Chinese-tied companies across those applications, per the report. The approvals, which don't necessarily indicate completed sales, included 75,000 for Alibaba, 150,000 for Tencent and its subsidiaries, 43,000 for Baidu, and 4,000 for BYD, according to the report. Each of those companies has been identified by the Defense Department as having ties to the Chinese military. The report shows the Commerce Department has a "long track record of transparency with Congress about licensing activity for the H200 and equivalent chips, including both approvals and rejections," a spokesperson for the Bureau of Industry and Security said in a statement Friday. The spokesperson said the Commerce Department's approach to H200 licensing is based on a rule in the Federal Register that was published in January. The rule imposes "significant additional national security-related requirements on license applicants in order to qualify for case-by-case consideration rather than a presumption of denial," the spokesperson said. An Nvidia spokesperson said in a statement Friday that the "limited shipments we made under the H200 program were legal and authorized" by the BIS. "The review and licensing process spanned more than half a year, with approvals subject to strict conditions and limited volumes," the company spokesperson said. WATCH: Trump says he would love former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang to 'be given a second chance' Earlier this week, Nvidia said it was no longer shipping H200 chips to China. The spokesperson said Friday that shipments had stopped despite prior approvals. AMD said it complies with U.S. export control laws and regulations and maintains "rigorous processes to ensure compliance across our global operations" in a statement from a spokesperson Friday. "We remain focused on serving our customers and upholding the highest standards of integrity," the spokesperson said. Chinese technology firms have been bracing for impacts on their ambitious AI development plans as scrutiny mounts on export controls in the U.S. Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick has been under intense scrutiny himself in the wake of the turmoil following the Huang affair. Last week, Bessent said he was frustrated with the Commerce Department's delay in placing restrictions on Nvidia chip exports to Megaspeed International, which is under investigation by the U.S. for potentially diverting restricted Nvidia AI chips to China. A former executive at the company who allegedly had an affair with Huang was reportedly suspected by U.S. intelligence agencies of being a spy for China. In an unusually public rebuke of a fellow Cabinet member, Bessent said his department wanted to place export controls on Megaspeed, but Commerce was in charge of the matter. Speaking to reporters on Friday, Trump said he has "not lost confidence" in Lutnick. Calling him a "different kind of guy," Trump said he "has a natural business instinct" and has "done a very good job." Huamani reported from Los Angeles. A British endurance swimmer has completed a three-day swim through the Strait of Hormuz to draw attention to what he says is the environmental cost of the conflict involving Iran.
Lewis Pugh, who is a UN Patron of the Oceans, swam about 15km (9.3 miles) through the strategic waterway, a key route for oil shipments from the Middle East.
Pugh, 56, who was born in Plymouth, Devon said "war causes immense human suffering" but nature is "another casualty that receives far too little attention".
He is calling for an end to the fighting, the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz and action to address environmental damage caused by the conflict.
The swimmer is believed to be the first person to attempt a long-distance swim in the Strait of Hormuz since the conflict began in March.
He swam from Musandam Island in the strait to the Cape of Hormuz, at the northern tip of Oman's Musandam Peninsula.
According to the Lewis Pugh Foundation, an oil tanker was struck by a projectile about 4km (2.5 miles) from where he was swimming on the first day.
On the second day, he saw flames rising above a headland separating him from the burning liquefied petroleum gas carrier Tara Gas and later passed close to the vessel while it was still on fire.
"My immediate thoughts were for the seafarers on board," Pugh said.
"The flames were enormous. These vessels carry highly flammable gases, and an attack on one can have catastrophic consequences - not just for crew members, but also on the surrounding marine environment."
Pugh said environmental damage caused by conflict often receives less attention than the human cost.
"War causes immense human suffering. Lives are lost, families are torn apart, and homes, hospitals and schools can be destroyed in minutes," he said.
"But there is another casualty that receives far too little attention: nature itself. And the damage can last long after the fighting has stopped."
The Strait of Hormuz is one of the world's most important shipping routes and is also home to wildlife including dugongs, sea turtles and whale sharks.
Pugh said oil spills and other contamination could have long-term consequences for marine ecosystems including coral reefs, seagrass meadows and mangrove forests.

36f54bef9a0c.text: President Trump on Saturday said the reported hack of a crucial FBI database might have a silver lining — it could, he claimed, expose more details of what he called the " Russia Russia Russia hoax ." Why it matters: The president remains laser-focused on many of his past grievances about the FBI , even as the public grows increasingly alarmed about the vulnerability of government infrastructure. Driving the news: CNN and NBC reported Friday night that the FBI was looking into an apparent breach of the National Crime Information Center, which connects local and national law enforcement for information sharing. That follows breaches and outages that struck the FAA, NSA and USDA, just in the last week. What they're saying: Trump was asked about the FBI reports in a Fox News interview Saturday morning. "Well we just heard about it and I will say that it's not good, I don't like that," Trump said. "But maybe we'll learn things that we would have never learned otherwise. You had the Russia Russia Russia hoax, you had all these other hoaxes," he added, referring to Ukraine in particular. "Maybe we'll learn about them. Maybe we'll learn about the voter fraud, all the voter fraud that took place." "I always like to put things in a positive spin," Trump added. "Wouldn't it be great to learn about Russia Russia Russia," he said. The intrigue: The president's comments come just days after a summit with Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese leader Xi Jinping in Asia, after which he described Putin as a " friend ." What to watch: It's not clear who breached the FBI database, or what they might do with the data obtained.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has justified Kyiv's repeated attacks on a critical bridge linking Russia to occupied Crimea, calling it a "fair response" to 109 separate Russian attacks on bridges in Ukraine.
In comments to the BBC in Kyiv, Zelensky said the intense attacks on Ukraine by Russia that have followed the strikes on the Crimean Bridge were only a "signal that Vladimir Putin does not want to stop. He wants a reason to escalate".
He rejected the claim by the Russian president that the bridge - which links Russia to the peninsula it illegally annexed from Ukraine - was "exclusively civilian" in use.
"There are facts, not just the words of Putin. We can see," he said.
The Ukrainian president pointed to images online of tanks and other Russian military hardware using the route from Russia into occupied Crimea as a supply line and for logistics.
"If Putin used the internet, he could see that."
The Ukrainian president added that Russia had carried out attacks with missiles and drones on bridges in Ukraine.
This week's combined missile-and-drone strikes by Ukrainian forces destroyed the central road section of the Crimean Bridge, collapsing part of it together with one of the two support arches into the sea and rendering the structure unusable for road traffic.
Russian attacks on Ukraine continued on Friday evening and overnight: a seven-year-old boy was killed in missile and drone strikes on Zelensky's hometown of Kryvyi Rih in the central Dnipropetrovsk region. Local officials say he had been in a playground at the time.
A 20-year-old female medic was also killed. A local official added that when rescuers rushed to the scene, the same site was targeted again with jet powered drones. Another 58 people were injured in the city.
Ukraine's state emergency service DSNS said 11 people were also injured in the north-eastern Kharkiv region, and one person in Rivne, in the north-west.
Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.
Zelensky was speaking ahead of a meeting in Kyiv with UK Defence Secretary Wes Streeting, who told the Ukrainian president he was here to show that Europe was united in its support.
"The more Putin tries to divide us, the more resolute we become," Streeting said.
He said that Russian missiles hitting Poland on Friday, during military exercises of the so-called Coalition of the Willing, was an "outrageous provocation".
The timing, Streeting said, seemed "more than a coincidence".
Asked by the BBC about Nato's response, he said the best way was to "do more for Ukraine" to defend itself against Putin who he called a "cold-blooded killer".
Streeting's description of Putin chimed with the comments made earlier by Zelensky, who described the Kremlin leader a "killer". This was done in response to US President Donald Trump referring this week to Putin as his "friend".
Streeting's visit to Kyiv came after European leaders meeting in Berlin on Thursday alongside US envoys said they were ready for negotiations with Moscow on ending the war in Ukraine.
"Europe has a clear and consistent and united negotiating position," UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham said, while German Chancellor Friedrich Merz stressed that Moscow's "maximalist demands are not realistic".
Donald Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner, one of the two US envoys who were in Berlin, said the US president - who had also dialled into the meeting from Air Force One - wanted to make a deal with Moscow "with Europe by his side".
Russia's Vladimir Putin has so far rejected any European role in the US-led peace talks - but earlier this week he invited European representatives to Moscow as it wanted to clarify "what Europe will bring to these talks".
That meeting in the German capital came hours after Putin had held historic trilateral talks in Shenzhen, China, with Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping.
Zelensky said he had been "sceptical" ahead of the latest round of talks, when US envoys claimed that Russia was prepared to make compromises to end the war.
"I thought [Putin] would find reason to escalate."
Speaking to the BBC, Streeting added: "Putin has absolutely no business playing the victim. He is the aggressor in this war. He provoked an illegal invasion of Ukraine. And all of us, right throughout the world, need to judge Putin not on his words, but on his actions."
In a separate development on Saturday, Finland said it "detected a drone strike on a Russian merchant vessel" in the eastern Gulf of Finland, "in an international maritime area".
The Finnish defence ministry said in a statement that the vessel was damaged, without giving any further details.
It added that "temporary restrictions on aviation and maritime areas in the eastern Gulf of Finland" were now reinstated for safety reasons.
Russia has not publicly commented on the issue.

A Mexican drug lord who was on the FBI's 10 most wanted list has been arrested following a shoot-out with Mexican authorities.
Fausto Isidro "Chapo Isidro" Meza Flores was detained along with his lieutenant by Mexican special forces in Guasave, Sinaloa on Friday, Mexico's defence secretariat said.
Meza Flores was wanted in Mexico on organised crime charges, while he has been accused of "flooding the US with fentanyl, cocaine, heroin and other deadly drugs" by the FBI. The US is seeking his extradition.
Mexico has stepped up efforts to tackle drug-related crime after coming under pressure from US President Donald Trump since he returned to the White House.
Meza Flores, the leader of the Meza Flores Organisation, also known as the Guasave Cartel, is thought to have been active in the drug trafficking trade since the 1990s but managed to evade authorities till now by maintaining a relatively low profile.
Using US intelligence on his whereabouts, Mexican special forces descended on his location using "stealth and surprise", establishing a perimeter to prevent him from escaping and reinforcements arriving, Mexico's defence secretariat said.
However, they "came under attack from gunfire and explosives" before entering the property and arresting Meza Flores and his second-in-command, it added.
Videos circulating online appear to show helicopters firing streams of bullets towards the ground in Guasave. Others appear to show people at a baseball stadium fleeing as they hear shooting sounds.
The two detainees were subsequently flown to Mexico City to face prosecution, the defence secretariat said.
When he was added to the FBI's most-wanted list in 2025, he was accused of "heinous crimes" including kidnapping, extortion and torture.
Then-acting FBI director Brian Driscoll said Meza Flores and his organisation had also unleashed a "scourge of illicit drugs" into the US via its southern border with Mexico.
He was initially charged with drug trafficking in the US in 2012 before being charged again in 2019.
The 44-year-old is alleged to have conspired to manufacture and distribute large quantities of cocaine, heroin, methamphetamine and marijuana between 2005 and 2019.
Meza Flores was originally a high-ranking member of the BeltrÃ¡n Leyva Organization, but a split between rival factions led to a surge of violence and prompted him to establish his own cartel by 2013.
His organisation has also engaged in what US officials described as an "extremely violent turf war" with the Sinaloa Cartel, one of the most powerful drug trafficking gangs, which operates in the same region.
Meza Flores was added to the FBI's most-wanted list after Mexican authorities reportedly linked his cartel to 20 million fentanyl pills they seized in 2024.
Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum has taken a tougher stance on the country's cartels in a bid to resist US intervention on Mexican soil. Mexico has welcomed closer collaboration but resisted US boots on the ground.
Trump made stemming the flow of drugs into the US across its southern border one of his key election pledges.
