With growing concerns that red squirrels could soon become extinct in England, one Channel Island is a corner of the British Isles where they maintain a stronghold.
Jersey is home to a thriving red squirrel population, thanks to the complete absence of grey squirrels, which carry a virus deadly to their red cousins.
Red squirrels are endangered in the UK, with about 120,000 to 160,000 left in the wild and various projects are aiming to boost those numbers.
There have some strongholds in England, external, particularly islands, and 75% of the British population is in Scotland, external.
However, despite not being native to Jersey, Henry Glynn, an ecologist with the National Trust of Jersey, said they "really are iconic for Jersey".
He said: "When you speak to people who have come over to visit the island from the UK, a lot of them will say that one of the things they want to do whilst here is to see a red squirrel, because they're so rare and so difficult to see in large parts of the UK.
"That is actually really special for them."
Red squirrels are not native to Jersey, having been introduced in 1885.
However, Glynn described them as "naturalised", having become "assimilated into the natural environment" over many years.
The animals have previously featured in Visit Jersey, external tourism campaigns, including one fronted by conservationist Ben Fogle.
The National Trust of Jersey said the island was an "important refuge" for the red squirrel, where they were "fairly widespread, external".
It said the inland valleys and woodlands were the best places to spot them.
The species is legally protected, which means it would be a criminal offence to harm them.
Nina Powell, senior animal carer at the JSPCA [Jersey Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals], said Jersey has a "good population" of squirrels and that "you can see them almost anywhere".
While the primary reason for their success is the lack of grey squirrels, Powell said they also thrived "because people look out for them".
She said: "A lot of people do support them, put out feeders and stuff like that.
"Their habitats are decreasing everywhere... but we do have quite a lot of nature reserves.
"In some places, we've got rope bridges which really help them cross the roads, and our speed limits are quite low, so that helps them as well".
She said the JSPCA had handled 50 red squirrels so far this year, including hand-raising eight babies, called kits (kittens).
She said: "We want to keep all animals as wild as possible, so we try and be as hands-off as possible.
"Some of them don't like us... some of them are quite sweet. They really do vary in personality."
Glynn agreed that their success had come in part because of the efforts of islanders.
He said: "They're really beloved amongst the local community as well. A lot of people put out squirrel feeders or love to see them in the garden.
"We get lots of reports from people who just want to tell us they've seen them because they're so happy to have them around."

29f32cf5304a.text: By — Madison Czopek, PolitiFact Madison Czopek, PolitiFact Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/nation/why-do-people-believe-recent-tech-failures-must-be-connected Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Why do people believe recent tech failures must be connected? Nation Nov 21, 2026 6:14 PM EST This article originally appeared on PolitiFact. It's been one thing after another. Companies including Microsoft, United Airlines, JPMorgan Chase and U.S. Bank experienced technical issues and outages that caused widespread banking issues, delayed plane departures and interrupted workdays across the world. Soon after, Marriott and Apple customers also experienced digital problems, and 178 companies reported being affected by a Nov. 16 cyberattack. At the same time, various U.S. government systems — the Federal Aviation Administration, National Security Agency and National Weather Service — fell into disarray, including a rare nationwide ground stop. For many people, the pile-on of concerning news alerts had a sinister feel. WATCH: Mounting tech disruptions raise concerns about U.S. cybersecurity "We're under attack in a way we've never seen before," wrote Nalin Haley, a conservative influencer and son of Republican politician Nikki Haley, on Nov. 17. "This is an AI cyberattack." On Bluesky, Christopher Webb, a self-described "lifelong Dem" and party strategist, questioned whether the issues were connected. "Coincidence??? 4 major banks reporting outages, a massive Microsoft disruption, and a nationwide FAA ground stop, all within days of each other," he wrote Nov. 16. The best available information points to mundane explanations such as routine maintenance, one-off problems or isolated cyberattacks, rather than an imminent systemic collapse or a coordinated attack on digital systems. But why can that be hard to believe? Human brains naturally detect patterns and reject uncertainty The rapid-fire succession of events didn't help. Neither did the timing of a planned, routine Nov. 17 test of the country's Emergency Alert System. Human brains are wired to make connections and spot statistical regularities in the world. "Detecting patterns is important for perceiving the world and learning about cause and effect," said Javier Granados Samayoa, a Texas Christian University psychology professor. This tendency "can sometimes lead people to see connections where none may exist." One paper about conspiracy thinking started with a coin toss. People who reported a tendency to notice patterns in a random string of coin tosses were more likely to also endorse conspiracy theories and supernatural beliefs. WATCH: Cascade of tech outages 'separate events' and 'under control,' Trump says Research also shows that when people lack control, they're more likely to detect nonexistent patterns. For people unable to access their work platforms or stuck at airports, powerlessness and confusion were all too familiar feelings. Those feelings contribute to embracing conspiracy theories. "People are looking for ways to understand what is going on and they don't like the uncertainty that often surrounds unfolding events," said Karen Douglas, a University of Kent social psychology professor. "Also, a simple explanation is often not very appealing. People assume that there must somehow be a bigger explanation, or more going on than people know about." Human biases and social media platforms can intensify the anxieties The flurry of frustration-inducing technical issues coupled with the known negativity bias observed across social media platforms can set people up to have outsized emotional reactions when things go wrong. Negativity bias means that negative information has a stronger impact and people tend to think about it more, said Granados Samayoa. On social media, content is more likely to prompt engagement and go viral if it uses negative language or prompts a strong negative reaction. WATCH: What a string of tech problems reveals about America's digital vulnerabilities Social media algorithms have continuously circulated some of the most alarming posts and conspiracy theories — an estimated 30% of which were pushed by suspected bots, including some with potential foreign influence, Axios reported. Sharing conspiracy theories on social media is easy, fast and difficult to untangle. "Once people believe in a conspiracy theory, it is often difficult to convince them otherwise," Douglas said. The events and concerns compounded as regular people and news reporters all began paying more attention to outages that would otherwise be routine. That's commonly called frequency bias. "United's outage this afternoon is so pedestrian, it'd be a non-story if not for what's happened the last four days," Kyle Potter, an editor at Thrifty Traveler, wrote Nov. 16. 1907e33f760b.text: By — Gary Fields, Associated Press Gary Fields, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/for-families-of-the-fallen-trumps-proposed-arch-casts-a-shadow-over-arlington-national-cemetery Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter For families of the fallen, Trump's proposed arch casts a shadow over Arlington National Cemetery Politics Nov 21, 2026 5:52 PM EST WASHINGTON (AP) — Cpl. Spencer Collart's headstone faces the rising sun and the Lincoln Memorial to the east. The Marine Corps War Memorial is nearby. Soon, President Donald Trump's gilded, towering arch could be, too. Collart's silent stone speaks volumes in its simplicity of courage, sacrifice and loss. It stands among thousands of uniform headstones and other monuments, each telling the story of the person, or persons, beneath it. WATCH: 2nd judge blocks construction of Trump's arch in D.C. But if Trump gets his way, a different story may be told. His proposed 250-foot-tall (76-meter-tall) arch could cast a long shadow on Arlington National Cemetery, with the potential to literally shade gravesites, disrupt solemn visits with the noise of construction and alter the carefully designed historic landscape of the nation's capital. For many veterans and their families, and the loved ones of others buried at the cemetery, the arch has no place so close to the Arlington, Virginia, burial grounds. That opposition has sparked lawsuits by veterans groups and others, including nine family members of the Kennedy political dynasty, who argue the arch, which would be built on a traffic circle about half a mile (0.8 kilometers) from Arlington's main entrance, will fundamentally change the experience of visiting the cemetery. "It's a billboard for an ego. It's a loud, boastful, gaudy piece of marketing dropped onto sacred ground," said Bart Collart, Spencer's father. His son, a young Marine who died at 21 trying to save fellow crew members in a 2023 Osprey crash in Australia, would see it as "dirtying hallowed ground." A skyline-altering arch could impact the cemetery The arch project is part of a series of renovations to Washington that Trump, a Republican, has set in motion to reimagine the city. When complete, the gold and granite arch will stretch taller than the Lincoln Memorial. Opponents say the arch would break the alignment between the Lincoln Memorial, the Memorial Bridge and Arlington House, which was formerly Confederate Gen. Robert E. Lee's home, and the symbolism of a reunited North and South. But behind the fences that line Memorial Drive is an active cemetery with more than 430,000 people interred there and dozens more added each week. They include retirees and their spouses and some dependents and a few eligible dignitaries. There are two presidents, John F. Kennedy and William Howard Taft, there, along with more than a dozen Supreme Court justices. Among the dead are an untold number who died while on active duty and eligible spouses. There are more than 400 recipients of the Medal of Honor, the nation's highest honor for valor in combat. The remains of military personnel from every war, dating back to the Revolutionary War, are there. WATCH: Retired general calls Trump's proposed arch near Arlington a 'sacrilege' An estimated 3 million to 4 million people visit annually. Walking among the stones or taking the tour is a lesson in the nation's military history. The Tomb of the Unknown Soldier is one prominent feature, as is the grave of boxing legend Joe Louis. Audie Murphy, an actor who was one of the most decorated U.S. soldiers in World War II, is also buried there. On a recent visit, a small group of about 10 men came quietly from Section 60, an area where soldiers who died in Afghanistan and Iraq are buried. Their young ages, "PH" for Purple Heart and the inscription Afghanistan or Operation Enduring Freedom mean premature loss. What comes through is silence and distant sound, except for the passenger planes flying over from nearby Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport. "I think you could, by any definition, consider it the most hallowed ground in the United States, but I think we're not even giving it credit for how hallowed, how representative, how much sacrifice and honor is there," said Micki McElya, a historian at the University of Connecticut and author of "The Politics of Mourning: Death and Honor in Arlington National Cemetery." She said the country's shifting values are represented there in all their complications, including slavery. Court battles over the arch are playing out Supporters of the arch say it completes a plan mandated by Congress in 1925 to add a monument to the circle. "It was always supposed to be a gateway to connect D.C. to Arlington," said Jared Craig, general counsel and national vice president for Veterans for America First, which joined several veteran organizations in a brief in the lawsuit supporting the arch. Craig argued the arch honors veterans and fallen service members. He said that the project does not impact the cemetery itself and requires no changes there. Jimi Shaughnessy, veterans program manager at the nonprofit National Parks Conservation Association, disagrees. A veteran, he visits his great-grandparents' resting place regularly. READ MORE: Trump says the towering arch he wants to be build might be dedicated to military veterans "The setting is open, it's quiet, it's peaceful, it is easy to navigate," he said. And there is space to transition "so I can properly acknowledge my great-grandfolks that are buried there." The sounds of major construction will intrude on that and funerals, and creating a tourist attraction at the arch will bring noise and distraction, along with a "looming dark shadow above me," he said. To the White House, the arch would serve "as a visual reminder of the noble sacrifices borne by so many American heroes throughout our 250 year history so we can enjoy our freedoms today," spokesm

A framed lock of hair from America's first president, George Washington, has been sold at auction for $4,000 (Â£3,058).
The hair once belonged to John Gadsby, who entertained Washington in 1799 just before the latter's death the same year, and was later obtained by a collector called John K Lattimer from a descendent of Gadsby's, according to Richmond Auctions, which sold the item.
Its new owner has not been named.
Saturday's sale is not the most expensive for Washington hair at auction. Three strands thought to have been removed from him close to or after his death stored in a locket sold for nearly $40,000 in 2021.
Gadsby, a resident of what in 1799 was the town of Alexandria in Virginia, entertained Washington for dinner shortly before his death later that year, according to a testament given in 1928 by Gadsby's granddaughter, Julia Ten Eyck McBlair, and which was posted on the Richmond Auctions website.
McBlair stated that her grandfather came into possession of Washington's hair "in view of the friendship and association with his last days" and had it framed and hung "under General Washington's portrait in our home in Washington City, there I have seen it all my life".
Gadsby hosted Washington's two birthday celebrations in 1798 and 1799, Richmond Auctions states.
Washington led American forces to victory against the British in the War of Independence and helped draft the US Constitution before becoming the country's first president in 1788. He stepped down in 1797 after serving two terms.
Several locks of Washington's hair have been preserved, including at least 50 examples that are in a collection at his former residence, Mount Vernon, which is now a museum.
"Public displays of hair from friends or loved ones peaked in the 19th century, but had long been popular among affluent families like the Washingtons," a blog on the Mount Vernon website states.
As well as lockets of his hair, other items associated with Washington have also done well at auction.
In July, a signed letter by Washington from 1776, in which he asks for soldiers for the Continental Army to fight the British, sold for $109,800.

f7f9724f890a.text: By — Ken Sweet, Associated Press Ken Sweet, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/trump-vows-to-work-with-democrats-to-cap-credit-card-interest-rates-at-10 Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Trump vows to work with Democrats to cap credit card interest rates at 10% Politics Nov 21, 2026 4:20 PM EST NEW YORK (AP) — President Donald Trump said Saturday that he would work with the incoming Democratic Congress to cap credit card interest rates, hoping to fulfill a promise he made on the 2024 campaign trail but couldn't deliver on because of industry pressure and a lack of interest from his fellow Republicans. "I would do it. These credit card companies have made a lot," Trump told Fox News Channel's "Saturday in America." Educate your inbox Subscribe to Here’s the Deal, our politics newsletter for analysis you won’t find anywhere else. Enter your email address Subscribe Form error message goes here. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. Democrats and the Republican president have both backed capping credit card interest rates, with the standard proposal being capping rates at 10%. It would substantially reduce what credit card companies can charge customers. The median credit card interest rate is roughly 22.2%, according to an August survey by the New York Federal Reserve. Trump proposed capping credit card interest rates in January, as part of the White House's affordability push. Banks and credit card companies immediately and aggressively opposed the proposal, saying any interest rate cap would force them to cancel cards for the poor and less creditworthy customers or substantially cut back on the rewards they offer when customers spend on their cards. The proposal also did not sit well with Republicans, and there was little effort by the GOP-controlled Congress to fulfill Trump's promise. WATCH: Credit card debt surges in U.S. as high interest rates make it harder to pay off That could change now that Democrats will control both the House and Senate. Sen. Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., who is expected to be the next chair of the Senate Banking Committee, has said repeatedly she wants to cap rates. In response to the Fox News interview, Warren said: "Let's cap credit card interest rates and save Americans money." Other Democrats have endorsed the idea in various ways, including Rep. Maxine Waters of California, a powerful Democrat who sits on the House Financial Services Committee. Among Republicans, Sen. Josh Hawley of Missouri has proposed several caps on credit card interest rates, as recently as this year when Trump made his proposal. "Congress should pass my bipartisan bill to cap these rates and deliver relief right away," Hawley said at the time. READ MORE: Voters demanded economic relief. Trump and Democrats face tough choices on how to deliver Researchers who studied Trump's campaign pledge after it was first announced found that Americans would save roughly $100 billion in interest a year if credit card rates were capped at 10%. The same researchers found that while the credit card industry would take a major hit, it would still be profitable, although credit card rewards and other perks might be scaled back. About 195 million people in the United States had credit cards in 2024 and were assessed $160 billion in interest charges, the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau says. Americans are now carrying more credit card debt than ever, to the tune of about $1.23 trillion, according to figures from the New York Federal Reserve for the third quarter last year. 8d643400db43.text: By — Eric Tucker, Associated Press Eric Tucker, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/ap-source-fbi-investigating-apparent-hack-of-its-key-national-criminal-justice-database Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter AP source: FBI investigating apparent hack of its key national criminal justice database Politics Nov 21, 2026 3:55 PM EST WASHINGTON (AP) — The FBI is investigating an apparent hack of a national law enforcement database that it maintains, a person familiar with the matter said Saturday. Educate your inbox Subscribe to Here’s the Deal, our politics newsletter for analysis you won’t find anywhere else. Enter your email address Subscribe Form error message goes here. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. The National Crime Information Center, known as the NCIC, is a computerized database of criminal justice information that is available to local, state and federal law enforcement agencies and includes records on fugitives, missing persons, criminal history data, stolen property and other topics. The FBI declined to comment Saturday on the apparent hack, which was first reported by CNN and confirmed to The Associated Press by a person familiar with the matter who was not authorized to speak by name and spoke on the condition of anonymity. The scope of the problem was not immediately clear. Asked about the subject on Saturday, President Donald Trump said in a Fox News Channel interview: "We just heard about it and I will say that it's not good." WATCH: Mounting tech disruptions raise concerns about U.S. cybersecurity News that the NCIC was targeted comes as the country has encountered a series of digital outages in the government and private sector that Trump administration officials have said were caused by routine efforts to upgrade computer systems and fix vulnerabilities, rather than a cyberattack. There was no immediate indication that the FBI incident was related to those outages. The bureau has historically been a frequent target for hackers. In September, for instance, the FBI said it was investigating a hack of its job portal website after a criminal hacking group known as ShinyHunters claimed it had obtained a massive trove of data on bureau employees and applicants. And in March, the FBI disclosed that it was investigating "suspicious activities" on an internal system that contains sensitive information related to surveillance operations and investigations. cdf7efb8596c.text: By — Reed Berger-Fleishman, The Conversation Reed Berger-Fleishman, The Conversation Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/health/a-doctors-guide-to-surviving-and-enjoying-holiday-feasting-while-on-glp%e2%80%911-medication Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter A doctor's guide to surviving — and enjoying — holiday feasting while on GLP‑1 medication Health Nov 21, 2026 2:46 PM EST This article originally appeared on The Conversation. Thanksgiving and the winter holidays bring celebration, connection and plenty of opportunities to come together with family and friends. But the holiday season also brings something else: more food-centered gatherings, larger portions and richer foods than most people typically eat throughout the year. Think whipped sweet potatoes, mac and cheese, decadent side dishes and an abundance of desserts. For people taking GLP-1 medications for diabetes management, weight loss or other medical reasons, these celebrations can present unique challenges. Changes in appetite, smaller portion tolerance, limits on alcohol consumption, medication side effects and the desire to maintain progress can make navigating holiday traditions feel a little different. WATCH: As GLP-1s reshape America, questions and new uses emerge As a physician specializing in obesity medicine, I encourage my patients to view GLP-1 medications as an advantage during the holidays. These medications can help regulate appetite, improve awareness of fullness, and reinforce healthier eating behaviors during a season when food often takes center stage. However, these medications don't eliminate the possibility of overindulgence. In fact, patients who previously experienced little or no nausea due to GLP-1s may suddenly develop significant nausea or even vomiting after eating beyond their new comfort level. Nothing can derail a holiday celebration quite like an upset stomach. Accounting for how these medications affect your body can help you avoid uncomfortable surprises while still enjoying the foods and traditions you love. Respecting fullness cues Whether taken by injection or orally, GLP-1 medications have become increasingly popular worldwide for managing Type 2 diabetes, obesity and other chronic conditions. In the United States, approximately 1 in 10 adults used these drugs in 2025, and prescribing rates continue to climb. GLP-1 medications work by reducing hunger, slowing stomach emptying and helping patients feel full sooner and stay full longer. Many patients also report fewer cravings for high-calorie foods and even a reduced desire to drink alcohol. In many ways, these effects can make holiday food temptations easier to navigate. My patients often tell me that they already know which dietary changes they need to make, but GLP-1 medications help them put those changes into practice. They find it easier to stop eating when they're satisfied, resist unnecessary snacking and avoid the constant thoughts about food that previously made weight management so challenging. The prices of Thanksgiving staples this year won't be too much higher than in 2025. Watch the video in the player above. One of the most important things you can do during the holidays is to learn to recognize your body's changing fullness signals. Pay attention to nausea, bloating and early fullness rather than pushing yourself to finish everything on your plate. These symptoms can serve as reminders that you've reached your comfortable limit. The best plan is to enjoy smaller portions, eat slowly and pause between bites to give your body time to recognize fullness. Rich, high-fat foods in particular can worsen nausea and prolong the sensation of fullness. A few bites of your favorite dishes may be much more satisfying than an entire serving. GLP-1 medications don't make these decisions for you – but they can reinforce healthier behaviors. A caution on alcohol Alcohol deserves special consideration during the holidays, when social gatherings and celebrations often revolve around drinking. Although you may have tolerated alcohol without difficulty in the past, GLP-1 medications can change your experience. Some patients report that GLP-1 medications reduce their desire for alcohol altogether. For them, the holidays may represent their first opportunity to drink since starting treatment. Alcohol can worsen nausea, acid reflux, dehydration and other gastrointestinal symptoms that some patients already experience while taking GLP-1 medications. If you choose to drink, consider these precautions: Limit your intake. Start with less than you might have consumed before starting your medication. Avoid drinking on an empty stomach. Eat beforehand, but avoid a particularly large or high-fat meal. Stay hydrated. Drink water throughout the occasion. Pay attention to how you feel. Stop drinking if you experience nausea, dizziness or other unpleasant symptoms. The safest approach is to be cautious and recognize that alcohol can aggravate medication-related gastrointestinal symptoms. Planning for travel Holiday travel can disrupt established routines, medication schedules and access to prescriptions. A little planning can help prevent unnecessary interruptions in treatment. Plan ahead for medication storage. Some injectable GLP-1 medications require refrigeration before use, while others allow room-temperature storage for a specified period after dispensing or first use. Storage requirements vary considerably by product. Check the prescribing information for your specific medication or ask your pharmacist before traveling. Don't assume that all injectable medications can remain unrefrigerated for the same length of time. If you're flying, keep your medication and supplies in your carry-on luggage. This helps protect them from extreme temperatures and prevents problems if your checked luggage gets delayed or lost. Please check your inbox to confirm. The companies must also coordinate with the White House and U.S. agencies on "appropriate responses" to any such requests, the order issued late Friday says. If they fail to comply, the White House warns their contracts could be terminated and their future work with the federal government suspended. The order is the Republican administration's latest effort to resist what are expected to be wide-ranging and aggressive oversight efforts from Democrats when they take over Congress in January. Democrats have made government contracts one of their top investigative targets, noting that federal money has been flowing to companies linked with Trump's family, particularly at the Pentagon. White House officials have already begun taking steps to exert more control over how agencies and officials respond to congressional requests, anticipating there will be a flood of investigations initiated by Democrats. Trump's counsel, Will Scharf, told federal agencies on Monday that they must seek approval from his office and the White House's Office of Legislative Affairs before agreeing to appear before Congress. Scharf also suggested in a recent letter to Rep. Robert Garcia of California, the top Democrat on the House Oversight Committee, that some congressional investigations may amount to "blatant criminality." READ MORE: Read the full White House memo requiring agencies to get approval before testifying in front of Congress Garcia sent letters this week directing members of Trump's family and top administration officials to preserve documents. Scharf sought to dismiss the requests, noting in a letter to Democratic lawmakers that they are not yet in the majority and cannot compel compliance. Responding to the new executive order, Garcia said it was part of the administration's "blatant attack on Congress' constitutional right to conduct oversight." He said that despite efforts to impede investigations, "we're just getting started." In a fact sheet, the White House framed the new requirements as "protecting executive privileges from congressional overreach," arguing that some congressional leaders have tried to intrude on executive branch privileges by "harassing private companies that contract with the federal government." Presidents of both parties have long used executive privilege to resist congressional inquiries, but the claims can set up messy, protracted legal fights as parties dispute whether it applies. Executive privilege allows the president to keep information from the courts, Congress and the public to protect the confidentiality of White House deliberations, but the protection is far from absolute. The latest executive order applies to all contractors and subcontractors, a universe of tens of thousands of businesses. A free press is a cornerstone of a healthy democracy. A Russian cargo vessel bound for the country's Baltic exclave Kaliningrad has been hit by a drone attack in the eastern Gulf of Finland, Russian and Finnish authorities say.
The ship - the Sparta II - caught on fire after the strike on Saturday morning, before drifting into Finnish waters. Finnish defence forces said Ukraine was likely behind the attack. Kyiv has yet to comment.
"War is spilling over into our immediate vicinity," Finnish Prime Minister Petteri Orpo said. "Ukraine has the right to fight back against the aggressor."
Kaliningrad Governor Alexei Besprozvannykh said two drones had been used, based on preliminary information, and there was "no threat" to the territory's supplies.
The Sparta II was sanctioned by the US in 2022 and Ukraine earlier this year, and is run by a Russian company, according to the Ukrainian and US governments.
The company says on its website that it was established within the structure of Russia's defence ministry in 2011 and since 2015 has been operating within the military construction complex.
Finland's coast guard said it had been alerted to the attack at around 08:50 local time (06:50 GMT) on Saturday and that the cargo vessel had been located approximately 50km west of the island of Suursaari in the Gulf of Finland.
This prompted "temporary aviation and maritime restrictions" around the area, Finnish border officials said.
Shortly after the incident, Finland's defence ministry said a Russian helicopter was suspected of violating the country's airspace, potentially linked to "rescue or tracking operations".
A Russian rescue vessel approached the ship and was told by the crew that they did not need to be evacuated, Kaliningrad's governor wrote on Telegram, adding: "The crew is currently carrying out the necessary work and plans to continue on its way."
The Finnish Border Guard later said the crew had been evacuated to another Russian vessel that was now already en route to Russia. The Russian rescue vessel had remained at the location of the stricken ship.
It added that no environmental damage had been detected and that there was no danger to maritime traffic or people.
Kaliningrad is a Russian exclave that sits between Poland and Lithuania.
Defence Minister Antti HÃ¤kkÃ¤nen said that the Finnish Border Guard were responsible for the investigation into the attack and were co-operating with other relevant authorities.
Nato has also been informed, the defence ministry said.
The Baltic Sea has become a flashpoint in the Russia-Ukraine war, triggered when Russia launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. Ukraine has recently ramped up its long-range attacks against Russia beyond the front lines.
Earlier this month, a Ukrainian drone strike hit a Russian warship in the Gulf of Finland.

5e5c12a8f2f0.text: By — Megan Janetsky, Associated Press Megan Janetsky, Associated Press By — Fabiola Sanchez, Associated Press Fabiola Sanchez, Associated Press By — Martín Urista, Associated Press Martín Urista, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/mexico-detains-top-cartel-boss-el-chapo-isidro-setting-off-a-burst-of-violence-in-sinaloa Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Mexico detains top cartel boss 'El Chapo Isidro,' setting off a burst of violence in Sinaloa World Updated on Nov 21, 2026 5:37 PM EST — Published on Nov 21, 2026 2:13 PM EST GUASAVE, Mexico (AP) — Heavy gunfire, helicopters and burning trucks marked Mexico's Sinaloa state Saturday after authorities captured cartel boss Fausto Isidro Meza Flores, known as "El Chapo Isidro," in an operation that left at least 11 people dead. Meza Flores, one of the FBI's 10 most wanted fugitives, was captured and flown to Mexico City on Saturday after the firefight between Mexican forces and cartel gunmen overnight left residents of the city of Guasave terrorized. Mexico's Defense Ministry on Saturday afternoon said that seven alleged cartel gunmen and four Mexican soldiers were killed. The capo climbed the cartel ranks to lead the Beltrán Leyva cartel and later became the leader of his own group, the Meza-Flores Transnational Criminal Organization. The United States had a $5 million reward offer for information leading to his arrest, and he was wanted for trafficking drugs to the U.S. and illegally carrying firearms. WATCH: Mexico's foreign secretary on Trump, cartel violence and U.S. trade talks Mexico's government said in a report early Saturday that intelligence from the Trump administration helped authorities capture him, but provided few details about how authorities in Mexico and the United States coordinated to detain Meza Flores. He was also a key ally to "Los Mayos," a faction of the Sinaloa Cartel, which was designated as a foreign terrorist organization by the Trump administration last year. His capture represents a blow to the cartel as it fights with another faction for control of the northern Mexican state. Authorities in the United States and Mexico celebrated the arrest as a security win. U.S. President Donald Trump has pressured Mexico's government to go after criminal groups. As a fierce firefight settled into a tense calm Saturday, experts warned that picking off capos could set off another wave of violence in a region already caught up in a power struggle between warring cartel factions. Mexican forces' move against cartel fuels violence The capture of Meza Flores and his No. 2 in the city of Guasave, Sinaloa, set off a wave of violence when a firefight broke out around 7 p.m. on Friday, according to residents of the 290,000-person municipality. Soon, military helicopters and drones were flying overhead, and helicopters opened fire on key locations across the city. Videos show screaming civilians fleeing gunfire at a baseball game, burning cars and businesses, and circling helicopters shooting at people below. Such shows of force by cartels are common following the capture or killing of leaders. "The fighting was happening all over Guasave," said Alma Camacho, a Guasave resident and local journalist. "It spread throughout the city." Mexican authorities said that they used "stealth and surprise" to arrest Meza Flores, establishing a security perimeter around the building where he was located. After coming under attack with guns and explosives from suspected cartel operatives, armed forces personnel entered a home and detained him. READ MORE: Why Mexican cartels are increasingly using car bombs and other explosives Video shared by Mexico's Defense Ministry shows Meza Flores and two others being marched by heavily armed soldiers onto a military aircraft to appear before prosecutors in Mexico City. A total of eight people were detained, according to authorities. Because of the violence, the Mexican army and National Guard special forces were unable to extract Meza Flores from Guasave until 4 a.m. on Saturday, said a federal official who spoke on condition of anonymity because he wasn't authorized to discuss the case. "Getting him (Meza Flores) out was extraordinary," the official said, describing an intense response by members of the criminal group who maintained at least "10 roadblocks" with burning vehicles on Guasave's streets. Terror in Sinaloa Vehicles burn on a highway near Los Mochis, Sinaloa, Mexico, on Nov. 20, 2026, following an announcement by the interim government of the arrest of Beltrán-Leyva Cartel leader Fausto Isidro Meza Flores, known as "El Chapo Isidro", in an operation between Mexico's Secretaría de la Defensa Nacional and U.S. intelligence agencies, in this still image taken from a video obtained from social media on Nov. 21, 2026. Photo by Yohari Leon via Facebook/via Reuters Guasave resident and firefighter Paola Sánchez said that thousands of people were terrorized late Friday as they took shelter from intense gunfire in grocery stores and other locations. "Last night, many businesses were burned ... along with cars and trucks," Sánchez told The Associated Press. She said that the city's firefighters had to take shelter at their station and wait until Saturday morning for orders from their superiors to dispatch the first crews to check whether any businesses or vehicles were still burning. An uneasy calm seemed to settle over the city Saturday. Mexican Security Secretary Omar García Harfuch wrote on X on Saturday morning that armed forces would remain deployed in Sinaloa state to protect civilians. He lamented the deaths of the four soldiers killed in the operation. Burned-out trucks continued to line the freeway leading into the town, blocking roadways on Saturday. Isabel Angelo spends her days searching the cosmos for exoplanets and signs of extraterrestrial intelligence. But Angelo’s head isn’t in the stars. It’s buried under mountains of 0s and 1s — data from space telescopes old and new.
To piece together a fuller picture of what’s out there (alien megastructures around nearby stars, perhaps?), Angelo and her colleagues at the SETI Institute in Mountain View, Calif., are turning to machine learning models. These tools are analyzing the troves of telescope data for anomalies — things that look “weird” in space that we don’t know how to explain yet.
Most of the space weirdos will probably turn out to be total normies — a comet, a newborn star or a star surrounded by lots of gas and dust. “These are things that I would expect [the models] to find,” Angelo says. “But the goal is to find something that’s not even in any of these categories.”
In the meantime, Angelo keeps her whimsy and wonder for space alive by remembering historic moments, like the reveal of the first portrait of a black hole in 2019. The scientists “put all of these telescopes all over the Earth. They wait for the Earth to rotate. They do all this math to construct this one image,” Angelo says. “I can’t believe how creative and innovative we have to be to learn about space. It’s such a specific and really fun challenge.”

Dor Minzer remembers sitting in an undergraduate computation class at Tel Aviv University. He was intrigued by his professor and soon found himself pulled into a new world: the mystifying intersection of math and computation, first laid out by Alan Turing during World War II. Working with the professor, Minzer became deeply interested in the limitations of what computers can and can’t do.
“My part is actually to prove not only do I not know how to do it, but I can prove that it’s impossible,” Minzer says. “You have to really be curious.”
Minzer’s hard work has paid off. In 2018, he proved a theoretical computer science problem called the 2-to-2 games conjecture. It asks whether computers can efficiently distinguish games where almost all rules can be satisfied from those where almost none can be satisfied, when the rules have a strict structure.
In September, Minzer and his two graduate students at MIT posted a 95-page milestone paper on the unique games conjecture, which builds off the 2-to-2 conjecture. The paper wasn’t quite ready, but they published to get ahead of a press release from OpenAI, describing its proof for the same problem, slated for only days later. It’s a situation that many mathematicians have found themselves in this year as AI companies flood the field with findings at lightning speed.
Minzer says it’s critical to remember that math, and all the research and contemplation behind it, is very human. “It’s a human activity,” he says. “Research is sort of a living organism, a living body.”
Minzer teaches his own students now. Some days, he talks to his class and gets the sense that nobody is paying attention. But other days, he gets a few students that participate. They have ideas, they’re excited, and they remind him of his own days as a graduate student.
“I feel like now I feel like I’m passing the torch,” he says. “Before you have a Ph.D. adviser, you’re like a new person in a dark room. There are infinite places to go. Your Ph.D. adviser is the person that holds your hand and says, ‘Okay, let’s walk here.’”

In an increasingly fire-prone western North America, Jennifer Grenz, an ecologist and member of the Lytton First Nation, looks at fire with a holistic eye. She considers her work with landscapes recovering from catastrophic wildfire to be “deliberately unfocused,” spanning soil microbial ecology, restoration ecology, invasion biology and historical biology.
Grenz analyzes historical ecological records, like how Indigenous people have shaped and cared for ecosystems over time, to paint a comprehensive picture. “I’m interested in how those histories leave ecological legacies and hints of the stewardship of the past,” says Grenz, who leads the Indigenous Ecology Lab at the University of British Columbia in Canada. “What changed on the land that made it more vulnerable?”
Grenz spends time with many kinds of specialists, such as archaeologists, anthropologists and Indigenous elders who provide oral histories.
Moving forward, her lab will examine ecology below ground, including soil, microbial communities and root networks. The goal is to understand the role of underground ecology in critical topics like carbon sequestration, climate change, biodiversity and sustainable management.
“My motivation is in our interior Salish Territories in the southern interior of British Columbia, where my ancestors rest and where my people are,” Grenz says. “The responsibility I feel to them and to our Tmícw, which means our lands, [is] to not take us back to the past, but to show that we have the deep knowledge to help us move forward.”

Yian Yin seeks to understand the dynamics of science itself. The computational social scientist is particularly interested in how innovations happen and how they may be accelerated.
“I want to understand what the secret sources or recipes of success are,” says Yin, of Cornell University.
He applied machine learning techniques to accepted and rejected research proposals to understand how scientists learn from failures. What he found was that scientists fail, and they fail often. Some switched gears after some rejections, but others who continued their research and incorporated feedback found success at a faster rate. Those who changed ideas or scrapped original proposals did not leverage a lot from their experience.
“A group that’s not only failing better and better,” Yin says, “is also failing faster and increasingly faster towards their eventual success.”
More recently, Yin has been investigating how generative AI is changing scientific publishing. Journals are receiving more AI-assisted submissions than ever before, which is leading the peer-review process to falter. More seemingly well-written papers that lack substance are getting through, he found. Coming up with large-scale solutions requires looking at the issue in a measurable way, Yin says.
“Considering both the technological and social side of scientific ecosystems would be something that’s really beneficial for the ongoing public debate and discussion about how we accelerate science in the age of artificial intelligence,” Yin says.

Sebnem Ece Eksi did a double take. Proteins typically studied in the brain were turning up in prostate cancer cells from high-risk patients. These proteins, called neuronal adhesion molecules, play a key role in the circuitry associated with memory.
The finding, made during her Ph.D. days at the University of Illinois Chicago, raised so many questions to which Eksi is still seeking answers. Now at the Oregon Health & Science University in Portland, Eksi has made it her lab’s goal to find out how nervous systems communicate with cancer. What were once two separate fields might be connected more closely than previously thought.
“What we’re learning is that tumors are actively communicating with the nervous system,” Eksi says. “In a way, it makes sense to me that a growing tumor in our bodies, in an organ, would be immediately sensed and detected by the nervous system.”
Eksi now plans to test an AI image-based recognition algorithm to identify nerve fibers in human patients. This is exciting, she says, because these nerves aren’t normally visible in patient tumors. But through biopsies, she hopes to map out and observe how the nervous system — which impacts sleep, cognition and pain — changes as cancer progresses. The implications are significant, she says. Could experts use the nervous system to detect cancer early? Can they improve patients’ quality of life?
“This field of cancer neuroscience can change all different stages of cancer diagnosis and treatments,” Eksi says. “It’s growing so quickly, the field itself.”

Wildlife enthusiasts have made a record-breaking number of sightings of an elusive moth at a nature reserve.
The Fisher's estuarine moth has been spotted 111 times at Abbotts Hall in Great Wigborough, near Colchester, in 2026.
Dr Zoe Ringwood, of Essex Wildlife Trust, said work to boost the highly threatened species' population had been an "important success story".
The charity has pledged to continue surveying new and existing plots on the Essex coast.
Fisher's estuarine moths can be recognised by their pale gold-brown wing colour with light and dark spots, and are naturally found in low-lying areas of natural grassland which are vulnerable to erosion.
They are reliant on rare hog's fennel for their survival, but the plant has been affected by rising sea levels.
To protect the species, Essex Wildlife Trust planted hog's fennel at Abbotts Hall in 2005 and introduced moth eggs five years later.
More than 100 of the scarce insect were recorded for the first time in 2025, before the record was broken again in 2026.
The charity said it was confident there was now a self-sustaining population at Abbotts Hall.
"[It is] a reflection of how taking evidence-based conservation action can achieve positive results for a threatened Essex species," said Ringwood, its senior conservation evidence manager.
Hog's fennel has also been planted at nature reserves in Fingringhoe, Wrabness and nearby Tollesbury.

At least three people have been killed and 36 were still missing after a fire at a confectionary factory in western Java on Saturday.
Firefighters were still tackling some flames on Sunday, while rescuers searched for the missing in parts of the damaged building where workers were believed to be trapped.
Indonesia's National Search and Rescue Agency said on Sunday 15 survivors had been located, and four others taken to hospital and a local clinic with undisclosed injuries.
The factory is in Serang district, Banten province, about 50km west of Jakarta. Authorities have not yet determined the fire's cause.
Banten Governor, Andra Soni, told media about 60 people were believed to be inside the factory when it caught fire.
Photos and footage of the scene showed the large factory taken over by flames during the night, firefighters battling the flames, and first responders retrieving at least one body from the wreckage on Sunday morning.
"All members of the joint SAR team are making every effort to locate the missing victims while prioritising the safety of personnel on the ground," the rescue agency said.
Relatives of the missing workers had gathered outside the factory waiting for updates, according to local broadcasts cited by AFP.
Firefighters had been called to the building at 1630 local time (0930 GMT) but it was already engulfed in flames, broadcaster Kompas TV reported, citing fire official Tubugas Machfudz.
"When we arrived (on location)... a large area was already on fire. So we could not determine whether the company's protection system was functioning properly or not," he said.
The factory is owned by PT Fonusa Agung Mulia, according to search and rescue authorities.
On LinkedIn the company describes itself as a subsidiary of UNIFAM, one of Indonesia's largest food and beverage companies.

Talks were set to resume at the UN COP31 summit on Sunday for a second day of overtime as countries struggled to reach a new global climate deal.
A new draft agreement was published in the early hours of Sunday which the Turkey and Australia co-hosts hoped would bridge the divide between nations.
Although it still includes no specific reference to "transitioning away from fossil fuels" - an omission in the previous draft that sparked threats of walkouts - it does acknowledge a previous commitment made by countries to do just that three years ago.
And it includes for the first time a recognition that the world is on track to miss the crucial goal of keeping temperatures below 1.5C of warming.
The president of the talks, Turkey's Environment Minister Murat Kurum, told the BBC he was "hopeful" of a breakthrough as he entered the summit on Sunday.
"We will be happy soon enough," he said.
But that outlook was not shared by the EU, which the BBC understands considers the new text to be a backward step.
The EU and Pacific states had been arguing against the removal of fossil fuels from the draft text. The EU has not yet reacted to this latest draft.
The Africa Group is likely to be disappointed at this latest iteration as it includes no specific figure on money for adaptation and instead kicks that decision to future meetings.
Countries were expected to reconvene at 09:00 local time (06:00GMT) to decide whether to approve a new deal, but that meeting has now been delayed further.
These talks are approaching the longest-running in the COP history.
If countries cannot reach consensus - as required by the UN's climate talks process - the negotiations could be suspended until next year. This has only happened once before since countries started holding COP climate meetings in 1995.
Just hours before the new text was published, EU Commissioner for Climate Wopke Hoekstra said if the bloc could not get "what is needed in terms of climate action... then there's no deal."
Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh, the UK's chief negotiator, struck a more hopeful tone, saying her team was still working to get an agreement.
A draft deal unveiled earlier this week called for a faster phase-out of fossil fuels, but a second, pared-down version released on Thursday stripped away all mentions of coal, oil and gas - sparking threats of a walk out.
The fallout led to the summit in Antalya blowing past the original deadline of Friday. On Saturday negotiating teams who had Sunday morning flights were rescheduling them - a sign a deal was still not in sight, and raising the risk that as teams eventually had to leave, the meeting could lose the critical numbers needed to pass an agreement.
As part of a last ditch effort to produce an acceptable text, the European Union and Saudi Arabia - who were deeply divided over the future of fossil fuels - were brought together on Saturday to seek a compromise.
COP31 President and Turkish Environment Minister Murat Kurum told delegates in the early hours of Sunday he believed concerns had been addressed.
"We ask you to look at this decision carefully," Kurum said. "We are closer than ever to agreement on the remaining issues."
What has the issue been?
Ministers from Panama, Solomon Islands, Cote d'Ivoire and the EU were fighting to have a commitment to move away from fossil fuels put back into the final agreement, after fossil fuel producers led by Saudi Arabia pushed for its removal.
"It is not acceptable to have a COP or a cover decision that does not even mention fossil fuels and we simply will not put up with it," said Juan Carlos Navarro, Panama's minister for the environment.
Tuvalu's Climate Minister Maina Talia told reporters it was a "red line" for the low-lying Pacific nation: "We're talking about the root cause of all of this".
France's Minister of Ecological Transition, Monique Barbut, took aim at several references in the text to carbon capture, use and storage (CCUS) - the technology that takes emissions when they are released and stores them underground - as a licence for other countries to keep burning oil and gas.
"We cannot be announcing to the world that we are now getting to 1.5 increase in the temperature and do business like nothing was happening," Barbut said.
In the latest text the commitments to CCUS have been reduced, which may be enough to alleviate the EU's concerns.
For the first time at a COP, the agreement - known officially as the Antalya Accords - could acknowledge that the goal set under the Paris climate accord of keeping global temperature rise below 1.5C has been missed.
The world is entering a period called "overshoot".
Beyond this point scientists warn millions more people will be exposed to sea level rise and extreme heat.
But Australia's Climate Change and Energy Minister, Chris Bowen, who is leading negotiations, pushed back on the need to include language on fossil fuels.
He argued the summit was about implementation, and should focus on the move towards clean energy sources.
'We did not come here to beg'
One of the other key issues raised by developing nations - the lack of money - appears unresolved in the latest draft agreement.
Earlier versions of the text included an agreement to ramp up money for adaptation to $120bn (Â£91bn) by 2035 - a figure that was then removed.
"We did not come here to beg, we came here to claim what is rightfully ours for our people who are suffering the brunt of anthropogenic activities of developed countries," said Zanetor Agyeman Rawlings, Ghana's Environment Minister and chair of the African Group of negotiators.
Climate activists and environmental groups, who are observers to these talks, have slammed negotiations.
"I can tell you without any doubt that this has been the worst COP ever," said Mohamed Adow of Powershift Africa.

Abdulhadi Dalhatu is something of a rarity in Nigeria politics.
At 38, he is among the young people seeking elected office in a country where about 80% of the population is under 40.
He hopes his age will stand in his favour as he campaigns for a seat in the state assembly in the northern Kano state in January's general elections.
"Younger people are the majority in this country and should be deciding the future," Dalhatu tells the BBC.
But Nigeria's political history suggests he faces an uphill battle.
Since the return to civilian rule in 1999, Goodluck Jonathan has been the youngest person elected president, taking office at the age of 53.
The current president, Bola Tinubu, is 74 and would be 79 by the end of a second term if he is re-elected in January.
His main challengers are also considerably older. Atiku Abubakar, seeking the presidency for the seventh time, is 79, while Peter Obi is 65.
Of the 18 presidential candidates, only one is under 40 - Moses Olusoji Adebisi, a 35-year-old businessman representing the Democratic Leadership Alliance (DLA).
Although he says he is confident of winning, few Nigerians appear to know much about him and he has not been seen much on the campaign trail.
The contrast is striking in a country with one of the world's youngest populations, where young people have repeatedly demonstrated their ability to shape political debate and mobilise for change.
In the previous election, Obi, then 61, galvanised millions of young Nigerians through a social media-driven movement known as the "Obedients".
His campaign promised a break from the established political order, appealing particularly to young people struggling to find jobs and earn a decent living.
But his failure to win the presidency left many of his supporters disillusioned.
"At the time we were so hopeful, but unfortunately the result wasn't what we wanted, which made many lose hope in the system," former Obedient Nonso Chukwudi tells the BBC.
The movement had built on the momentum of the EndSars protests in 2020, which grew into one of Nigeria's biggest youth-led movement in decades.
Initially sparked by anger over police brutality, the demonstrators developed into a wider call for political reform, accountability and greater youth participation in governance.
But the protests were eventually crushed by the authorities. About 56 were reportedly killed, although officials dispute this figure, while hundreds were arrested and some had their bank accounts frozen.
Both EndSars and the Obedients demonstrated the capacity of young Nigerians to mobile around political causes.
But turning that enthusiasm into sustained electoral participation has proved much harder.
Hajara Musa, 33, is among those who have lost faith in the political system. She has no plans to register or vote in the near future.
"I just feel like things are already determined and I'll just be wasting my time. It is going to be the same people all over again," she tells the BBC.
The electoral register appears to reflect this growing disillusionment.
Although the number of registered voters has increased by 10 million to over 103 million since the last election, enrolment of those under 35 has actually fallen, by about seven million.
Young people now account for just 29% of registered voters, down from 40% in 2023.
Nigeria's electoral commission, Inec, says it has made efforts to encourage more young people to register ahead of the 2027 general elections.
This includes appointing nine ambassadors from the entertainment industry, spanning film, music and comedy, to reach younger audiences.
But the figures suggest these efforts have yet to make a significant difference.
Dalhatu says he understands the frustration but argues that young Nigerians cannot expect change, if they stay away from the political process.
"Unfortunately, many prefer to just post on social media" instead of getting involved, he says.
Of course being young does not mean you are necessarily the best candidate.
For those who want to participate, there is a formidable obstacle to getting into politics - money.
Dalhatu dreams of becoming president one day, but says he has previously had to abandon campaigns because he could not raise enough funds.
The cost of running for office in Nigeria is notoriously high.
Under the Electoral Act, presidential candidates were allowed to spend up to 5bn naira (Â£2.8m; $3.7m) on campaigns ahead of the 2023 elections. That spending limit has since been doubled.
The cost of nomination forms alone puts the presidency beyond the reach of most aspiring young Nigerians.
The ruling All Progressive Congress (APC), along with the Peoples Democratic Party (PDP) and the African Democratic Congress (ADC) have each set their presidential nomination fee at 100m naira ($74,000; Â£56,000), making it extremely hard for new challengers to emerge.
Since the return to democracy in 1999, only two parties have governed Nigeria - the PDP from 1999 to 2015 and the APC since 2015.
These parties, alongside the ADC, formed last year by politicians who had defected from the other two, have established nationwide network of branches, supporters and campaigners.
Those aspiring candidates without the financial resources to secure nomination forms and compete in the internal party contests of the main parties have little chances of becoming president.
The barriers are also evident in the National Assembly.
Not one of Nigeria's 109 senators is under 40, while only 14 of the 360 members of the House of Representatives fall into that age group.
"I have been in politics for many years and I will tell you that young people in this country lack the resources to become president," says Dalhatu, who is running under Obi's Nigeria Democratic Congress.

Sixteen-year-old Landon Tresp was in the bedroom of his family's Colorado mountain home, playing an online game after finishing his daily chores, when he began chatting on his laptop with another player.
She was also a teenager, and the pair "kind of just clicked," he tells the BBC.
He told her he liked her name, and she confessed that it was an alias. She was a runaway, she said - and was being held against her will, hundreds of miles from home, though she didn't know exactly where. The girl, 17, and had been missing for more than a year.
Stunned, Landon felt "helpless," he says - and, after learning more details over two weeks of chatting, he decided to tell his mother, Khristina on 31 October this year. The 41-year-old nurse and mother of five was putting Halloween makeup on her younger children for trick-or-treating when he briefed her.
That set the mother and son on a path to track down his friend, contact her mother, cooperate with the FBI - and ultimately witness the rescue of the teen - only 24 hours after Landon first alerted Khristina to her plight.
"She had one opportunity to reach out her hand and ask for help, and she chose me," Khristina says of the girl, who was 15 when she went missing.
The Tresps have shared with BBC screenshots of communication with the girl and a photo matching the criminal complaint to corroborate their story.
Landon first told his mother about "Jenny" - whose identity the BBC is protecting - in mid-October, a few weeks before the rescue.
"He had mentioned something about maybe a week or so into talking to her that he met a girl online, and she was really sweet," says Khristina - who cautioned him that "you don't always know who's on the other side of the screen".
"She's just having a really hard time and looking for a friend," he told her.
But Landon was becoming increasingly concerned as Jenny told him more about her situation.
They'd met playing Among Us, a game Landon describes as "kind of like online space Clue".
After telling Landon that she was a runaway, "Jenny" said an older man had taken her across state lines and wouldn't let her leave. She was the subject of a missing person investigation, and she sent Landon links to stories about her disappearance. But she believed police were no longer looking for her.
Jenny was scared and desperate, and that's why Landon went to his mother.
Her maternal instincts on high alert, Khristina contacted Jenny herself on Discord, the encrypted platform.
During the conversation, Khristina said she told the Colorado mother how she'd been through "years of abuse in her life and lots and lots of problems".
Within hours, Jenny started calling Khristina "mama".
The Colorado mother knew things were serious when she read the missing persons articles. Jenny knew she was in Oregon and gave the name of a city, but she didn't know where she was being held exactly. Khristina knew she needed more. She told Jenny to find a piece of mail or another document in the house that had a full name on it, which the girl did.
"That's when I went to work," Khristina says, delving into tax and property records.
Khristina narrowed down addresses, then searched them on a real estate site to find pictures. She showed the photos to Jenny, who confirmed that the second one was where she was being held.
The "next thing she asked me was to please not tell anyone until [her captor] was gone - that he did have weapons in the house and she was very scared," Khristina said.
Jenny promised Khristina she'd call her back through the game platform when he left the next morning, and in the meantime Khristina began looking for the law enforcement agency that had been assigned to the missing teen's case. She contacted Jenny's mother on social media, spoke briefly to her on the phone and then got a call from an FBI agent.
"Have you seen her alive?'" the agent asked Khristina.
"And I said: 'I have; I video chatted with her, I've seen her, and she goes 'Oh my God, I cannot believe any of this'," Khristina recalled.
When Jenny called Khristina back after her alleged captor left home, the FBI monitored their conversation. According to the criminal complaint's record of the conversation, Jenny explained how she'd met Adam Hunter Harmel on social media in May 2025.
He'd told her he was disabled and his hips were "messed up," offering Jenny money if she'd help get him to Oregon.
After he picked her up in Utah, however, Harmel threw her phone into a river, drove her to Oregon and kept her in the basement. He forced her to sleep against the wall in his bed, with a knife under his pillow, to prevent her from escaping. He gave Jenny a cell phone with no ability to make calls, but it could connect to wifi, which is how she played the online game.
The 39-year-old "would become violent and aggressive", the document says, which included hitting her and sexually assaulting her.
He also allegedly forced Jenny to remove her braces with pliers so she wouldn't be identifiable.
As Khristina and the FBI heard all of this, law enforcement were staging to bring Jenny to safety, after being alerted to her whereabouts.
While Harmel was out of the home, officers were sent to the street and the address, and Khristina was prepping Jenny for her run to freedom.
She'd unsuccessfully tried escaping before, she told Khristina.

Canada joins NATO innovation fund, promises ‘business as usual’ with US
But the investment is a pointed reaction to the Trump administration’s dwindling cooperation with its northern ally.
HALIFAX, Nova Scotia—Hours after news broke that the United States would limit defense cooperation with Canada, the Canadian government announced plans to pour 100 million Canadian dollars into a NATO defense-innovation fund. “As far as we're concerned, it's business as usual,” Defense Minister David McGuinty said when asked about the news.
It was a calm reply about an extraordinary development between formerly close allies, but in one sense, it was quite true. As the Trump administration reduces its contributions to the alliance—and in some cases threatens military action against its members—they are increasing their efforts to build their own militaries and industry.
The Canadian decision pushes total commitments to the NATO Innovation Fund past 1.1 billion euros. Joining the fund also makes Canadian defense startups eligible to draw upon it, giving them another source of capital and access to the fund’s network of venture capitalists.
The NIF is a way to connect startups with investors and military users across the alliance to “help successful solutions reach scale,” Tarja Jaakkola, NATO’s assistant secretary general for defense industry, innovation, and armaments, said at a recent NATO conference in Izmir, Turkey.
In June 2024, for instance, German ground robot maker ARX Robotics raised 9 million euros in a seed round. The NIF led the round and provided more than half the money. In April 2025, ARX raised 31 million euros in a Series A round led by HV Capital. In July, Austrian venture capital firm Speedinvest led an 11 million euro extension, bringing its Series A total to 42 million euros.
But competition for the money is stiff. In April 2025, NIF partner Patrick Schneider-Sikorsky said the fund had seen “thousands” of deals and invested in about 10 companies.
Canada’s pledge is a bet on collective action. The funds could have gone directly to Canadian firms, and there’s no guarantee that any of the money will come back home.
There is “no pro rata in the NATO Innovation Fund. It is finding the best technologies that best address the capability needs of the alliance,” NIF President Ari Kristinn Jónsson said here on Saturday.
The announcement came hours after a White House news conference at which President Donald Trump again accused Canada, the United States’ second-largest trading partner, of unfair trade practices.
“For some reason they feel emboldened and we can’t let them feel that way anymore,” Trump said.
Over the summer, the president imposed 50-percent tariffs on several types of Canadian products, claiming that Canada discriminates against American autos, alcohol and cheese. But, as PBS has reported, Trump’s argument “rests in large part on retaliatory actions taken by Canada after the U.S. president imposed tariffs on Canada under the pretext that it should do more to stop fentanyl smuggling.”
Shortly afterward, the Washington Post reported that Pentagon leaders had issued a secret memo restricting military cooperation between the United States and Canada.
Canadian officials said they had learned of the memo from news reports and had yet to see it.
In Halifax for the 18th Halifax International Security Forum, Sen. Mike Rounds, R-S.D., said the memo was months old and limited only flag officers’ participation in social events. Rounds said it “does not impact any DoD personnel that are in Canada today. It does not impact NORAD. It does not impact NATO operations or [the Five Eyes intelligence sharing partnership]]. Does not impact general or flag officer meetings.”
McGuinty pointed to more than 70 years of military cooperation between Canada and the United States.
“We have Canadian vessels interdicting drug trafficking in the Caribbean, working alongside American vessels. So that cooperation remains ongoing,” he said, adding that, as far as he knew, cooperation through NORAD and intelligence-sharing agreements continued as before.
“As far as we're concerned, it's business as usual.

9fffc85d9ad1.text: We've talked to more than 50 leaders in government, AI, business and cyber — from let-'er-rip AI accelerationists to shut-'er-down critics — and they were unanimous on one chilling assessment: Cyberattacks on business and critical infrastructure will be constant, increasingly sophisticated and highly disruptive over the next 18 months. These leaders describe 2027 as the year cyber becomes like weather: Outages will be frequent, disruptive, occasionally scary, and something people and companies must learn to navigate and live with daily. The chances of widespread disruption or real damage are rising fast. Why it matters: We write this neither to forecast nor frighten. Rather, we're sharing what government and AI leaders say privately but won't say publicly. The big picture: The disruptions of the past two weeks — from a global Microsoft outage to the FAA grounding air travel to a consumer banking glitch at Chase — were a mild preview of what experts expect is coming. Bridgewater Associates, the world's largest hedge fund , put it bluntly in an assessment this month: "[We] are managing money based on a one-in-three chance of an economically destabilizing attack within the next year." Horacio Rozanski , chairman and CEO of Booz Allen, calls this the "fog before the war" — a foretaste of greater chaos to come, when agentic invaders reach their full potential and can attack "at the speed of thought." "Now is the time to take as many precautions as you can," Rozanski said. "Recognize that this is coming." Most of these malfunctions appear to have resulted from companies and government trying to secure their computer and infrastructure systems against future large-scale cyberattacks. This pattern will persist. Many future ones will be actual cyberattacks, carried out by U.S. rivals or smaller bad actors, using increasingly powerful AI to spot and exploit security vulnerabilities across society and our daily lives. Most top AI and government leaders expect at least small-scale strikes and fear much larger ones. The best-case scenario described to us: regular, random outages and small-scale scares like losing bank access or air travel for a day. The reason: Every government agency and company will mobilize to upgrade their software systems. So errors are inevitable. These are assumptions based on private intelligence and an understanding of AI's capabilities, both to cause and fix glitches. What worries top officials most : With thin AI expertise, an understaffed government and major companies are trying to keep pace with a technology that improves daily. Even if government were loaded with competent experts, which it decidedly isn't, the sheer scale of vulnerabilities across federal, state and local government, not to mention all of business, would make it impossible to reliably secure. Think of it as whack-a-mole with infinite moles. Until this past month, the White House and Congress have focused largely on safety regulations and data centers, not imminent cyber risks. Now, even the White House's Super Intelligence Force ( SIF ) is scrambling to get its head around the rising risks while appraising near-daily reports of possible breaches. And President Trump just ousted the White House national cyber director and named Kirsten Davies, who was the Pentagon's chief information officer, as the replacement. Davies has deeper subject-matter expertise than her predecessor, former RNC official Sean Cairncross . Step back: Only by understanding the state of AI + cyber can government and business mobilize to prevent possible shutdowns across critical banking, electricity and water systems. This is our crack at distilling our conversations in a digestible way for Axios readers: The double-edged sword. The good news: America's frontier AI labs (Anthropic, OpenAI, Google, etc.) built the most powerful AI on the planet, especially for building software. The bad news: AI that's great at building software is equally great at finding — and exploiting — its vulnerabilities, often called "bugs" or "holes." The new dangers of old technologies. Government and business operate mostly on computer systems that were built for a pre-AI world. They're full of those bugs and holes. One vulnerability — exploited by a bad actor, or even triggered by someone trying a repair in good faith — can shut down an entire company or all air travel, as we just witnessed. China foresaw this moment. A Beijing-sponsored hacking group, Volt Typhoon, has lurked in American critical infrastructure — water, energy, transportation and communications networks — for more than five years. A sister group, Salt Typhoon , broke into major U.S. phone carriers and took call records and wiretap data. The full number of compromised systems is unknown. The administration's view is that China isn't slowing down and the U.S. can't cede any advantage. America is scrambling — and struggling — to catch up. Remember when Anthropic held back its Mythos AI model because of its breathtaking and scary cyber capabilities? Since then, some global companies , including JPMorgan Chase, have used Mythos and other technologies to locate and repair their vulnerabilities. Our intelligence agencies did the same. But most of government and American business haven't. Cyber defense is costly. Lots of government agencies and businesses simply can't afford to safeguard their systems. The biggest companies can outbid others for top-tier cyber protection. The best firms are largely booked. Bluntly, many businesses hesitate to spend millions on pure loss unless they're convinced a threat is imminent. The coming swarm. AI is getting better and better. And the ability of swarms of agents to act autonomously rises each week.
