ABOARD THE MV SHARKWATER—At 5 a.m. on a Sunday in September, crew members aboard the MV Sharkwater, a ship operated by the Sea Shepherd Conservation Society, readied a small inflatable motorboat tied alongside the larger vessel for a pre-dawn mission.
The night before, the crew received a report about an illegal sport fishing boat anchored just off Isla Desterrada, a sandy islet inside the Alacranes Reef National Park, a federally protected area located about 70 miles off the northern coast of the Yucatán peninsula. At more than 1,300 square miles, the park includes the largest coral reef in the Gulf of Mexico.
Images captured by a drone pilot for Sea Shepherd, an international marine conservation nonprofit, showed seven men from the boat setting up camp on the island. The crew was eager to confront them before they headed out to sea.
“We want to catch them before they leave to go fishing,” said David Hance, Sea Shepherd’s director of operations, slipping on his lifejacket as he prepared to step onto the smaller vessel rocking in the dark early-morning swells. They would need to move fast, though, he said.
Since the 1970s, Sea Shepherd has dispatched crews around the world to investigate, document and disrupt activities that jeopardize marine life. They run direct-action campaigns to stop industrial krill fishing in Antarctica, mass dolphin hunts in the Faroe Islands and poaching in the Upper Gulf of California.
Combating illegal fishing inside Alacranes Reef National Park—commonly referred to as Scorpion Reef—is one of the organization’s newest initiatives aimed at helping Mexico safeguard some of its most prized marine protected areas where fishing and other potentially harmful activities are banned or highly regulated to safeguard important ecosystems like coral reefs.
Globally, coral reefs provide vital habitat for at least 25 percent of all marine life, including at least 4,000 types of fish. But climate change is jeopardizing their future. Rising ocean temperatures and frequent marine heat waves are driving 96 percent of the world’s shallow reefs towards collapse.
To conserve coral reefs and boost their resilience, many scientists say it is vital to include them in marine protected areas where local pressures like overfishing, illegal fishing and pollution are alleviated.
Coral reefs need abundant fish populations to thrive. Herbivorous species like parrotfish feed on algae that can take over a reef, especially when corals are stressed by heat, disease and other disturbances. Predators like grouper and snapper also help keep smaller fish populations in check, maintaining a healthy, balanced ecosystem.
“Effectively managed marine protected areas are one of the strongest tools we have in protecting coral reefs and protecting the biodiversity that they host,” said Mishal Gudka, a coral reef scientist from Kenya who recently spearheaded a global assessment of shallow coral ecosystems for the International Union for Conservation of Nature.
But turning that promise into reality requires more than drawing boundaries on a map. These areas need people to actively defend them.
Flying Drones
The day before Hance set out on the early morning mission to Isla Desterrada, the 141-foot Sharkwater, a former Japanese fishing vessel, had anchored off Isla Perez, the only island inside the park that has a lighthouse and a small Mexican Navy outpost.
Another smaller live-aboard vessel owned by Sea Shepherd called the MV Roger Payne hung closer to Isla Desterrada, which in English means “Exiled Island.”
Every few hours the two crews surveyed much of the area with drones. From this viewpoint, they could not only spot other vessels, but also identify their names, registration numbers and how many people they had on board. This information is then cross-referenced with a daily list the National Commission of Natural Protected Areas keeps of vessels they’ve authorized to be in the park. If they’re not on the list, the crew goes to inspect them. And the fishers spotted on Isla Desterrada were not on the list.
From the drone photos, the crew could see several men making a campfire on the beach. Others rested on inflatable sleeping mats or chairs wedged into the sand where sea turtles are known to nest nearby. Hance and the rest of the crew decided the best plan of action would be to surprise the fishers the next morning.
30×30
In 2022, Mexico joined nearly 200 countries in adopting the Kunming-Montreal Biodiversity Framework, a landmark United Nations agreement aimed at halting and reversing the widespread biodiversity loss driven by climate change, pollution and other human activities that alter natural ecosystems.
As part of this agreement, participating countries have committed to conserving 30 percent of Earth’s terrestrial, inland waters and coastal and marine areas by 2030. Since then, Mexico has made significant progress towards achieving that goal, often referred to as 30×30. Around 25 percent of the country’s marine areas are legally protected or conserved—at least in theory.
At least a quarter of ocean areas designated for marine protection around the world lack adequate funding, surveillance and enforcement, clear rules or regulations. As a result, many become what scientists refer to as “paper parks”—areas that are legally recognized on paper, but don’t have the proper safeguards in place to achieve their conservation goals.
For many years, Scorpion Reef had come close to being one of them, said Tomás Camarena, director of the Alacranes Reef National Park and two other marine protected areas managed by Mexico’s National Commission of Natural Protected Areas.
According to the park’s rules, anyone who enters the area must first obtain a permit from the national commission, which sets limits on the number of people and boats allowed inside each day. South Korea's Education Minister Choi Kyo-jin has resigned over an exam cheating scandal that shocked the nation.
He said he took full responsibility for the confusion caused by last-minute measures aimed at stopping AI-assisted cheating during Thursday's annual college entrance exam, known as Suneung.
A week ago, the top scorer in the national tax accountancy exam admitted using a mini-camera, mobile phone and AI tools. This prompted officials to act urgently to detect hidden devices, including sending emergency alerts to every single mobile phone in the country.
The Suneung takes up to nine hours to complete, and it plays a big role in career trajectories of millions of South Koreans.
"As the minister in charge, I believe I cannot escape criticism that we failed to prepare in advance," Choi was quoted as saying on Sunday by South Korea's Yonhap's news agency.
"Now that the exam has concluded, I feel a deep sense of responsibility and am offering my resignation," the minister added.
South Korean President Lee Jae Myung - who has been calling for an overhaul of the current exam system - later accepted Choi's resignation.
The education ministry earlier said 111 candidates had been found with unauthorised smart devices during this year's Suneung, which was taken by about 500,000 students.
Concerns over academic dishonesty during the fiercely competitive exam had been brewing in recent weeks, after reports of candidates cheating with the help of AI devices.
These fears came to a boil last weekend, when Han Won-seok, the top tax accountancy exam scorer in April, admitted to cheating.
His confession came amid speculation over his unusually high score, with just one out of 160 questions wrong.
"I used a microcamera to photograph the test questions and sent them to an AI, then checked my answers on my smartphone to commit the cheating," the 34-year-old said in a video message.
This prompted the authorities to introduce urgent measures, with just days ahead of the Suneung.
This included sending nationwide emergency alerts on the exam day.
Three alerts were sent between 08:00 and 15:00 local time on Thursday, causing phones across the country to blare out in unison - even if they were on silent mode, and even if they belonged to tourists using data roaming.
The phones did not ring out if they were switched off or on airplane mode.
It was the first time that South Korea used its national disaster alert system to catch exam cheaters.
Candidates also had to cover up the buttons on their shirts and jackets to block any hidden cameras, and authorities conducted inspections of eyewear.
All this made even honest test takers paranoid.
Ahead of the Suneung, one high school senior told the Korea Times he was worried his horn-rimmed spectacles would be mistaken for smart glasses.
Another told Yonhap he usually wore glasses but made an effort to put on contact lenses for the Suneung to avoid raising suspicions.

Italian jeweller Paolo Bulgari, who helped turn his family's business into a global luxury brand, has died in Rome aged age 89.
His family announced the news, remembering him as "the greatest jeweller of our time", according to Italian media.
Paolo Bulgari was Chairman of the Bvlgari Group since 1984 and its jewellery pieces have adorned Hollywood stars and royalty including Diana, Princess of Wales.
The company Bvlgari posted an online tribute to the "true creative soul", whose work would "continue to inspire generations to come".
The firm, Bulgari, was set up by his grandfather, Greek silversmith Sotirios Voulgaris, in Rome in the late 19th century - who later adapted his name to Bulgari in Italian.
Originally from Paramythia, a mountain village in the Epirus region of northwestern Greece renowned for its silver jewellery, Voulgaris fled Ottoman rule and settled in Naples before opening a shop in Rome.
Paolo Bulgari joined the company shortly after leaving school, becoming an expert in gemstones - eventually leading the business and overseeing international growth.
The Bulgari family favoured bold gemstones, rich yellow gold, generous proportions and unexpected colour combinations to set them apart from the delicate asethetic associated with Parisian jewellery houses.
The business broke into luxury markets and diversified beyond jewellery into watches, perfumes, leather goods and hotels.
"Paolo Bulgari began collaborating with his father in 1960, specialising in the knowledge of precious stones, of which he was one of the world's leading experts, and refining the sensibility and aesthetic sense that are at the root of the Bvlgari style," the Bvlgari company posted on social media., external
"He poured his heart into his craft and into nurturing the talents of young designers, leaving an indelible mark on the world of jewellery.
"Thank you, Mr. Paolo, your legacy as a brilliant beacon of creative inspiration will continue to inspire generations to come."
The post included a quote from Paolo Bulgari: "Everything can be a source of inspiration. There are no rules in creativity. Never."
The designer brand's celebrity clients have included Elizabeth Taylor, Audrey Hepburn, Marilyn Monroe, Ingrid Bergman, Sophie Loren, Anne Hathaway, Zendaya and Rihanna.
In 2011 the family sold its controlling stake to the French luxury group LVMH, in a deal worth about 3.7 billion euros.
In 2019, he and his wife established the Paolo Bulgari Foundation to support young people through schooling and job training in disadvantaged neighbourhoods on the outskirts of Rome.
The funeral will take place in Rome on Monday, 23 November in the Basilica of Santa Croce in Gerusalemme.

Miley Cyrus has married her partner of four years Maxx Morando during a ceremony in Palm Springs, California.
A string of black and white photos shared by the Flowers singer on Instagram showed the pair kissing while surrounded by white roses.
Her mother, Trisha Cyrus, and sister, Noah Cyrus, could be seen in the background of one image. Her father Billy Ray Cyrus was not in the picture but was at the ceremony with his partner, actress Liz Hurley.
Grammy-winning Cyrus, 33, wore a white silk dress designed by Anthony Vaccarello for Saint Laurent, while 28-year-old drummer Morando said "I do" in a black suit from the same fashion house.
In one of the photographs, which was the first in a series of images shared by the singer in an Instagram post, the newly weds posed next to a golden retriever.
The post was captioned with "M+M" followed by a white heart and the ceremony date, 21 November.
Miley's sister Brandi Cyrus, singer Doechii and fashion designer Donatella Versace were among those to congratulate the couple in the comments.
The ceremony reportedly took place at a resort formerly owned by Fly Me To The Moon singer Frank Sinatra.
Guests stuck to an all-black dress code, according to reports.
The American singer confirmed her engagement to the 28-year-old drummer during an interview with US TV show Good Morning America last year.
She said Morando had got down on one knee for the proposal during a trip to Asia.
"I am not easy to surprise because I love to control every situation and I had completely surrendered and I'm telling you, I was so, so, so surprised," she said.
During an interview with Wonderland, Morando said he "had to be really sneaky" to keep his proposal plans a secret.
"We went to Tokyo first for a couple days, and then on to Kyoto. I think she had a sense that it was coming, so I was waiting until the very last moment of the very last day to throw her off the scent as much as I could," he said.
Cyrus, 33, had previously been married to Australian actor Liam Hemsworth but the couple separated in 2019.
The singer, whose hits include Party in the U.S.A and Wrecking Ball, married Hunger Games star Hemsworth in 2018 after the couple were in a relationship for a decade.
Speaking to British Vogue in 2023, Cyrus said she and 28-year-old Morando met after being "put on a blind date".
Morando is a drummer with LA-based band Liily. The band participated in NBC's Miley's New Year's Eve Party - hosted by Cyrus - in 2022, alongside musicians including Cyrus's late godmother Dolly Parton and David Byrne.

49dfa92aa0ba.text: By — Dee-Ann Durbin, Associated Press Dee-Ann Durbin, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/nation/appeals-court-says-federal-law-requiring-accommodations-for-pregnant-workers-is-unconstitutional Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Appeals court says federal law requiring accommodations for pregnant workers is unconstitutional Nation Nov 22, 2026 4:21 PM EST An appeals court has struck down a federal law that requires workplaces to provide accommodations for pregnant women, saying Congress violated the U.S. Constitution when it passed the law in 2022. The New Orleans-based 5th Circuit Court of Appeals issued its 9-8 decision on Friday. Advocates of the Pregnant Workers Fairness Act said the decision invalidates the law in Texas, Louisiana and Mississippi, which are covered by the 5th Circuit, and could imperil the law elsewhere. WATCH: The state of anti-discrimination laws for pregnant workers in America The appeals court said the act was unconstitutional because a majority of U.S. House members weren't physically present when it was approved as part of a spending package in December 2022. At the time, the House was operating under COVID-era rules that allowed members to vote by proxy. "The (Quorum) Clause's text, context, original understanding and unbroken historical application all indicate that members of Congress must be present for quorum purposes — as the Supreme Court expressly held over 125 years ago and as Congress has done ever since the founding," the court said in its decision. "'Proxy presence' does not count." A Better Balance, an advocacy group that spearheaded the law's passage, said in a statement Friday that the circuit court ruling would likely be appealed to the U.S. Supreme Court. Inimai Chettiar, the group's president, said the ruling was "legally unsound and short-sighted." "The 5th Circuit has put the health, livelihoods, and economic security of millions of American women and their families at risk," Chettiar said in a statement. The law, which passed with bipartisan support, strengthens the rights of women to receive workplace accommodations for needs related to pregnancy and childbirth, such as time off for medical appointments and exemptions from heavy lifting. Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton sued to block the act in 2023 on grounds that it was unconstitutional. In 2024, a federal judge agreed and blocked enforcement of the law for Texas state employees. But in 2025, a three-judge panel on the 5th Circuit court disagreed, finding that the law was properly passed under Congress's pandemic-era rules. That decision was appealed to the full 5th Circuit. In their dissent, the eight judges who would have upheld the law noted that no member of Congress objected that a quorum was lacking when the $1.7 trillion government funding bill was passed. "The State of Texas, having accepted the vast majority of the funds that Congress appropriated to it, now contends that the portion of the bill providing protections for pregnant women and workers violates the Quorum Clause," they wrote. While the law was passed during the Biden administration, the Department of Justice under the Trump administration has continued to fight Paxton's lawsuit, which — if successful — could open the door to legal challenges of other pandemic-era laws passed by proxy. A message seeking comment on the appeals court decision was left Sunday with the Justice Department. A free press is a cornerstone of a healthy democracy. ef8996ba043d.text: The Pentagon accused Canada of failing to become a "credible partner" due to its faltering military readiness and low defense spending, according to a sharply worded fact sheet issued by the Pentagon to justify new restrictions on America's northern neighbor. Why it matters: The restrictions deepen tensions between the U.S. and Canada over trade and defense, as Ottawa reconsiders billions of dollars in purchases of American weapons. The new restraints — which do not affect defense or intelligence sharing— limit U.S. military personnel from fraternizing with their Canadian counterparts at official events without prior authorization from the Pentagon, an official told Axios. The Pentagon fact sheet has not been reported. But the Washington Post first reported the restrictions, followed by the New York Times . Zoom in: At the heart of the dispute are NATO defense spending goals and military readiness under the bilateral North American Aerospace Defense Command where, the memo says, Canada falls short in three ways: 🛩️ Air: Only 41.9% of the Royal Canadian Air Force fleet "was serviceable from 2025-2026, largely due to ageing equipment and personnel shortages," the Pentagon fact sheet says. The shortfall limits Canada's "ability to meaningfully contribute to air defense commitments … to defend our North American airspace against all threats." Canada relies on the U.S. and NATO for airborne early-warning aircraft but is negotiating to buy its own from Sweden's Saab. ⚓️ Sea: Just 53.9% of Canada's naval fleet was "serviceable" from 2025-2026, limiting its "ability to monitor maritime approaches to North America," the fact sheet says. Only one of Canada's "four ageing Victoria-class submarines" is "seaworthy at any given time." Canada has a new fleet of conventional submarines, manufactured by ThyssenKrupp Marine Systems, coming on line, but until then, its undersea "capability will be limited." 🪖 Land: The Canadian Army had an operational readiness rate of 48% from 2025-2026. The other side: Canada's own defense department reported the same equipment shortages while finding that 61% of its military units were ready for operations. Canada's defense ministry could not be reached. Friction point : NATO defense spending has been a constant sore spot for President Trump. Canada first agreed to spend 2% of GDP on defense spending in 2006, but it was only at 1.5% until 2025, according to the Pentagon. Canada announced in March that it had achieved 2% GDP-defense spending, but now the target is 5% by 2035 and U.S. policy makers say Ottawa "has yet to articulate a resourced path to reach this target. "Canada must get serious and focused," the fact sheet said. The big picture: More defense spending by NATO allies is a revenue generator for the U.S., which has the globe's largest military-industrial complex. "Since March 2025," the Pentagon fact sheet noted, "Ottawa has been reviewing its decision to procure 88 F-35s to replace its ageing fighters and is considering a mixed fleet that will compound existing personnel shortfalls." Canada is increasingly looking to European manufacturers for its military buildup. Context: Relations between the two countries soured when Trump scrapped a free-trade agreement he insisted on in his first term, began a tariff war and threatened to annex Canada as the 51st state. At a Friday news conference, Trump complained about Canada and trade imbalances between the two countries. The bottom line: The two nations remain allies and work closely together on defense issues. Canada has an office in the Pentagon next to the joint staff. The limited restrictions imposed by Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth on official interactions between U.S. and Canadian personnel are a "shot across the bow," a U.S. official said. "Unfortunately," the Pentagon fact sheet said, "Canada has yet to make the hard decisions and tradeoffs needed to put it on track to fulfill its NATO Defense Investment Pledge and become a credible partner in the defense of our shared continent. Canada's defense shortfalls speak for themselves."

An explosion on a Russian ship docked at Benghazi naval base port was caused by a suspected drone attack, Libya's eastern government has said.
The explosion happened at dawn on Sunday, while the ship had stopped for fuel and supplies on its way back to Russia, Libya state media reported, citing the eastern government.
The statement said there were no casualties. Moscow has yet to comment.
Later on Sunday, the health ministry said it had received injured from another vessel, a commercial ship, that was also targeted off the coast of Benghazi, state media reported. Their injuries were minor and their condition stable, the ministry said.
Videos posted on social media and geolocated by BBC Verify show the ship that was struck in the morning engulfed in flames and smoke. Satellite imagery from Planet Labs PBC also shows a boat on fire at 05:47 GMT at the Benghazi port.
US-based intelligence firm Vantor collected high-resolution images that it said showed Project 20380 Steregushchiy-class corvette (Merkury) - a Russian navy ship - moored in the port on Saturday, and on Sunday showed most of the same ship capsized and sunk with only the forward bow still visible.
The eastern-based Government of National Stability (GNS) said the Russian ship - which it did not name or identify - was using the Benghazi port within the framework of an existing maritime agreement.
Sunday's incident is under investigation, and authorities are coordinating with their Russian counterparts to determine the source of the suspected attack and who is responsible for it, GNS added.
GNS condemned the attack on a ship inside a Libyan port, and called it a violation of maritime safety and an attack on their sovereignty. It said Libya was not party to the Russia-Ukraine war, or any other conflict beyond its borders.
Separately, Libya's internationally recognised government in Tripoli - the Government of National Unity (GNU) - warned against hosting foreign forces and allowing them to use facilities in a statement published by state media.
GNU said such activity raises "serious fears" about "risks that may result from involving ports and civilian facilities in activities related to external conflicts, and the resulting threat to the lives of citizens and the safety of national facilities and assets".
Libya fractured into violence and instability after its leader Muammar Gaddafi was overthrown in 2011, leading to the opposing governments.
Benghazi is more than 2,000 km (1,243 miles) away from the Russian capital Moscow.
Although it has not been officially confirmed who was behind the attack, there is little doubt, according to Jalel Harchaoui, Libya specialist at the Royal United Services Institute (RUSI).
"Ukraine is the only actor brazen enough to pull something like that off," he told the BBC. "If I were to bet my own money, I would bet that it was the Ukrainians."
If confirmed, it would not be the first time Ukrainian forces had carried out an operation of this sort. In March, Russia accused Ukraine of targeting the Russian tanker Arctic Metagaz in the Mediterranean between Libya and Malta with "uncrewed sea drones" launched from the Libyan coast.
As well as having an economic impact on Russia, hampering the ability of their so-called shadow fleet of tankers to export oil and gas, attacks like this are seen as humiliating to the Kremlin, according to Harchaoui.
But it is not only Moscow that will want to react to this latest incident. The ship was in the region as part of a deal with the government of eastern Libya - allied with Khalifa Haftar, commander of the Libyan National Army.
Harchaoui said Haftar will take the attack as a personal slight. "You're going to have a response by the Haftar family. They will ask questions about who is hosting the Ukrainians."
Additional reporting by Benedict Garman and Shayan Sardarizadeh

The Democratic Party has won the largest majority in the US House of Representatives since 1992, after Democrat Chuck Hubbard unseated Republican Representative Virginia Foxx in North Carolina.
The race was called on Sunday, with Hubbard beating Foxx by 330 votes with 99% counted. It was one of the closest contests of the recent midterm elections, in which Democrats also secured the Senate.
The party has now won at least 258 House seats in the midterms compared to Republicans, who hold at least 173 seats, with four races still yet to be called.
Neither party had won as many House races since 1992, when Bill Clinton won the presidency and Democrats won a total of 258 seats.
Sunday's result came after Foxx, who has represented North Carolina's 5th Congressional District since 2005, requested a recount. This is allowed under state law when the margin of victory is under 1%.
She conceded on Sunday, saying in a statement: "After running a campaign focused on my track record of commonsense solutions and conservative values, I'm humbled and grateful that so many North Carolina voters responded by supporting my candidacy, even if we came up just a few votes short."
Hubbard, meanwhile, wrote on X that he had spoken to Foxx, "who graciously conceded following the results of the recount process".
He added: "I deeply appreciate her commitment to a smooth transition of the office and constituent casework. We may not always agree, but we both love North Carolina and the people of the Fifth District."
Hubbard's win, which comes after he lost to Foxx in the 2024 midterms by nine percentage points, followed a number of Democratic victories in deeply Republican districts including South Carolina, Texas, Alaska and Iowa.
Hubbard, like many Democrats running in the midterms, focused on the rising cost of living in the US during the war with Iran - a top issue for voters.
President Donald Trump himself has suggested inflation caused by the war in Iran was probably to blame for the Republican losses, as well as Vice President JD Vance.
Hubbard has also said he will also prioritise working families and small businesses, supporting public education and expanding access to affordable healthcare, according to his website.
The remaining House races yet to be called are in Tennessee and Minnesota, while two elections in Louisiana will go to a runoff in December. In Tennessee's fourth district, Democrat Victoria Broderick leads by fewer than 300 votes, and in Minnesota's first district, Democrat Jake Johnson is winning by fewer than 500 votes.
Democrats may use their upcoming majority in the House and control of the Senate to investigate conflicts of interest and other actions by the president and those close to him, while the Senate also has the power to confirm or block the president's cabinet and judicial nominations. They will also be able to pass legislation through Congress easily, though Trump still has to give final sign off for it to become law.
However, even with control of both chambers of Congress, they will still have limits on their power as Trump can veto legislation.

0250dcc570c8.text: By — Jacques Billeaud, Associated Press Jacques Billeaud, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/nation/u-s-army-plans-to-invoke-emergency-provisions-to-detonate-bomb-making-chemicals-in-iowa Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter U.S. Army plans to invoke emergency provisions to detonate bomb-making chemicals in Iowa Nation Nov 22, 2026 3:18 PM EST The U.S. Army plans to invoke emergency provisions to avoid a court order that had put on hold plans to detonate several tons of bomb-making chemicals in Iowa, saying that continued delays will make it more dangerous as the weather starts to turn colder. "To protect its personnel and the surrounding communities, the Army needs to take swift action," government lawyers told the 8th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals in a filing late Saturday. "Protection of human health and the environment demand action now, not delay." WATCH: Court halts Army detonation of bomb chemicals in Iowa Environmental groups criticized the government's move, decrying it as a maneuver to get around a court order and avoid public demands for safety and transparency. The appeals court on Thursday granted a request by environmentalists to put on hold a permit that cleared the way for the detonation in Middletown, a small community about 160 miles (257 kilometers) southeast of Des Moines. It was initially planned for Friday, but the Army later announced that it would push the operation to Monday following an outpouring of public concern about potential health and environmental effects. Environmentalists have called for a review of the emergency permit that was approved earlier this month by the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency. In a statement Sunday, the Iowa Environmental Council, Sierra Club, and Earthjustice questioned claims that all alternatives were given appropriate consideration. "The Army seemed more concerned over the weekend with finding a way to sidestep the judicial process than on meeting the public's demands for greater transparency, notice to affected communities, and far stronger protection of people, property, and the environment from serious harm," said Earthjustice Attorney Thien Chau. Officials contend that the chemicals are unstable, and the risk of an uncontrolled explosion is growing, particularly as temperatures drop. They said there is a risk that the chemicals may explode as temperatures are expected to drop below 30 degrees Fahrenheit (-1 Celsius) in the coming days. READ MORE: Iowans brace for lead dust cloud as Army plans to detonate 5 tons of bomb-making chemicals In March, staff at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant found several dozen barrels of degraded lead azide, which is used in munitions production. Crystallization of the material created an unstable and dangerous situation, prompting the Army to assemble experts in munitions chemistry, engineering and environmental safety to come up with a plan. According to EPA documents, alternatives such as neutralizing and decomposing the drums' contents with other chemicals were considered. But officials said handling the drums would increase the probability of an accidental, fatal detonation. The environmental groups disagreed, arguing in their petition that other alternatives were not fully considered. They also criticized officials for not sharing more information with the public. The Army had shared details during a public meeting in Middletown in October, but a public advisory a week ago was the first time other communities — some as far away as 100 miles (160 kilometers) — became aware of the potential impact. Nearly 400 people live in Middletown but thousands more in surrounding areas could be affected by detonated material that could disperse in the air and land on the ground. Vibrations from the two planned blasts were expected to be quick, but they could break old windows. That led officials to recommend some residents in Middletown vacate the area. Iowans in the region were told to stay inside; keep windows and doors closed; bring pets and livestock indoors; and clean cars, windowsills and outdoor surfaces afterward. "The detonation will result in an air plume with some lead-containing particles which will disperse in the air and deposit on the ground," an advisory states. "Lead is toxic to humans and animals." 8c9cb5e3819c.text: By — Claudia Ciobanu, Associated Press Claudia Ciobanu, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/poland-says-russia-allegedly-twice-tried-to-kill-a-ukrainian-american-rapper Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Poland says Russia allegedly twice tried to kill a Ukrainian American rapper World Updated on Nov 22, 2026 4:27 PM EST — Published on Nov 22, 2026 2:58 PM EST WARSAW, Poland (AP) — Denmark has expelled a Russian official after it said it had thwarted an alleged plot to kill a Ukrainian American citizen on Danish soil. The case took a new twist Sunday when Polish authorities revealed that the same man was allegedly targeted by Moscow's intelligence services last summer in Poland. Denmark is expected to ask the European Union this week for more decisive action stemming from the case, perhaps restricting Russian citizens from entering and traveling freely within the EU. Poland said it would support such measures. READ MORE: NATO calls Russian missiles landing in Poland a 'grave violation' of airspace European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said Russia's threats were becoming more real, reaching EU soil as the bloc continues supporting Ukraine as Moscow's full-scale invasion nears the five-year mark. The case involves Albert Vasiliev, a rapper who performs under the name Kyivstoner and holds Ukrainian and U.S. citizenship, according to Danish media. The assassination attempt in Denmark was planned for Sept. 25 during a concert north of Copenhagen, according to the Danish Security and Intelligence Service, known by its acronym PET. It said the plot was "planned and initiated by Russian intelligence services." The plot was thwarted by authorities, the Danish prime minister's office said Friday. PET said two men were charged with attempted murder and assisting a foreign intelligence service in operating in Denmark. They were linked to Loyal to Familia, it said, a banned gang known for "extensive, serious and violent criminal activity." WATCH: Ukrainian refugees face growing hostility in Poland Russia dismissed the allegations through its embassy in Copenhagen, saying the accusations were unsubstantiated. Denmark responded by expelling Russia's defense attaché. "In our assessment, the individual concerned was a particular target of the Russian intelligence services," said Rasmus Kieffer-Kristensen, director general of PET. "The case demonstrates that Russian intelligence services are both willing and capable of initiating an assassination attempt on Danish soil — at a public event and using individuals from Danish criminal gangs. This is a concrete indication of the heightened threat posed by Russia." Poland reveals a plot against the rapper in August As Denmark announced the plot against the rapper on Friday, the Polish Foreign Ministry posted on X that it was noting the news with "outrage and concern." "This is another assassination attempt against this person — the first took place on Polish territory in August 2026 but was thwarted thanks to the efforts of the Polish services and the would-be perpetrator, a Russian citizen, was detained," the ministry said. The suspect, who was allegedly recruited by Russia's secret services, was detained by Polish authorities on Aug. 7. READ MORE: Poland says it thwarted Russian plot to kill an American citizen in a NATO country Maciej Wewiór, a Foreign Ministry spokesman, confirmed to The Associated Press the previous attempt to kill Vasiliev in Poland. On Aug. 13, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk disclosed the plot to kill a Ukrainian American citizen in Warsaw was thwarted, noting it was the first time that "someone on the order of Russia" sought to attack a U.S. citizen on the territory of another NATO country. Tusk did not, however, disclose Vasiliev's name, saying only that the target "was uncomfortable" for Russian President Vladimir Putin's government. The rapper left Ukraine after the full-scale invasion Vasiliev was born in Kyiv in 1991, according to Polish media. He posted online comedy sketches and was a former member of the Ukrainian band Hryby. He also was popular in Russia before the full-scale invasion of Ukraine. But he left Ukraine after the war broke out and lived for two years in the U.S. before moving to Slovakia. He has expressed his support for Ukraine against Russia. He performed across Europe this year before his concerts were cancelled for security reasons. Russia's domestic security service, the FSB, accused Vasiliev of being involved in supplying drones for an alleged Ukrainian attack on a defense enterprise in the Moscow region. It said he was "acting under the patronage" of Ukraine's internal security service, the SBU. Danish broadcaster DR reported that Vasiliev denied the FSB accusations. He did not comment on social media about the plot against him in Poland, but DR reported that he announced on Instagram that "the intelligence service banned us from holding the concert," referring to the cancellation of his event in Denmark. Western officials have accused Russia and its proxies of staging dozens of attacks and other incidents across Europe since the invasion of Ukraine. "Russia's hybrid threats are becoming less and less hybrid, and more and more real," said von der Leyen, the EC president, who condemned the alleged plot against Vasiliev in Denmark. The Polish Foreign Ministry said in a statement that "the events in Denmark are another example of Russia's criminal activity on the territory of an EU member state, aimed at intimidating and destabilizing our societies." Russia has denied accusations by Western officials that it was conducting a sabotage campaign in Europe. Joanna Kozlowska in London contributed. A free press is a cornerstone of a healthy democracy. What's next after no deal at COP31 climate talks?
The COP31 climate summit in Turkey has officially come to an end after countries failed to come to a consensus on a new deal.
The European Union and some other countries rejected a fourth draft agreement over its failure to mention a need to phase out fossil fuels, the largest driver of global climate change.
An EU representative accuses some oil states of hijacking talks, as Russia defends opposing the inclusion of such a commitment and levels direct criticism at the EU in its speech.
The talks have been the longest-running in the summit's history, with negotiations breaking down two days after they had been due to end.
BBC climate and science reporter Esme Stallard reports from Antalya, in Turkey.

00f1b41a1557.text:
ANTALYA, Turkey—By the time the United Nations COP31 climate talks ended Sunday afternoon, the conference center resembled a going-out-of-business sale at a pawnshop for broken dreams.
As cleaning crews cleared away the debris left by more than 100,000 participants, Murat Kurum, president of the Conference of the Parties and Turkey’s minister of environment, urbanization and climate change, tried to tie together disparate parts of a draft climate deal with a shiny ribbon of multilateralism.
Many countries were not buying it.
For the first time since 2009, the conference ended without consensus on a cover decision, the concluding statement that typically signals global solidarity on how to confront the worsening climate crisis. Countries did adopt several decisions, including a program to help workers and communities transition away from fossil fuels, and a plan to assess progress on climate adaptation.
The failure to agree on an overarching conference statement reflected deep divisions over whether the agreement should mention fossil fuels and carbon capture, as well as how much climate financing developed countries should provide to developing nations hit by costly climate disasters.
The European Union, as well as several Latin American countries and Pacific Island states, said they would not accept the proposed text from the conference leaders.
Cover decisions at the annual conferences usually focus on new steps or language that could reinforce international efforts to slow global warming. A central aim at this meeting was to set quantifiable but voluntary global goals for the widespread electrification of economies, and to increase funding from developed countries to help developing countries adapt to climate impacts.
In 2022, the U.N. conference in Egypt agreed to establish a loss and damage fund to help vulnerable countries pay for irreversible climate impacts. A year later in Dubai, delegates from more than 190 countries agreed, for the first time, that a “just and orderly” transition away from fossil fuels in energy systems is needed to slow global warming.
Since then, international collaboration on climate issues has declined amid increased conflict, rising oil and gas prices and economic insecurity. The talks in Turkey ran two days beyond the scheduled end without reaching broad agreement on potential next steps, an outcome that won’t kill the global effort but is widely viewed as a serious setback.
But compromise for the sake of consensus is not enough, said Kathy Jetn̄il-Kijiner, a climate envoy for the Marshall Islands Ministry of the Environment.
“We will not be forced to accept false solutions,” she said. “We will not compromise our future to benefit fossil fuel interests.” As written, she added, the Antalya Pact undermines her country’s security and threatens its future.
“People are dying, seas are rising and ecosystems are collapsing,” Jetn̄il-Kijiner said. “Are we so divorced from reality that we take backward steps, even as overshoot threatens to overtake us? To accept this deal would be a betrayal to the Marshallese people.”
It’s not the first time Pacific Island nations threatened by rising seas have objected to the outcome at one of the United Nations’ annual conferences. During the 2023 U.N. talks in Dubai, a final text was adopted even though a delegation representing 39 small island developing states objected because they were still outside the plenary meeting, trying to coordinate their position.
But in Antalya, the divide ran much deeper. The economically powerful and politically influential European Union, representing 28 member countries, also rejected the proposed agreement.
Ireland’s climate, energy and environment minister, Darragh O’Brien, said the European countries formally objected to the cover decision because it fell short of what the global climate crisis demands.
“We will not endorse a decision that does not even mention fossil fuels, the key driver of climate change, and not accept a COP that greenwashes fossil fuels,” said O’Brien, speaking on behalf of the EU during Ireland’s rotating presidency.
Egypt and Brazil, hosts of the U.N. climate talks in 2023 and 2025, also criticized the text proposed by COP31 president Kurum of Turkey and Chris Bowen of Australia, president of the conference negotiations.

Mohammad Ayoub, a climate negotiator with the Saudi Arabian energy ministry, said the 22-member League of Arab States supported the proposed Antalya Pact. He criticized developed countries for using up most of the global carbon budget, the amount of fossil fuels that can be burned without overheating the planet, and then asking developing countries to give up the very energy sources that fueled their own growth.
Ayoub condemned some countries’ opposition to including references to carbon dioxide removal and carbon capture and storage in the pact, calling their resistance to those technologies unscientific.
Carbon capture and storage are not close to being deployed fast enough “to keep 1.5 degrees within reach,” he said, referring to the long-term goal of limiting the average global temperature increase established by the 2015 Paris climate agreement.
“We believe that climate change requires all solutions on the table, and that countries select from these solutions depending on their national circumstances.”

The US Army plans to move ahead with detonating five tonnes of degraded explosives in Iowa despite a ruling to halt it indefinitely, a new court filing shows.
"To protect its personnel and the surrounding communities, the Army needs to take swift action," the justice department notified the court on Saturday. "Protection of human health and the environment demand action now, not delay."
The court had ordered a pause after environmental groups sued to stop the detonation, arguing the army failed to consider safer alternatives.
The detonation was originally scheduled for Friday at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown. The army now plans to act by 24 November under an emergency exemption.
In the new filing, the Department of the Army argued that a controlled detonation was necessary to protect the public from an unplanned explosion, a risk it said would become more likely as temperatures were set to fall in the coming days.
"There is an immediate risk that the lead azide at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant will explode as temperatures are expected to drop below 30 degrees Fahrenheit (-1C) in the next several days," the filing states.
It argued that the army had removed the doors to the bunker where the barrels were stored in preparation for the detonation and that made the explosives more "vulnerable to temperature changes".
The government has not released details for the rescheduled detonation.
Earlier, the army had warned residents to leave their homes for six hours on the original scheduled day of the explosion, for the duration of the explosion and until the dust settled. An advisory warned "all humans" to avoid being outside in the affected areas while the demolition detonation was set to take place.
Lead azide is a highly volatile compound used as a detonator. Earlier this year, the IAAAP found that the material had degraded over time to the point where it was now too risky to move the material, according to Iowa Public Radio.
On Friday, the military said it was working with the Department of Health and Human Services and the EPA to ensure the explosion was done in the safest manner possible.
Military and environmental officials determined that detonating it in place was the safest way to eliminate the explosive safety hazard.
The EPA, which granted an emergency permit to detonate 68 drums of the material, said it did so because the explosion risk "presented an imminent and substantial threat to human health and the environment".
One of the Environmental groups suing to pause the detonation, the Iowa Environmental Council, argued that many Iowans living within the risk-zone were unaware that the explosion was scheduled to happen.
"There is no safe level of lead exposure, and Iowans were given just days to prepare for the November 20 detonation," the organisation said in a press statement.
The Iowa Environmental Council and Sierra Club, which filed the lawsuit on Thursday that prompted the court-ordered pause, filed a new motion on Sunday in response to the army's filing.
The group asks the court to pause proceedings so that it may submit additional information before the scheduled detonation.
The motion includes declarations from environmental experts and local officials who support pausing the detonation, citing a lack of public notice and questioning the Army's claim that delay would cause significant risks.

4319c416d268.text: By — Jill Colvin, Associated Press Jill Colvin, Associated Press By — Lisa Mascaro, Associated Press Lisa Mascaro, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/democrats-clinch-a-historic-house-majority-of-at-least-258-seats-the-largest-since-1992 Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Democrats clinch a historic House majority of at least 258 seats, the largest since 1992 Politics Updated on Nov 22, 2026 3:10 PM EST — Published on Nov 22, 2026 1:24 PM EST WASHINGTON (AP) — House Democrats have secured their best general election result in decades, winning at least 258 seats in an election sweep unseen since 1992 that creates not only vast opportunities to govern but also intense pressure to deliver on campaign promises and priorities. Democrats have gained 44 House seats so far, four more than the 40 they picked up in President Donald Trump's first midterm in 2018. The 258-seat tally was reached Sunday after Democrat Chuck Hubbard defeated Republican Rep. Virginia Foxx in North Carolina. Four other House races remain outstanding: one each in Minnesota and Tennessee and two in Louisiana that are heading to a December runoff. Please check your inbox to confirm. Republicans will have at least 173 seats in the minority. The milestone in the 435-member House sets up divided government, with the Senate also in Democratic hands and with a Republican president in the White House. Emboldened Democrats are preparing a 100-day agenda to address high costs of living while also confronting Trump with a vast oversight agenda for the remainder of his second term in office. The Democrats' majority will be bigger than any the party has seen in elections since Bill Clinton was first elected president in 1992 (258) or the election of Barack Obama in 2008 (257), yet not quite the high-water mark of the Franklin D. Roosevelt-era, which saw House Democratic majorities swell past 300. WATCH: Tennessee Democrat describes how she won a Trump district with almost no ad money It presents opportunities and challenges ahead. "Like, hell yeah, we should feel pressure," said Democratic Rep. Jason Crow of Colorado, a former Army Ranger. "There are people dying in this country and people losing their healthcare, losing their livelihoods, losing their farms, being terrorized from ICE," he said earlier this month at the Capitol, referring to U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement. "If you don't feel a sense of urgency and pressure in this job, and a desperation to deliver for folks, then you don't belong under this Capitol dome." Election rout creates a mandate to govern The numbers underscore the extraordinary scale of Democratic wins, which spanned from the strongest Republican states to the Midwest and East Coast, as voters, angry over high prices and the Iran war and concerned over corruption, made clear their discontent with Trump. Taking control of both the House and the Senate come January, the Democrats will carry with them the backing of voters and the expectations to deliver. The Senate Democrats won a 56-seat majority in the 100-member chamber, their biggest advantage in over a decade. The Democrats, as part of their 100-day agenda, are planning swift votes to reverse the Republicans' Medicaid cuts and restore the Affordable Care Act tax credits the Republicans allowed to expire. Democrats have vowed to marshal their subpoena powers and launch a flurry of investigations to exert the role of Congress as a check on presidential power. That includes plans to probe how Trump and his family have become wealthier since he returned to office. Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries of New York, who is in line to become House speaker, has not ruled out trying to impeach Trump for a third time. READ MORE: Here are some of the House seats that Democrats didn't expect to win — but did "This is a historic moment for our country. This is one of the largest classes we have seen," said progressive leader Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y., at the Capitol. She called the big numbers "a mandate for change." Rep. Tom Suozzi, a centrist Democrat from New York and an accountant by profession, said the House Democrats should focus 75% of their time on affordability issues and 25% on accountability. "Everything should be tied back to the people — and how it's affecting the people," he said. For example, he said, as the Democrats launch investigations into Trump's financial dealings, they should be connecting the dots: "How does that affect people's pocketbooks?" The White House has issued a warning to Democrats over their planned probes into the administration, going as far as claiming that such investigations — a standard oversight function of Congress — may amount to "blatant criminality." A new generation of leaders After House Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., struggled to keep the House functioning for the past two years with a narrow single-digit majority — meaning a few GOP lawmakers could derail the agenda — the Democrats will have a wide margin that provides the new leadership much more room to maneuver. Jeffries, who is poised to make history as the first Black speaker of the House if his colleagues elect him to the job on Jan. 3, 2027, will be able to lose dozens of Democrats on any given vote and still have the 218 needed for passage, in the face of GOP opposition. "We're not a monolith — people come to the caucus with different ideas — it's OK," said Rep. Troy Carter, D-La., who is expected to lead the Congressional Black Caucus. Countries have failed to reach a major new deal to tackle climate change after deep divisions over fossil fuels and money emerged at the UN COP31 talks in Turkey.
Negotiations were due to finish on Friday but ran late into Sunday in search of common ground, becoming the longest UN climate conference in history.
But the final deal proved unacceptable to the EU, Pacific island nations and others because it failed to directly mention fossil fuels, the main cause of global warming.
Meanwhile, many poorer countries objected to the absence of any clear financial commitments from richer nations to help them adapt to the impacts of rising temperatures.
The last time a COP's main political agreement collapsed like this was in 2009 in Copenhagen.
UN secretary general Antonio Guterres, in his last COP before he steps down, said he was "deeply disappointed".
He took aim at what he called "powerful fossil fuel interests" who he said were taking "a page from Big Tobacco's playbook: distorting the science, delaying policy, blocking action, and piling up huge profits while people everywhere pay the price".
After two weeks of negotiations, exhausted delegates were presented with a new, draft deal in the early hours of Sunday morning to try to break the deadlock.
But the words "fossil fuels" did not appear anywhere in the text. The only indirect reference to coal, oil and gas was a nod to a deal agreed at COP28 in 2023, when countries agreed to "transition away" from fossil fuels in energy systems.
The EU's representative, Irish Minister Darragh O'Brien, made it clear that the EU "strongly" objected, saying that the "decisions go nowhere near the level of ambition needed to tackle climate change".
"It is unconscionable that we would have a climate pact that makes no mention of fossil fuels," he said.
Other countries, such as Panama and the Marshall Islands, also criticised the deal for doing nowhere near enough to tackle the pace of climate change.
A first draft of the deal on Monday mentioned "fossil fuel" or "fossil fuels" six times, but that was unacceptable to oil-producing nations.
Saudi Arabia's delegate Mohammad Ayoub said that Arab countries "continued to engage in good faith" but argued that they only accounted for a small proportion of historical greenhouse gas emissions.
Russia warned not to "turn to slogans" over coal, oil and gas, claiming that if countries moved away from fossil fuels too quickly it would lead to "fuel poverty".
Another major sticking point has been money for poorer countries to adapt to the impacts of climate change, such as more intense heatwaves and more severe droughts.
Last year at COP30 in Brazil, nations agreed to triple the finance for that purpose.
But this year's deal contained no reference to concrete figures, nor the baseline against which that pledge would be measured. This raised fears it would give richer nations too much wriggle room.
"Rich nations and polluting governments cannot keep arriving empty-handed," said Mohamed Adow of Power Shift Africa, an African climate and energy think tank.
The UK's Energy Secretary, Miatta Fahnbulleh, described the failure to reach a political agreement as "immensely disappointing".
"This only strengthens our resolve to work with partners around the world on the genuine progress made in Antalya on tackling the climate crisis," she said, adding that the UK's commitment was "unwavering".
Climate talks in an age of 'overshoot'
While talks were hosted in Antalya in Turkey, Australia led the official negotiations - creating what some observers described as a chaotic dynamic.
Chris Bowen, Australian government minister and COP31 president of negotiations, said that there were "unbridgeable red lines" in the discussions.
He pointed to "the most complicated and fraught geopolitical environment in living memory". At the same time, "the impacts of climate change are getting worse", he said, raising the stakes.
The year 2026 could end as the hottest on record and has brought extreme weather and natural hazards to much of the world, from summer heat and drought in Europe to flash flooding in Nepal.
And COP31 was the first annual UN conference to formally discuss how one of the key international targets for limiting climate change would be missed.
In the Paris talks of 2015, nearly 200 countries agreed to try to limit global warming to 1.5C above pre-industrial levels of the late 1800s, aimed at avoiding some of the worst effects of climate change.
The UN says that the Paris deal has driven "near-universal" climate action. In the early 2010s, global warming of 4C or more was thought to be a serious possibility by the end of the century.
Now, the world is likely to limit warming to about 2.8C by 2100 based on current government policies, the UN says.
But action has not been fast enough to meet that Paris goal, with the world likely to "overshoot" 1.5C of long-term warming in the next few years.
Many countries say they are committed to eventually bringing warming back down to 1.5C, but that will require an ambitious ramping up of technologies - which do not yet exist at scale - to remove carbon dioxide from the atmosphere.
Although the main deal fell through, some agreements were reached, including progress on a "just transition mechanism" - a framework to support workers and communities as economies shift towards clean energy.
The COP31 president also said that more than 80 countries backed Turkey's target to increase the share of global energy use met by electricity to 35% by 2035
But following today's events, some have questioned whether the UN climate process - which relies on consensus - can succeed in a geopolitically divided world.
The UN's climate chief, Simon Stiell, said he would seek advice on potential reform to the process, with the next conference scheduled for November 2027, COP32 in Ethiopia.
"[The consensus process] has worked to get us where we are," he told the BBC. "It got us through Paris... so it can work,

86b3fcf538a0.text: By — Nancy Jiang, Associated Press Nancy Jiang, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/health/scientists-are-fighting-for-their-halted-funds-trust-of-black-communities-may-be-harder-to-win-back Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Scientists are fighting for their halted funds. Trust of Black communities may be harder to win back Health Nov 22, 2026 1:02 PM EST People in a historically Black corner of Pittsburgh took memory tests, tracked their sleep and blood pressure and shared stories of their past to help scientists unravel risks for Alzheimer's disease. But they may never get answers. The study was among broader research into why Black Americans are twice as likely as their white peers to develop Alzheimer's, but the Trump administration abruptly halted it in its final stretch. Researchers say the move not only wasted more than $8 million in taxpayer money already spent but also is a blow to the hard-earned trust of anxious study participants who won't even learn if their brain tests showed signs of trouble. WATCH: 'The Price of Exclusion' explores lasting impact of racial inequality in medicine "The community will look like, 'Oh, they came in here, they took all our stuff, they checked us out. Now they're gonna leave us hanging,'" said Roderick Blair, 70, who had participated in the study for four years. Trust in U.S. health institutions has long been strained in the Black community, stemming from the nation's long-standing racial health inequities, unequal access to care and bias within the nation's medical system. The legacy of the Tuskegee study, which withheld treatment from Black men who had been infected with syphilis in the 1930s, still casts a shadow. The Pittsburgh study overcame that mistrust. Getting people involved in the city's Hill and Homewood communities helped get people talking about memory loss, dementia and Alzheimer's and helped challenge misconceptions about it, according to La'Vette Wagner, the Pittsburgh study's field coordinator. Studies are mislabeled as diversity, equity and inclusion Families who once dismissed memory loss as depression began asking about dementia, and people outside the study called her to ask if family members could join, she said. More than half of Black Americans, or 55%, believe that a significant loss of memory or cognitive abilities is a natural part of aging rather than disease, according to the Alzheimer's Association. As Blair said, "You start forgetting things and you start to wonder, do you have Alzheimer's? You wonder, do you have dementia?" Then the study, which had been near completion in its fifth and final year, was stripped of funding last year by the National Institutes of Health, on the grounds that it was "not science," according to the study's researchers, despite a rigorous review and vetting from a community advisory board. "It wasn't a Black study or a DEI study," Wagner said. "It was something that was happening that was real." WATCH: Scientists sound alarm on Trump administration's dismantling of research funding Similar terminations happened all over the country. Negar Fani, a neuropsychologist at Emory University in Atlanta, was two years into a five-year, $2.9 million project on how daily experiences of racial discrimination affect the brain and body of Black Americans when NIH terminated it in July. While Fani tries to find the roughly $2.3 million she needs to complete the study, she and her team were left to try to explain the situation to participants who feel abandoned. "It takes a lot to restore trust with the Black community, who has experienced so many different betrayals," she said. Like the Pittsburgh study's funding, Fani's grant had been terminated for being "not scientific" and "subjective" — after the study had been approved and had enrolled 66 of the 220 people it. "It's simply brain science research," she said. Fewer grants awarded for multiyear studies In Pittsburgh, study lead researcher Andrea Rosso is one of numerous scientists in a recently filed lawsuit against NIH and its parent Department of Health and Human Services, one of a growing body of legal actions as the administration continues to hunt for and halt medical grants with descriptions that include the words "disparities," "minority" and "racial." Ann Cohen, a director of Pittsburgh's Alzheimer's Disease Research Center, also is part of that lawsuit after her separate, complementary study of Alzheimer's risk also was halted -- after spending $5.2 million over three years. She, too, has a troubling ethics question: What to do with blood samples collected from the participants? "You lose trust a hell of a lot faster than you build it," she said. A spokesperson for HHS said "Massive amounts of DEI grants have failed to translate into better health outcomes for minority populations. Following President Trump's directives, NIH is shifting money into rigorous research that will help Americans — including minority populations — live longer, healthier lives." WATCH: Black midwife's death highlights racial gap in maternal mortality This year, the NIH has awarded 2,000 fewer grants for multiyear studies worth a total of $200 million compared with 2025, according to an Association of American Medical Colleges report. "It's unprecedented. Many of the decisions are based on political biases and based on what politicians think is valuable rather than peer review processes, evidence-based decisions about where to invest our research dollars," said Jill Rosenthal, the director of public health policy at the Center for American Progress. "We're wasting resources, we're wasting the opportunity to identify cures for diseases," she said. Researchers in Pittsburgh are especially concerned that promises made to the community will remain unfulfilled. 'Danger seems greater all the time': Ukrainians search for missing after Russian strikes
At least three bodies have been recovered the site of a residential building that was hit by a Russian strike in the Kyiv region, Ukraine's State Emergency Services said.
A woman in her forties and a teenage boy have so far been identified as rescue workers continue to search the rubble for those who are still trapped.
Continued warnings of further drone threats near the site are hampering efforts, the service added, but some people were successfully evacuated earlier in the day.
"We are living a nightmare... only God knows when it will end," one woman told the BBC's Sarah Rainsford, who's reporting from Ukraine's Kyiv region.

4a0db0857164.text: By — Sylvie Corbet, Associated Press Sylvie Corbet, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/health/french-activists-demand-a-tear-gas-suspension-over-reported-menstrual-changes Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter French activists demand a tear gas suspension over reported menstrual changes Health Nov 22, 2026 12:34 PM EST PARIS (AP) — French activists and lawmakers are demanding after recent street protests that authorities suspend the use of tear gas to disperse crowds over concerns it's caused menstrual changes and other reproductive health problems, though scientists have not confirmed a medical connection. WATCH: Why French students are leading massive protests across the country The demands come after police used tear gas during student protests and demonstrations over the cost of living, some marred by violence. Some women reported painful cramps, unexpected bleeding and disrupted menstrual cycles after exposure, and an advocacy group says it has collected more than 10,000 complaints. Opposition lawmakers are seeking a ban and independent research into possible health effects. Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez has rejected the calls, saying police use of tear gas is essential to crowd control as an alternative to using more dangerous weapons. Here's what is known — and what is not — about tear gas and reproductive health. Tear gas is commonly used by police to disperse crowds Tear gas grenades used by French police contain CS, a chemical irritant that affects the eyes, skin and respiratory tract. CS is a crystalline powder dispersed into the air as fine particles. Its effects depend upon how much is used and how long people are exposed to it. Those exposed during the protests include peaceful demonstrators — including children, pregnant women and older people — and residents near the sites of protest marches. Women reported pain and unexpected bleeding after exposure A member of the French gendarmerie shoots a tear gas canister during a demonstration as part of a nationwide day of strikes and protests over wages, the cost of living and public services called by French labour unions, and joined by high school and university students calling for better education conditions, in Nantes, France, on Nov. 5, 2026. Photo by Stephane Mahe/Reuters Mélina Galland, 24, was working as an independent photographer during Oct. 17 protests in Paris that were marred by rioting and looting. She wore a double surgical mask along with a diving mask when tear gas grenades were fired. "Heading back home, I felt intense belly pain which was unusual because I never experience pain that intense at that stage of my period," she said. Chloé Baroux, 25, also a photographer, first noticed pain and irregular periods after covering protests against a security bill in 2020 and 2021. She said her menstrual cycles eventually became more regular, and she didn't think of a potential link to tear gas until she covered the recent protests, noting, "over the past two months, it's become irregular again." WATCH: French authorities impose curfews after weekend rioting Eva-Luna Tholance, a former journalist who investigated the issue six years ago, decided to found the "Lacrymos de sang" ("Tears of blood") advocacy group during the protests to raise awareness about possible effects on menstrual cycles and pregnancies. The group asked people last month to complete a questionnaire describing their exposure and symptoms. Its collection of accounts doesn't establish how common symptoms are among those who say they were exposed to tear gas, and they were not reviewed by independent doctors. Still, Tholance said, many women described pain or unexpected bleeding, and thousands are asking questions about what's happening in their bodies. "Some people experience mild cramps, but a huge number tell us about cramps that are far worse than what they normally experience during their periods," she said, adding that bleeding reports range "from spotting to extremely heavy bleeding lasting several days. Some people bleed for weeks." Others reported bleeding despite being postmenopausal or taking hormonal contraception that normally prevents menstrual bleeding, Tholance said. Investigations have yet to establish a causal link An Associated Press investigation during the 2020 Black Lives Matter protests in the U.S. found there had been limited study and oversight of tear gas, though it did raise concerns about tear gas exposure in confined spaces, excessive use and canisters fired directly at people. A recent study collected accounts of symptoms reported after the BLM protests. It found a "potential relationship" between exposure and "adverse reproductive health outcomes" but did not prove cause and effect. That's in part because the study relied on self-reported information collected at one point in time — similar to the French group's questionnaire — and because people who felt most impacted may have been more likely to respond. "There's a lot of theories. We don't really 100% know," said the study's lead author, Asha Hassan of the University of Minnesota Medical School. The study calls for more research "urgently." WATCH: French students lead massive protests against education policies Hassan said much early research on tear gas involved healthy young men in military settings, which could help explain why menstrual and other reproductive health effects have gone undocumented. Alsetex and Nobel Sport, two leading suppliers of tear gas grenades to French law enforcement, did not respond to requests for comment. The Interior Ministry says no published scientific studies show that CS causes menstrual changes or miscarriages. It said other effects of tear gas generally resolve within hours, although it acknowledged that some longer-lasting symptoms affecting the skin and eyes "cannot be ruled out." Some other possible effects in the body "have been suggested, but not demonstrat

30228365a20f.text: By — Loreben Tuquero, PolitiFact Loreben Tuquero, PolitiFact Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/nation/as-ai-detects-flaws-in-computer-systems-is-it-causing-more-tech-outages-and-disruptions Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter As AI detects flaws in computer systems, is it causing more tech outages and disruptions? Nation Nov 22, 2026 12:13 PM EST This article originally appeared on PolitiFact. In the span of one week, Microsoft services went down, flights were grounded nationwide, some banks' services briefly stopped working and an internal platform for the National Security Agency went dark. It left people wondering: Is artificial intelligence the culprit? In a Fox News interview, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said he asked someone in the tech industry what could be causing the outages, and that person believed it's "super intelligence," the Trump administration's preferred term for AI (they're not the same thing). "That kinda makes sense to me, because I can tell you with 98% certainty, we're not seeing the cyberattack, no one's out there taking claims for it," Mullin said Nov 17. WATCH: Mounting tech disruptions raise concerns about U.S. cybersecurity In a separate Nov. 17 Fox Business interview, National Intelligence Director Jay Clayton pointed to flaws that AI detected in a programming language used in systems across the world, and he said fixing them caused unexpected problems. "The patching that has gone on following that has caused some of these systems to not come back up when you patch them as expected. That is what has happened at the NSA today," he said. Senate Intelligence Committee Vice Chairman Sen. Mark Warner, D-Va., said some of the recent outages were "AI-related." "What's happened is that these AI tools, what they've been able to do is spot vulnerabilities in all of our existing systems," Warner said in a Nov. 18 CNBC interview. "Then all of these companies are in this mad rush to create patches because nobody wants to have their system vulnerable." High-profile AI hacks have happened this year, but there's no indication that the recent outages were the result of AI-related cyberattacks or rogue AI agents. Experts say AI is boosting companies' ability to detect weaknesses in their systems, and therefore requiring more fixes, which could lead to outages. But no evidence has shown that caused the recent string of tech disruptions. "Vulnerabilities are being discovered and exploited faster than ever before, especially with increasingly capable AI models," said Bryan Ward, a Vanderbilt University computer science assistant professor. How AI is helping detect system flaws In the past, organizations would task specialists with finding flaws in their software systems, said Stuart Madnick, an MIT Sloan School of Management information technology professor. Now, AI is often able to do this 10 to 100 times faster than humans, Madnick said. If an organization previously found four or five flaws in a year, they would now be aware of 40 to 400. "The question is: Is (it) the fixing that's causing the problem, or the fact you got 400 open windows and doors in your system that are now known that's causing a problem?" Madnick said. WATCH: Cascade of tech outages 'separate events' and 'under control,' Trump says Leading AI companies, such as OpenAI and Anthropic, have released sophisticated models that have uncovered serious vulnerabilities in software. On Nov. 17, a cybersecurity start-up using an OpenAI model found a critical software flaw in a programming language used by government agencies, banks, hospitals and the majority of Fortune 500 companies. To give a sense of the volume of fixes deployed by one major company, the cybersecurity firm Qualys reported that Microsoft addressed 1,235 vulnerabilities in November, compared to 68 in November 2025. More secure software systems must be built in the future, Ward said, but there is an immediate need to fix problems now. No evidence so far that the tech outages are connected to each other Based on what the government and affected companies have reported so far, the outages did not happen because of a common weakness. Microsoft said it had a technical issue unrelated to AI or AI agents, and the problem stemmed from a "network capacity upgrade." It hasn't given more details. The nationwide ground stop happened after a router upgrade disrupted the FAA telecommunications infrastructure, government officials said. Investigators haven't determined whether there was an installation error or a faulty router, but they have ruled out an AI system the FAA recently rolled out. WATCH: What a string of tech problems reveals about America's digital vulnerabilities JPMorganChase attributed its outage to a "temporary issue related to a software bug in on-premise hardware systems." Unintended consequences, such as services becoming unavailable, can be a trade-off when companies update their systems, said Nicholas Leiserson, president of the Center for Advancing Cybersecurity at the Institute for Security and Technology. "That's like a perennial challenge that has existed in information technology operations for a long time, and AI can potentially accelerate it," he said. Before an outage, people can protect their personal devices and information by: Keeping software updated. Using strong passwords, and not reusing them across websites. A password manager can help store passwords securely. Using multifactor authentication. Keeping a data backup. "I think recent events should be a wake-up call and the public should take the opportunity to improve their cybersecurity posture," Ward said. "Recent outages demonstrate how critical and intertwined software systems have become in our society today, and how important cybersecurity truly is."
