e99e0449a122.text: By — Marcia Dunn, Associated Press Marcia Dunn, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/science/mercury-gets-its-first-visitor-in-years-as-a-pair-of-spacecraft-loop-into-orbit Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Mercury gets its first visitor in years as a pair of spacecraft loop into orbit Science Nov 22, 2026 11:41 AM EST CAPE CANAVERAL, Fla. (AP) — A pair of spacecraft slipped into orbit around Mercury on Saturday after an eight-year cruise through the inner solar system to unravel our littlest planet's mountain of mysteries. The linked robotic explorers — one European, the other Japanese — will separate from one another next month in order to map and study the scorching little planet from different altitudes. The $2 billion (1.7 billion euros) mission is known collectively as BepiColombo. Grow your mind Subscribe to our Science Newsletter to explore the wide worlds of science, health and technology. Enter your email address Subscribe Form error message goes here. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. The European Space Agency announced BepiColombo's arrival via social media. A series of thruster firings slowed the spacecraft enough to be captured by the planet's weak gravity. But it took several anxious hours before flight controllers in Germany — 94 million miles (152 million kilometers) away — could confirm that BepiColombo had achieved orbit. Teams pored over the data streaming back; additional information was not immediately available. BepiColombo is only the third spacecraft to visit Mercury — the sun's closest planet and barely bigger than our moon — and the first in more than a decade. NASA's Mariner 10 flew past Mercury three times in the mid-1970s. The team included the late Italian mathematician Giuseppe "Bepi" Colombo, for whom this latest mission is named. NASA's Messenger spacecraft entered orbit around Mercury in 2011 and, after running out of fuel, crashed into the planet in 2015. Launched in 2018, BepiColombo took a slower, more roundabout route to get to Mercury, flying once past Earth, twice past Venus and six times past Mercury for gravity-guiding assists. All those loop-de-loops put more than 6 billion miles (10 billion kilometers) on the odometer. The conjoined spacecraft shed their mother ship in September for the final leg of the journey. WATCH: Astronauts reflect on living aboard the International Space Station Lead project scientist Geraint Jones said he and others can't wait for all the new data to start streaming down in the spring. The mission will provide the ability to compare "unprecedented measurements taken by two spacecraft at the planet at the same time," he noted. Once orbiting separately, the European Space Agency's satellite and the Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency's smaller craft will study Mercury's dense interior and exterior magnetic field, as well as everything in between: impact craters, volcanic plains, mountain ridges and peaks jutting as high as 3 miles (4 1/2 kilometers). The mercury at Mercury can hit more than 800 degrees (427 degrees Celsius), adding strain to electronic and engineering systems. Space agency officials want to keep the mission going for at least one Earth year — or the equivalent of four Mercury years. "The spacecraft and its instruments need to be kept as cool as possible, which is a huge technical challenge in itself," Jones said in an email. Despite its relative proximity to Earth, Mercury is one of the solar system's least explored planets. Only outer planets Uranus and Neptune have had fewer visitors — a lone Voyager 2 back in the 1980s. Delgado, Associated Press By — Sibi Arasu, Associated Press Sibi Arasu, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/un-climate-talks-break-down-over-bitter-disagreements-on-fossil-fuels Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter UN climate talks break down over bitter disagreements on fossil fuels World Updated on Nov 22, 2026 3:35 PM EST — Published on Nov 22, 2026 11:30 AM EST ANTALYA, Turkey (AP) — United Nations climate talks fizzled out Sunday without reaching an overarching agreement because of disputes over whether to mention the fossil fuels that cause global warming. Expectations had already been low heading into the two-week negotiations in Turkey, but impasses over explicitly including fossil fuels and other issues, including money, proved irreconcilable. Nations' negotiators, activists and even organizers used the word "disappointing" to characterize the discussions. Though the talks, called COP31, failed to reach a main agreement, known as a cover decision, the meeting had already made progress on smaller issues. The two-week session ended Sunday night, after running more than 50 hours overtime at the resort town of Antalya. READ MORE: Climate talks in overtime as nations wrestle with response to worsening global warming This all happened as global warming accelerates with ever-worsening heat waves, floods, storms and droughts. The U.N. said it is now inevitable that the world will soon blow past the warming threshold established by the 2015 Paris climate agreement. And there is also a global energy shock due to the war in Iran. On top of that, a strong El Niño amplifies human-caused warming and causes more weather disasters. "I am deeply disappointed that COP31 has ended without consensus on an overarching outcome," United Nations Secretary-General Antonio Guterres said. "Temperatures keep shattering records. Climate extremes keep intensifying. Emissions remain far too high. And every delay makes our task harder and more costly." Upset youth representative Oumnia Anfer told the negotiators "you have let us down." Any pact approved at the talks requires near-unanimous consensus. Several countries and the 27-nation European Union said they could not accept the final proposal from the joint Turkish-Australian leadership, which didn't mention fossil fuels. A considerably larger number of nations accepted the decision, often reluctantly, saying consensus on something was more important, though it ultimately failed. Russia and Saudi Arabia sought to keep fossil fuels out of the document. "It's unconscionable that we would have a climate act that makes no reference to fossil fuels," Darragh O'Brien, Ireland's climate minister, said on behalf of the EU at the climate talks. Impasses over draft agreements Previously, fossil fuels went unmentioned in COP final decisions for more than 25 years, said Alden Meyer, with the think tank E3G. Then, three years ago in the oil-rich United Arab Emirates, a groundbreaking agreement called for "transitioning away from fossil fuels" but since then there's been no explicit mention of fossil fuels. The Turkish-Australian proposal recalled the Dubai agreement in its entirety, but that wasn't enough for many nations and environmental groups. "Fossil fuels are driving the climate crisis," said Guterres. "The continued addiction to coal, oil and gas is fueling climate chaos, exposing economies to price shocks and undermining energy security. We can't put out the fire while pouring fuel on it." Adding to the disagreement was the fact that the draft included explicit language and a goal for carbon capture and storage for industrial polluters, which many nations and activists said would undermine efforts to reduce overall emissions. READ MORE: Activists, leaders criticize COP31 climate talks as fossil fuels go unmentioned in draft deal "The failure of COP31 is an outrage — it is outrageous that a handful of petrostates have veto power over any mention of fossil fuels," said former U.S. Vice President Al Gore. As the proposed deal fell apart in the plenary session, Turkish Environment Minister Murat Kurum, the president of COP31, was absent, leaving it to Elchin Allahverdiyev of Azerbaijan to announce the failure. "Unfortunately, we were unable to reach agreement on a cover decision. And that's disappointing, very disappointing," said Australia's Chris Bowen, COP31's president of negotiations. Bowen said the Dubai agreement's explicit call to wean away from coal, oil and natural gas that cause climate change is still in force: "Transition away from fossil fuels in the real world is happening. It's happening. It's happening at speed and it's irreversible." Other issues left unresolved Other climate issues weren't settled, and many were deferred to next year's negotiations in Ethiopia. They include details on transitioning away from fossil fuels, financial help for poorer nations to adapt to the warming world and action on gender and climate. For this year's negotiations, Turkey made global electrification its signature issue. A proposal introduced separately from the main agreement calls for countries to increase the share of electricity in total final energy consumption from about 21% today to 35% by 2035. This would require nations to commit to measures such as switching transportation — including cars, trucks and planes — from fossil fuels to electricity and using electricity instead of coal to make industrial products. Nearly 100 nations signed up for this goal as part of the separate pledge. Meyer, with E3G, also hailed progress on global adaptation goals and on a program that helps countries achieve their emissions-cutting goals fairly. c52a26a8a044.text: By — Christopher Weber, Associated Press Christopher Weber, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/nation/immigration-officers-make-arrests-at-seattle-airport-in-distressing-scene-delaying-flight Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Immigration officers make arrests at Seattle airport in 'distressing' scene, delaying flight Nation Nov 22, 2026 11:18 AM EST Masked immigration officers detained two people on a crowded airport jet bridge in Seattle as people were boarding Saturday, causing what the airline called a "distressing" scene for passengers and employees and delaying the Los Angeles-bound flight. Video of the incident showed officers dragging away at least one person at Seattle-Tacoma International Airport as a woman screams that her daughter is being taken and she has a work permit. WATCH: Lawmakers press Mullin on flight disruptions and ICE tactics Immigration and Customs Enforcement said in a statement that its officers conducted a targeted enforcement operation to arrest Ricardo Larrondo Mendoza, an immigrant from Mexico who "overstayed his visa in violation of our nation's laws." During the confrontation, another passenger "hurled hot coffee on the officers," the ICE statement said. That woman, Sofia Hernandez Mejia, was determined to be in the U.S. illegally from Mexico and to have also overstayed her visa, ICE said. She could be charged with assaulting a federal officer. Online flight data showed that Alaska flight 1306, which had been scheduled to depart at 8:10 a.m., was delayed. Alaska Airlines said ICE officers gave no advance notice of the enforcement action, which occurred during a busy travel weekend ahead of the Thanksgiving holiday. "We are concerned by this morning's law enforcement action during the boarding of Alaska Flight 1306," the airline said. "We recognize how distressing this incident has been for affected employees and guests." It added that the airline is committed to "treating every guest with dignity and respect." The arresting officers wore unmarked jackets and khaki pants. The video showed them struggling with someone on the ground as passengers surrounded by rolling suitcases look on. ICE has stepped up arrests at airports since the summer, especially targeting people who overstayed visas in the past. WATCH: ICE touts record number of deportations in agency's history Alaska Airlines said it was working with the Port of Seattle, which manages the airport, to see if protocols were followed, and also that it has raised concerns "directly with the appropriate authorities." The Port of Seattle said in a statement that the arrest was distressing not only for the affected family but for other passengers, and that local authorities would "engage federal officials to understand more about what occurred." Washington Gov. Bob Ferguson, a Democrat, said ICE's tactics were "deeply un-American" and called for the agency's abolition. "The video is horrific and it is chilling," Ferguson said at an afternoon news conference with labor leaders and local elected officials. "We need a system of immigration enforcement and border security that is effective, ethical and humane. And ICE is not it. It is beyond reform." Ferguson also said he was looking into how ICE agents accessed the jet bridge and he believes they violated a state law he signed in March limiting facial coverings on law enforcement officers. April Sims, president of the Washington State Labor Council, AFL-CIO, representing over 600,000 workers, said union members were aboard the flight. She said the action disrupted travel during one of the busiest times and only days after flights were grounded nationwide due to a communications problem. "Airport workers are already managing extraordinary stress, passengers are already anxious and instead of restoring calm and confidence, federal agents introduced more fear and more chaos," she said. The News
The COP31 climate summit in TÃ¼rkiye collapsed on Sunday without agreement on a final deal, over deep disagreement over the negotiationsâ most basic provision â the first time the talks ended unsuccessfully since calamitous 2009 meetings.
After negotiations stretched to their longest in three decades, Murat Kurum, the summit president, finally acknowledged that a meeting meant to drive forward the âimplementationâ of countriesâ existing carbon-cutting commitments could not even agree on what their overarching goal should be. âThere is no consensus on this document,â he said, marking the first time for COP to conclude without an agreement since the calamitous 2009 summit in Copenhagen. âTherefore, these decisions have not been adopted.â
Timâs view
The breakdown effectively marks the demise of a 2023 consensus, reached in Dubai, on the long-term phaseout of fossil fuels in the global economy. The years since then have been marked by successive global energy crises, including the biggest oil and gas supply disruption in history. While these crises have driven a faster pivot from fossil fuels in some importing countries, they have reinforced othersâ conviction that more, not less, investment is required in the legacy energy system for the sake of security and affordability. COP31 shows that climate action was a casualty of that turmoil.
Overlapping wars and US President Donald Trumpâs rambunctious foreign policy have also undermined multilateralism in general, a critical problem for a negotiating process that requires consensus (a requirement that former Vice President Al Gore criticized this week as âinsaneâ for an issue on which some countriesâ interests are so diametrically, inherently opposed).
In Dubai, it took an oil executive â Sultan Al Jaber, CEO of ADNOC â to bring fellow exporters onboard for the most pointed critique of their own industry in COP history. But that consensus proved fragile. At last yearâs COP in Brazil, the final deal didnât include the words âfossil fuelsâ but did encourage countries to take the Dubai consensus âinto accountâ when developing national policies.
By this year, the most delegates could muster was merely ârecallingâ the consensus, without any indication of what that memory was meant to instigate. Instead, the draft decision included new calls for carbon capture that â while clearly necessary to bend the curve on global emissions â are seen by many negotiating teams as a cover for extending the lifespan of fossil fuels.
Negotiating blocs that supported adopting the draft included the Arab Group, which includes the UAE, as well as China, India, and Japan. But the COP process requires consensus, and the draft was adamantly opposed by the least-developed-countries bloc, as well as the UK and European Union. The US has not been represented at the talks since President Donald Trump returned to office.
While the failure to adopt a conference-wide deal indicates that universal agreement on global energy pathways has become more elusive than ever, smaller groupings did manage to find common ground on the issue. More than two dozen countries (albeit relatively minor carbon emitters) have now adopted some form of policy guidelines for a âtransition away from fossil fuels.â And during COP31, nearly 90 countries signed on to pledge to turbocharge the electrification of their economies.
COP, in other words, has not completely imploded â but it has become deeply fragmented. And meanwhile, the real economy doesnât need a UN-brokered summit to set either the floor or the ceiling for change.
âThe green economy will not win because a text tells it to,â Juan Carlos Monterrey GÃ³mez, Panamaâs former climate envoy, wrote. âIt will win because it is cheaper, smarter and creates more jobs. The future will not be negotiated.â
Notable
- Throughout the summit, Beijing remained focused on lowering trade barriers to its green tech exports. Protectionism is an obstacle to global electrification goals, Chinaâs delegates to COP31 warned.

The News
Semafor is facing scrutiny for hiring high-profile Washington consultants to assist with event bookings, a revelation that underscores the murkiness embedded into a high-level convening business thatâs become a vital and growing revenue source for some global media companies.
As online web traffic and the associated advertising dollars have diminished across the industry, publishers have leaned into sponsored in-person events to support their newsrooms. The growing importance of these events has raised thorny standards and ethics questions regarding sponsors who pay to be onstage at places like Fortune, The Wall Street Journal and The Atlantic â even if their sessions are clearly labeled as sponsored â or regarding media CEOs who strike deals with advertisers while interviewing those same CEOs.
Of the last decadeâs crop of digital media outlets, none have leaned further into the events-driven business than Semafor, which has hosted hundreds of high-profile gatherings since launching in late 2022.
While Semafor primarily relies on an in-house events team to secure bookings of business, political and government leaders, for its flagship April gathering, Semafor World Economy, the Washington Post reported on Thursday that the company enlisted a handful of external consultants to recruit politicians for onstage interviews. Among the consultants were former Trump advisers Jason Miller and Kellyanne Conway, as well as former Kamala Harris and Joe Biden adviser Adrienne Elrod. Miller is no longer on contract, but Conway and Elrod remain consultants at Semafor.
The contracts were intended to help secure the best guests for its flagship Washington event, a multimillion-dollar revenue-driver for the four-year old company. A spokesperson for Semafor said in a statement that âwe donât pay speakers and both our speakers and guests come for tough, fair, and independent interviews,â noting that âmany other media companiesâ employ consultants from across the political spectrum to recruit high-profile guests to attend their events.
But others saw it as a potential conflict of interest.
âBad look all around,â one anonymous media executive told Puckâs media analyst, Dylan Byers.
âWe shouldnât have to learn from court documents in a child support case that Semafor paid Jason Miller $100,000 because Semafor should have disclosed that,â the editor-in-chief of the left-leaning publication MeidasTouch posted.
On Friday, the publication updated 11 stories disclosing the companyâs financial relationship with Miller, Conway, and Elrod.
Maxâs view
The death of the previous generation of digital media startups like BuzzFeed News and Vice, and taught many in the news media a lesson: the free, ad-supported model of digital startup journalism is unsustainable.
In this environment, Semaforâs success has aroused some suspicion. At a moment when many media companies have struggled to stay afloat, Semafor has built a profitable news outlet thatâs still free for online users, prompting some skeptics to wonder what the real reason is for the businessâ growth.
As a four-year veteran of the company, I can say Semaforâs viability is the result of a hardworking and creative commercial team, fairly shrewd financial planning, and talented journalists producing an editorial product readers find to be important. In my time here, Iâve never been asked by any editor â explicitly or implicitly â to lay off a guest or subject for commercial reasons. Iâve watched our editors defend our critical coverage and skeptical questions at events from subjects that arenât always pleased with the content, and, when our offices were much smaller, I occasionally caught a glimpse of our revenue team navigating skittish sponsors who werenât always comfortable with sensitive topics in the news cycle. At Semafor World Economy earlier this year, which occurred weeks after the Iran war began, a number of high-profile guests dropped out after asking us if our journalists could avoid asking about the war. They were told no.
But media organizations are built on trust, and few institutions are less trusted in 2026 than the news media. America is cynical about the real and perceived coziness between politicians, lobbyists and the media companies that cover them. Compensating well-known political hands to ask important players to appear at events deepens that perception, even if they had zero influence on questions that the journalists asked once they got there.
Semafor is not wrong that the use of external firms to help with high-profile events isnât unusual. Many Washington organizations hire strategic public affairs firms for events that require executive wrangling. Two people familiar with the arrangement told me that former Harris adviser Shari Yost Gold had been enlisted for the White House Correspondentsâ Association dinner and Politicoâs major Sunday brunch (though unlike Conway, Yost Gold has not worked in the federal government). Bloomberg has enlisted FGSâ Capricia Marshall, a veteran of the Clinton and Obama White Houses, for its events.
âEvery public affairs firm offers this,â one industry insider told me.
But even if you accept the premise that it is a routine practice, Miller was not just a normal lobbyist; at the time that he was an adviser for Semafor, he was also working for Paramount to help secure its bid for Warner Bros. Discovery, and get the resulting Skydance megamerger approved by federal regulators.
The Semafor reporters and editors covering the deal considered Miller a part of that story, and were completely unaware that he was simultaneously being paid by the commercial side of the business. Miller has also been so close to the White House at times that itâs hard to consider him an outside actor. The directors of You Can See Everything are pushing back against new reporting about the filmâs controversial subject.
At the end of the documentary, which follows disgraced pharmaceutical entrepreneur Elizabeth Holmesâ final days before going to prison, it is revealed that her husband, Billy Evans, negotiated â and later relinquished â the rights to payment for the familyâs role in the film.
Last week, The Hollywood Reporter published a story saying the film had omitted key details that made Evans look slightly better â principally, that he âdid retain rights to the payout on You Can See Everything after all.â
âThe payout still went out; it was just redirected to a charity, in a move that puts Evans in a slightly warmer light,â the outlet reported.
But during a Q&A Saturday night at the Darryl F. Zanuck Theater on the Fox studio lot, Lance Oppenheim and Nathan Fielder said that the THR storyâs framing and wording was inaccurate, and that none of the documentaryâs subjects were paid, according to one person in attendance.
An A24 spokesperson declined to comment. But a studio source said that after Evans negotiated a profit participation deal, he ultimately relinquished his right to it. He and A24 mutually agreed to donate the proceeds to charity; as a part of the deal, the source said, Evans gave up his right to participate in the filmâs profits.
Oppenheim told the audience he was surprised by the story because The Hollywood Reporter is a âgreat publication.â
âIt is?â Fielder replied.
In an email, THRâs editor-in-chief, Maer Roshan, said that the organization stood by its reporting, and that A24âs view âseems like a pretty semantic argument.â Further, he noted that THRâs Julian Sancton raised the story with Oppenheim during THRâs yet-to-be-released directorâs roundtable yesterday featuring the You Can See Everything director, plus Alex Gibney, Ron Howard, and Ava Duvernay, among others.

d7cbd5a20071.text:
Two years out from the âmanosphere election,â Joe Rogan remains American menâs most trusted voice in media, even as their electoral sympathies have swung back towards the Democratic Party. Thatâs according to a sweeping post-midterms report conducted by Precision Strategies and data firm Tunnl â titled Beyond the Manosphere: The Vote Moved Together. The Culture Didnât â that found an American populace riven by economic anxiety and split across race and gender lines.
Meanwhile, the survey found, thereâs no equivalent consensus voice for female audiences: Forty-nine percent of men (including 41% of Democratic men) said they trust Rogan, a greater share than any other figure polled, while no one person earned more than 22% of womenâs trust. One possible reason why: Sixty-three percent of men said they had no male role models to turn to in their lives, and the potent parasocial relationships Roganâs intimate longform chats can foster have inspired imitators from Theo Von to the US military. (See video podcaster aesthetic, above.)
âThe landscape of influence is changing, and understanding who people trust â and why â is becoming just as important as understanding what they believe,â said Tunnlâs Brent Seaborn.
Another data point from Precisionâs survey may disquiet journalists: Half of Republicans (51% of men, 50% of women) say the US government should be able to restrict media access for outlets that it believes to be biased, while a slight majority of the overall population say press access takes precedence.
On partisan politics, the report broadly tracked with other midterms polling: Americans, particularly Gen Z, shifted towards Democrats without developing an abiding loyalty to the Democratic Party as their fears about job losses and financial difficulties continued to mount. Forty-five percent of men under age 30 reported identifying as independents, despite that groupâs noted Democratic swing.
But some findings underscored a growing weariness with some of MAGAâs cultural agenda: Only 16% of men and 11% of women said the Trump administrationâs crusade against DEI had helped them in some way, while most reported no difference. And just 13% of women and 19% of men want more women to be full-time homemakers, something the Trump administration has sought to incentivize.
Americans also report varying attitudes towards AI usage: A fifth of respondents said theyâd used AI chatbots for companionship, with higher rates among younger Americans. Asian, Black, and Hispanic Americans also said they used AI more often than white Americans.

ceeb4cc8f83a.text:
The highest-grossing film of all time, Avengers: Endgame, grossed $2.9 billion during its theatrical run. Grand Theft Auto VI, the long-awaited next installment of the video game franchise, recorded $3.8 billion in sales on its first day.
In a rave review, The New York Times called it âa game about love and relationships, their joy and heartache, and the work required to make them successful,â while The Washington Post gushed that the game was âan astonishing American epic.â The Miami Heat released special-edition Vice City jerseys.
The record-setting release represents the cultural acceptance of a franchise that was once the center of a backlash to violent video games.
During a press conference in 2005, then-Sen. Hillary Clinton said that the âdisturbing material in Grand Theft Auto and other games like it is stealing the innocence of our children,â and The House of Representatives passed a resolution (by a bipartisan 355-21 vote) asking the FTC to investigate Rockstar, the studio that makes Grand Theft Auto. The late Sen. Joe Lieberman (who some GTA fans suspect is parodied by the weedy in-universe character âChaz Liebermanâ) denounced GTA for years.
The franchise outlasted and outgrew the backlash. The game added layers of narrative tenderness in between some of the brutal and comic setpieces, and expanded its range of playable tasks into the comically mundane, like painting your characterâs house and picking up groceries for his girlfriend. Years of research also tamped down some fears about links between video games and real violence.
Beyond some segments in conservative media, the criticism this time around has been fairly muted; in some corners of the incel right, the game has been criticized as, if anything, too respectful to women. The mainstream acceptance of GTA has even reached Fox News, where a former police captain, brought on to warn parents about GTAâs influence on children, admitted: âItâs probably a really fun game.â

873d35bb929d.text: Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton will also serve as acting national cyber director while Kirsten Davies awaits Senate confirmation to lead the office, Axios has learned. A White House official said the strong support Davies received convinced Trump to nominate her to lead the office permanently rather than keep her in an acting capacity. Why it matters: Clayton, the nation's top intelligence official, will now coordinate cybersecurity policy as outages and reported cyberattacks expose vulnerabilities in America's digital infrastructure. Catch up quick: President Trump announced Thursday he was tapping Davies, the Pentagon's chief information officer, to replace Sean Cairncross as national cyber director. Davies will assist Clayton as a senior adviser in the Office of the National Cyber Director until she is confirmed. Trump has increasingly turned to Clayton. He became director of national intelligence in August, and then Trump named him AI czar coordinating the government's approach to AI. Now he will temporarily lead the office responsible for coordinating cybersecurity policy. What they're saying: "I'm excited to work more with Kirsten, who has the experience and capabilities needed to help America navigate our increasingly complex and powerful digital infrastructure as our next National Cyber Director," Clayton said in a statement to Axios. "I look forward to working with the ONCD team to ensure Kirsten has a seamless transition into the role upon her confirmation by the Senate." The big picture: Two critical national security roles will temporarily fall under one official as President Trump shakes up his cybersecurity team amid the growing threat of AI-powered attacks. The disruptions have raised concerns about the vulnerability of the nation's digital infrastructure, although administration officials say there is no evidence they were caused by coordinated cyberattacks. Clayton himself has played a prominent role in the administration's response, telling lawmakers Wednesday that the outages appeared to stem from unrelated technical problems and system upgrades. Driving the news: Clayton spent Sunday morning on CNN's "State of the Union," ABC's "This Week" and "Fox News Sunday," explaining recent technology disruptions and national security concerns. On CNN, he warned that Americans should expect more "glitches, gaps, interruptions in service" as government agencies and businesses modernize their systems. On ABC, Clayton maintained that recent widespread outages were neither coordinated nor state-sponsored, but declined to discuss reported cyberattacks on the FBI and Department of Agriculture. On Fox News, he said AI is giving malicious actors more powerful tools and warned that critical infrastructure will need upgrades. Zoom in: Davies oversees the Pentagon's information technology and cybersecurity strategy, including efforts to modernize aging systems and protect military networks. She has nearly two decades of technology experience, including senior roles at Unilever, Estée Lauder, Barclays Africa, Hewlett Packard Enterprise and Siemens. Behind the scenes: Clayton has already worked closely with the Office of the National Cyber Director, National Security Council, National Security Agency and other agencies through his AI leadership role, according to the White House official.

a9c608bb8196.text: By — Kathy McCormack, Associated Press Kathy McCormack, Associated Press By — Patrick Aftoora Orsagos, Associated Press Patrick Aftoora Orsagos, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/nation/lawyer-father-and-daughter-detained-by-ice-at-seattle-airport-were-traveling-to-family-baptism Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Lawyer: Father and daughter detained by ICE at Seattle airport were traveling to family baptism Nation Nov 22, 2026 6:46 PM EST A father and daughter detained by masked immigration officers on an airport jet bridge in Seattle, causing chaos in front of other passengers, were heading to a family baptism ceremony in California, their lawyer said Sunday. READ MORE: Immigration officers make arrests at Seattle airport in 'distressing' scene, delaying flight Other passengers boarding the Alaska Airlines flight at Seattle-Tacoma International Airport on Saturday used their cellphones to film the father and daughter being detained by the officers, who were wearing unmarked jackets and khaki pants. The recordings were widely viewed on social media. The videos show the officers struggling with someone on the ground. The flight, bound for Los Angeles, was delayed. The father and daughter were traveling to attend a baptism ceremony in California and are seeking asylum in the U.S., where they have lived since 2015, their lawyer, Olia Catala, told The Associated Press in a telephone interview. They have no criminal record, Catala said. "They've done everything correctly, and these are educated people," Catala said of the father and daughter. "She went to college, to university, she worked for a nonprofit. No criminal history (for) any of them. So it's just heartbreaking." Immigration and Customs Enforcement said in a statement that its officers detained Ricardo Larrondo Mendoza, an immigrant from Mexico who it said had overstayed his visa "in violation of our nation's laws." During the confrontation, another passenger "hurled hot coffee on the officers," the ICE statement said. That woman, Sofia Hernandez Mejia, was determined to be in the U.S. illegally from Mexico and to have also overstayed her visa, ICE said. She could be charged with assaulting a federal officer. Mejia, in her mid-20s, had married a U.S. citizen and filed paperwork for adjustment of her status, her attorney said. Mejia's husband was accompanying Mejia and her father when they were detained Saturday, Catala added. The husband was not detained, the attorney said. WATCH: Lawmakers press Mullin on flight disruptions and ICE tactics Both were being held at the Northwest ICE Processing Center in Tacoma, Catala said. She said Mejia was carrying a cup of coffee when the confrontation occurred. "When somebody's charging at you, you're going to drop a cup of coffee," Catala said. "It was just a lot of commotion, and honestly, if somebody is running at you or charging at you and they're not wearing a uniform, you don't know who they are," Catala said. "There was a lot of panic, chaos, not knowing what's going on." Alaska Airlines said ICE officers gave no advance notice of the enforcement action, which occurred during a busy travel weekend ahead of the Thanksgiving holiday. ICE has stepped up arrests at airports since the summer, especially targeting people it says have overstayed visas. Alaska Airlines said it was working with the Port of Seattle, which manages the airport, to see if protocols were followed, and also that it has raised concerns "directly with the appropriate authorities." The Port of Seattle said in a statement that the arrest was distressing not only for the affected family but for other passengers, and that local authorities would "engage federal officials to understand more about what occurred." Washington Gov. Bob Ferguson, a Democrat, said ICE's tactics were "deeply un-American" and called for the agency's abolition. 2738467f9fa8.text: By — Suzan Fraser, Associated Press Suzan Fraser, Associated Press By — Anton L. Delgado, Associated Press Anton L. Delgado, Associated Press By — Sibi Arasu, Associated Press Sibi Arasu, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/in-their-own-words-leaders-at-un-climate-talks-discuss-why-negotiations-ended-without-deal Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter In their own words: Leaders at UN climate talks discuss why negotiations ended without deal World Nov 22, 2026 6:00 PM EST ANTALYA, Turkey (AP) — The words of negotiators and other leaders at the U.N. climate talks illustrate why the meeting failed to reach a final agreement. Each year the annual meeting seeks to hammer out a document known as a cover decision that gives direction on how countries around the world should fight climate change. But at the meetings in Turkey this time, negotiators could not overcome impasses on whether the final document should mention fossil fuels. The burning of fuels such as coal, oil and gas is what causes global warming. READ MORE: UN climate talks break down over bitter disagreements on fossil fuels After reviewing a draft of the agreement released by co-host Turkey, a number of countries spoke up during the final meeting Sunday to say they couldn't accept a deal that failed to include wording on fossil fuels. Others spoke to reporters on the sidelines of the plenary sessions. The co-hosts Turkey and Australia also offered their thoughts. Below are the views of the players at COP31, in their own words. Darragh O'Brien, Irish climate minister speaking on behalf of the European Union's 27 countries: "I want to clearly state that the European Union and its member states object to this cover decision in both its iterations, and that we're saying that on behalf of our citizens, our member states, because these decisions go nowhere near the level of action or ambition that are required for us to tackle climate change, it is unconscionable that we would have a climate act that makes no reference to fossil fuel." Ana Aguilar, Panama's chief climate negotiator and a senior leader in the Climate Change Directorate at Panama's Ministry of Environment: "Our responsibility is not to negotiate the minimum threshold, our responsibility is to do what is right. Our responsibility is to protect the planet. ... This is an issue of justice. President, please allow us to explain briefly why Panama cannot support this decision. One, because it repeats previously agreed to commitments without closing the gap between reality and what science demands. Two, because it (relies) too much upon technologies such as, CCS capture storage of carbon, instead of calling for deep changes. And, three, because it weakens language agreed in previous decisions. This is a setback, a rollback." The Marshall Islands delegation: "We came here expecting the world to deliver a comprehensive and urgent response on reducing emissions, on protecting our people and on providing the finance. To do this, we have been let down on all sides. We were presented with the worst possible response to overshoot. A response that will enhance oil and gas. We will not be forced to accept false solutions. We will not compromise our future to benefit fossil fuel interests. We will not accept an outcome that undermines our security and threatens our future." Australian Minister for Climate Change and Energy and President of COP31 Negotiations Chris Bowen looks on before the plenary session at the UN Climate Change Conference in Antalya, Turkey, on Nov. 22, 2026. Photo by Murad Sezer/Reuters The United Kingdom government: "The United Kingdom does not believe the cover decision proposed by the Presidencies meets the moment. We believe it moves us backward on the science when we must accelerate implementation. It has compromised where it should have presented bold collective ambition on climate action." Steven Victor, Palau's minister of agriculture, fisheries and environment: "Palau will support this text, not perfect as it is. We support this because there's clean electrification, there's ocean, there is finance. The only thing that we had issues with, and we were willing to engage in trying to improve it, is carbon capture. But unfortunately, others all forget about all these other good things and focus on one aspect of the negotiation." "Although there's no cover decision, there are these other work programs that got approved today and the last couple of days. So it's not a failure." Chris Bowen, COP31's president of negotiations and minister of climate change and energy for co-host Australia: "Unfortunately, we were unable to reach agreement on a cover decision. And that's disappointing, very disappointing. Ultimately, looking back, many parties were people of good faith who had very strong red lines on a couple of key issues ... An obvious issue is the transition away from fossil fuels where some parties insisted that it must be mentioned. ... Transition away from fossil fuels in the real world is inevitable. It's happening, it's happening at speed, and it's irreversible." The Associated Press' climate and environmental coverage receives financial support from multiple private foundations. e604e64dcce1.text: To the surprise of many Democrats and even some of their former aides, Pete Buttigieg and Amy Klobuchar now consider themselves friends after their bitter clashes during their campaigns for president in 2020. Their journey from snarky tension to "real respect and friendship," as Klobuchar describes it, is a story of how two ambitious Democrats came to appreciate each other once the heat of a presidential primary had subsided. Why it matters: It's also a reflection of how Buttigieg — who's weighing another run for president — has become a well-regarded Democratic stalwart after many in the party viewed him as a presumptuous lightweight when he ran six years ago as a little-known 37-year-old former mayor of South Bend, Ind. "I'm sincerely grateful for Amy's friendship," Buttigieg, who was President Biden's transportation secretary, told Axios. "My appreciation has continually grown for her substantive leadership and sense of humor alike." "I know there are people that run against each other for president and literally hate each other," Klobuchar, who's in her fourth term in the Senate but will leave in January to become Minnesota's governor, told Axios. "That was far from the case for us." Flashback: A casual observer might see that as a bit of revisionist history. The Buttigieg-Klobuchar spats during the 2020 Democratic primary were some of the most vicious of that campaign. Aides from both sides can still quote the barbs, word for word. "I wish everyone was as perfect as you, Pete," Klobuchar sniped at one debate in Las Vegas before saying "You've memorized a bunch of talking points and a bunch of things." She added after the debate that Buttigieg was "haughty" and that "given the guy [Trump] we have in the White House, maybe you need someone who's a little more humble." Buttigieg repeatedly mocked Klobuchar for not remembering the name of the president of Mexico in an interview. He said Klobuchar was "not able to speak to literally the first thing about the politics of the country to our south." She shot back: "Are you trying to say that I'm dumb?" Asked today about those mutual attacks, Klobuchar says simply: "We both wanted to win." Many Democrats laughed that their feud appeared to continue into 2021, when the two wrote books with opposite titles — "Trust" by Buttigieg, and "Anti-Trust" by Klobuchar. When Buttigieg announced recently that he has a book coming out in January titled "Next," he texted Klobuchar: "Please tell me you're not putting out a book called 'Last.'" Zoom in: Klobuchar said their relationship has become increasingly warm through the years. "We kept consistently in touch, and not just over work. We had lunch when he first got into Washington. I remember I saw their apartment at the time," she said. "I also worked with him extensively on transportation issues." She added that she came to appreciate "how smart and even-keeled he is" at a time when "'hair on fire' is kind of cool to be." Buttigieg, who campaigned with Klobuchar during the 2026 midterms, said he's "looking forward to seeing all that she accomplishes as governor, and also to my next opportunity to join her at the Minnesota State Fair." What they're saying: A former Klobuchar aide told Axios that it's a "very Midwestern friendship story." "You meet someone new with a healthy dose of competition, skepticism, and a little frostiness. And along the way, you find out you genuinely like each other. That's Amy and Pete." What's next: Klobuchar, who has said she's not running for president, didn't want to weigh in on 2028 because she knows many people who are likely to run. As for what she thinks of Buttigieg's potential candidacy: "He has always been impressive."

7af0bf3d71f1.text: By — Jamie Stengle, Associated Press Jamie Stengle, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/nation/automation-system-problem-at-delta-causes-flight-delays-as-americans-travel-for-thanksgiving Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Automation system problem at Delta causes flight delays as Americans travel for Thanksgiving Nation Nov 22, 2026 5:40 PM EST Well over half of Delta Air Lines flights were experiencing delays Sunday afternoon following a problem with an automation system during a busy time for travel ahead of the Thanksgiving holiday. The airline said its teams were using manual workarounds to get flights off the ground while they continued to work to restore automation of a system that calculates weight to ensure an aircraft isn't too heavy to fly. Hours later, Delta said that system was once again working, though flights were still not back to normal. About 1,000 of the airline's flights were delayed as of Sunday afternoon. READ MORE: Travelers' concerns spike as Thanksgiving nears and tech hiccups grow, but few are dissuaded Earlier Sunday, the Federal Aviation Administration issued about an hourlong ground stop to some flights into Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta International Airport, which is Delta's hub and one of the busiest airports in the world. Complying with the weight and balance limits of an aircraft is critical to flight safety, according to an FAA document, and going above the limit can compromise the structural integrity of the aircraft. The agency said on X that the delays weren't related to FAA air traffic systems. Earlier this month, a malfunction in the FAA's network led to the longest nationwide ground stop in 25 years. The stop lasted for more than four hours, and carriers canceled and delayed swaths of flights as they worked to recover. Just days after that, United Airlines saw its own system outage — forcing it to delay departing flights. The Delta delays come as Americans have been encountering a growing number of problems with technology that are increasingly disrupting their lives. As of mid-afternoon Sunday, the flight-tracking website FlightAware said 67%, or about 1,000, of Delta's flights were delayed. FlightAware said that 54% of flights out of the Atlanta airport were delayed while about 50% of flights destined for the airport were delayed. Delta said about 70% of the delays and cancellations noted by FlightAware were connected to the automation issue and the rest were because of inclement weather. By mid-afternoon Delta was apologizing for the delays, and said it was rebooking customers and providing meals and hotel rooms where needed, and offering refunds if a flight was canceled. According to FlightAware, 2% of the airline's flights were canceled. A free press is a cornerstone of a healthy democracy. Support trusted journalism and civil dialogue. 7759c31f2325.text: Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis is quietly working on a book, two sources tell Axios — a project likely to fuel speculation about his making another run for the White House. Why it matters: DeSantis hasn't publicly acknowledged the book project or disclosed what it will be about. But writing a book is often the first step toward a presidential campaign, and it could give the term-limited governor a platform to lay out his vision for the Republican Party's future. DeSantis' state was a rare bright spot for Republicans in this month's midterms, as Democrats made historic gains across the nation. Driving the news: Word of DeSantis' book comes as he's become increasingly outspoken on a range of policy issues, particularly the economic and social impact of artificial intelligence — potentially offering clues about what the book might address. DeSantis has become a vocal critic of the potential dangers of AI, warning that it could eliminate jobs, threaten children's safety and privacy, and drive up electricity bills as data centers expand. DeSantis has pushed for an "AI Bill of Rights" and signed state legislation aimed at preventing tech companies from passing the costs of data centers on to residential consumers. His stance has put him at odds with the Trump administration's efforts to limit states' ability to regulate AI. DeSantis has emphasized affordability, immigration and education — issues likely to remain central to national politics long after he leaves office. Zoom out: DeSantis has made other moves that could keep him in the national spotlight after he leaves office in January. NBC News recently reported that DeSantis is preparing to launch a conservative think tank, which could enable him to retain a political and donor infrastructure. After the midterms, DeSantis embarked on a flurry of media appearances that resembled a victory tour, highlighting how Florida Republicans had largely escaped the Democratic wave. Yes, but: Some DeSantis allies are highly skeptical that he'll mount another presidential campaign after his unsuccessful 2024 bid. DeSantis has sent mixed signals about his political future. He downplayed the prospect of another presidential bid last year and, after the midterms, questioned how much a Republican president could accomplish with Democrats controlling Congress. He also disputed a report that he was building a campaign operation. But he hasn't ruled out a 2028 run, saying he'll assess the political landscape after leaving office. What they're saying: DeSantis' spokespeople did not respond to requests for comment about the book.

bcdded504cd6.text: By — Samira Mehta, The Conversation Samira Mehta, The Conversation Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/nation/todays-thanksgiving-holiday-was-invented-amid-the-civil-war-to-unite-a-divided-country Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Today's Thanksgiving holiday was invented amid the Civil War to unite a divided country Nation Nov 22, 2026 5:18 PM EST This article originally appeared on The Conversation. It is hard to imagine a more American holiday than Thanksgiving. Every year, elementary schoolers learn about the first celebration: that after surviving a terrible year, New England's first European immigrants, the Pilgrims, invited their Indigenous neighbors to a feast in gratitude for their help and God's providence. READ MORE: A historian explains how the Pilgrims took over Thanksgiving – and who has been erased Children learn the story as if it were history — and as though Americans have commemorated Thanksgiving the same way ever since. The only existing eyewitness account of this event does not, however, say much about what was eaten. A slightly later account of the 1621 harvest mentions seasonal food such as venison, corn — and, yes, turkeys. The idea of a straight line connecting that "first Thanksgiving" to Thanksgivings today is, in fact, an American myth. It is a story created in the 19th century to unify a nation and long used to assimilate new immigrants into it. Creating today's Thanksgiving The Pilgrims and Puritans, who started arriving in Massachusetts shortly afterward, regularly held fasts and feasts. On fast days, the community atoned for sins they believed they had committed. On feast days, they gave thanks to God. Some governors of colonies — and later, states — declared fall holidays of thanksgiving, but did not coordinate with each other. The Thanksgiving that we know, with the traditional recipes and the close connection to the Pilgrims, was largely the creation of one woman: Sarah Josepha Hale, who was born in New Hampshire in 1788. In the 1830s she became the editor of Godey's Lady's Book, which had the largest circulation of any U.S. magazine before the Civil War. Godey's included clothing patterns, recipes, articles on home management, essays on educating children, recipes and fiction. Hale believed that the woman was the heart of the home and responsible for creating an upstanding, God-fearing, wholesome family. She was also deeply committed to her young country and believed that homemakers could help create its national identity. According to historian Elizabeth Pleck, Hale began publishing editorials calling for a national Thanksgiving, along with instructions for what the day could look like. READ MORE: The botany behind why cranberries became a Thanksgiving staple Godey's taught readers how to celebrate the day, with recipes for seasonal food such as turkey and cranberry sauce. The centerpiece of the table was the pies, which featured elaborate pastry decorations: the Mayflower or a cornucopia, created out of pie crust. The full table was a celebration of "women's work," at a time when the Industrial Revolution was shifting the economy toward factories and other business, making the importance of unpaid domestic labor less obvious. Hale's idea of Thanksgiving also emphasized returning to loved ones, as those factories were drawing many workers away from home. She saw it as a day to tell family stories — and the story of the nation, starting with the first Thanksgiving. Hale petitioned five presidents to declare Thanksgiving a national holiday. Abraham Lincoln finally took her up on it, hoping that a national holiday emphasizing the country's origin story would prove uniting during the Civil War. Northern women sent pies to the families of soldiers and turkeys to the men at the front. Pleck notes that abolitionist Sojourner Truth went door to door, collecting funds to provide Thanksgiving dinners to African American troops. The holiday caught on gradually. Given the Protestant origins of early Americans' feast and fast days, Catholics were slow to embrace it. Given its association with Lincoln and the war, the South was also late to adopt it. And given the day's emphasis on family, it was less celebrated on the frontier, where single men dominated. Wherever Thanksgiving was celebrated, however, Godey's Lady's Book taught Americans how to celebrate it. The magazine's op-eds connected the holiday menu and the past, using the Pilgrims' courage to inspire 19th-century Americans dealing with massive changes in their own lives: war, industrialization, urbanization and the frontier. Assimilating immigrants Before long, Thanksgiving was also seen as a way to assimilate immigrants. This vision was, in part, popularized by political cartoonist Thomas Nast. "Uncle Sam's Thanksgiving Dinner," which appeared in Harper's Weekly in 1869, depicted Americans from any number of races and ethnicities in their national dress: men, women and children sitting as equals around a dinner table, with portraits of presidents on the wall, while Uncle Sam carved a turkey. The image suggested that immigrants could be incorporated into the nation – and formerly enslaved people, too. It was printed just one year after the 14th Amendment granted citizenship to anyone born in the U.S. and four years after the 13th Amendment formally ended slavery. Nast's image contrasted sharply to another cartoon, also called "Uncle Sam's Thanksgiving Dinner," that G.F. Keller drew for the San Francisco Wasp eight years later. Keller's disheveled and entirely male collection of diners each ate their own national food, or offensive stereotypes thereof, suggesting immigrants could never truly become American. But many Americans believed they could — although they demanded most immigrants give up their "Old World ways" and take on customs of their new country. Thanksgiving was part of the engine of that assimilation. WATCH: How teachers are debunking s

US immigration authorities faced criticism after Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officers arrested two passengers as they were boarding a flight in Seattle.
The incident happened on Saturday morning local time at the Seattle-Tacoma International Airport (SEA), when ICE said a man and a woman, both Mexican nationals, were arrested for allegedly overstaying their visas.
It said that, during its arrest of the man - named as Ricardo Larrondo Mendoza - "other travellers began to obstruct and assault our law enforcement officers", which it described as a "federal crime and a felony".
The Port said in a statement that it was "outraged" about the incident.
Alaska Airlines said the incident happened during the boarding of one of its flights to Los Angeles and that it was not given "appropriate notice of the enforcement action".
It also said it was "concerned" about the arrests and recognised "how distressing this incident has been for employees and guests".
Both the airline and the Port of Seattle, which owns and runs the airport, said they were looking into whether the proper protocols were followed.
The Port said: "Immigration enforcement actions at SEA are conducted without the Port's participation or knowledge."
According to ICE, the woman they arrested - named as Sofia Hernandez Mejia - "hurled hot coffee on the officers" and would be charged with assaulting a federal officer.
Olia Catala, a lawyer for both Mendoza and Mejia - who are father and daughter - told local NBC affiliate King 5 News that they have "absolutely no criminal history".
"They're not fugitives. They're going through a legal process," Catala added.
The family has reportedly said that the ICE officers were in plain clothes and approached Mendoza and Mejia without identification.
"You can imagine if somebody's running at you who is not dressed as an officer, you don't know who they are," said Catala.
"So, there was a lot of panic, a lot of chaos, officers grabbing her, coffee spilling."
Video of the arrests taken by eyewitnesses appears to show two agents wearing masks, plain jackets and khaki trousers.
One eyewitness, John Gaedeke, who was also boarding the plane, told the Reuters news agency he thought the agents were passengers and that they "didn't have any identification".
Gaedeke said the agents "pointed and then they said now, and then they just lunged forward, didn't identify themselves" before "tackling" a man.
"Coffee definitely went flying, but to me, it looked like the passenger was holding it in their hand, and when they were tackled, it went everywhere. I didn't see anyone throw coffee," he added.
The Port of Seattle said it had "continually asked, and local federal immigration authorities have previously agreed to protocols at SEA, and we are in conversation with DHS [the Department of Homeland Security] on whether any of these protocols were breached".
According to the port's website, federal agents have access to airport property and port officials cannot interfere with operations. It says that the port has not historically been given advanced information about immigration enforcement, even when this takes place on its property.
Alaska Airlines said it is "required to comply with applicable laws and regulations when interacting with law enforcement officials".
"We do not direct or coordinate immigration enforcement activity, and we remain committed to protecting the privacy and safety of our guests and employees wherever possible," it added.
Washington's Democratic Governor Bob Ferguson told a press conference on Saturday that "ICE is completely out of control".
"We need a system of immigration enforcement, border security that is effective, ethical, and humane and ICE is not it. It is beyond reform."
Katie Garrow, the executive secretary of MLK Labor - which represents flight attendants, pilots and airport employees - said the incident had been "so upsetting and disturbing to workers" that four of the six crew on the flight chose not to fly.
Deportations of people found to be in the US illegally have ramped up significantly under Donald Trump's presidency but the tactics used by ICE have made many Americans grow uncomfortable, including many of those who supported stricter restrictions broadly.
Immigration raids have caused controversy in a number of US cities, including Minneapolis, Minnesota, where ICE agents killed Renee Good and Alex Pretti earlier this year.

African governments have spent decades promising to turn their countries from exporters of raw materials into manufacturing economies. But concrete progress has been limited. Now, after years in which Chinese companies appeared mostly focused on extracting African resources, a new report shows they are pivoting to building a manufacturing presence across the continent.
At least $19 billion in Chinese manufacturing investment was made across 113 projects in 19 African countries between Sep. 2024 and June 2026, according to Development Reimagined, a consultancy. Thatâs nearly double the $10 billion pledged by Chinese companies at a 2024 China-Africa summit in Beijing, and is separate from $41.2 billion in mining and mineral processing investments identified in a companion study.
âWe last saw a big government push on Chinese FDI into Africa around 2015/2016, it seems now, post-COVID, that push is back, and it seems with more gusto than ever,â said Hannah Ryder, chief executive of Development Reimagined.
The renewed interest comes as Chinese manufacturers deal with excess capacity and intense price competition at home, while trade barriers in the US and Europe make these export markets harder to access. But itâs also clear Africa offers growing consumer markets, lower-cost production opportunities and, since May, duty-free access to China for 53 of 54 countries.
A bigger Chinese manufacturing footprint does not mean Africa is about to become the worldâs next industrial hub. The continentâs share of global manufacturing output has actually fallen to less than 2% today from about 3% in the 1970s, according to the UN Industrial Development Organization. Familiar obstacles still give investors pause including unreliable electricity, poor transport links, and limited access to finance.
But the opportunity remains significant: Global supply chains are shifting just as demand grows for locally made construction materials and clean-energy equipment. Chinese companies that already operate on the continent are expanding, Ryder said, suggesting the trend has commercial momentum.
The question to consider is whether African governments can turn that interest into something more durable with local suppliers, skilled jobs, and technology transfer. Attracting manufacturers is a start but ensuring more of the value stays in Africa is the harder test.

Nigeria's President Bola Tinubu says the presidential villa suffers from cuts in electricity and water - issues that are all too common for the country's ordinary citizens.
He said he was shaving last week when the water supply cut at the villa, known as Aso Rock, in Abuja.
He is seeking re-election next January and vowed to address these issues.
Tinubu made the disclosure on Sunday at a special prayer session organised in his honour by members of his family in Lagos.
He explained: "On the Wednesday of last week, I was shaving, and the water went off. In the villa, you won't know punishment dey dia too [thereâs punishment there too in Nigerian pidgin].
"The water went off. So we will correct all this. No light, no water, no electricity, no development. We have just started. We can do it, and we will do it for Nigeria,â he said.
Aso Villa serves as both the office and official residence of the Nigerian president. It is situated at the base of Aso Rock in Abuja.
Nigeria has long endured electricity shortages, but recent severe disruptions have been caused primarily by insufficient gas supplies and declining hydropower output, rather than the usual nationwide grid collapse.
Persistent blackouts in Lagos, Abuja and elsewhere have forced distribution companies to implement rotating power cuts, severely impacting households and businesses.
The country also suffers from chronic water shortages, the result of a structural crisis rooted in the gap between rapid urban population growth and decaying, inadequate public water infrastructure, leaving millions without reliable supplies, especially in Lagos.
Tinubu made a high-profile electricity promise during the 2023 election campaign, but the exact wording and how binding it is has become a major point of contention ahead of the election on 16 January 2027.
In 2022, months before the last presidential election, Tinubu said: "Whichever way, by all means necessary, you will have electricity, and you will not pay for estimated bills any more. A promise made will be a promise kept.
"If I don't keep the promise and I come for a second term, don't vote for me, unless I give you adequate reasons why I couldn't deliver,â he said.
Despite the continuing power cuts, some of his supporters point to improved electricity supplies in rural areas as well as a recently approved $2bn (Â£1.5bn) investment in a new EastâWest Super Grid, designed to expand electricity transmission capacity and strengthen the national grid, as evidence that he is doing his best to keep to his promise.
Tinubu defeated the countryâs former Vice-President Atiku Abubakar as well as former Anambra state governor Peter Obi in 2023 and the three are seen as the strongest contenders once again.

Hundreds of flights have been cancelled and train services have been severely disrupted across Belgium as a result of a strike against planned austerity measures.
All air traffic has been halted in Zaventem airport in the capital, Brussels, as well as Charlerois, home to low-cost airlines such as Ryanair.
Trains and underground services have also been halted in Brussels where large numbers of people joined a protest march.
The protest comes as Prime Minister Bart De Wever continues talks with his coalition allies over a budget to cut borrowing costs. King Philippe declined his resignation earlier this month, giving De Wever more time to negotiate.
No flights are taking off or landing at Brussels Airport between 07:00 and 21:00 local time (06:00-20:00 GMT) as a result of the strike by air traffic controllers. More than 50,000 travellers' plans were being disrupted - with more expected to be affected overnight and on Tuesday.
A similar situation has affected Charlerois, where all flights were shown as "scheduled", regardless of the time of departure of arrival.
"Without air traffic control, no flights can take off or land," the airport said on Saturday when the strike action was announced, warning of "disastrous consequences".
As thousands descended on Brussels for the protest march, the leader of one of the country's main unions, FGTB, said the government had alternatives to "dismantling the social protection system".
"A genuine wealth tax, fair taxation, and the elimination of tax loopholes," Bert Engelaar, head of FGBT, said.
"Political responsibility is not about keeping a government afloat at all costs. It's about knowing when to stop," Engelaar said, praising the left-wing Vooruit party - the only member of the five-party governing coalition reported to have stalled efforts to agree the budget.
Vooruit wants to raise taxes on the rich, and fewer cuts to pensions and the health sector.
Another union leader, Ann Vermorgen of the CSC, criticised government plans to cut bank holidays when they fall on weekends.
Public transport, schools and other public services are also facing disruptions.

Russia and Ukraine carried out weekend strikes that pointed to an expansion of the war despite a recent diplomatic push. Kyiv sank a Russian warship moored off the coast of Libya the day after striking a cargo ship in the Baltic Sea it said was being used to ferry weapons for Moscow.
The Kremlin retaliated by unleashing a fierce attack on Ukraineâs energy infrastructure and hitting civilian sites, including an apartment block and shops, killing at least a dozen people. The expansion in hostilities, as well as the recent resumption of strikes in the Gulf, pushed up benchmark European LNG prices ahead of what could be a difficult, and expensive, winter.

The UK National Health Service launched what it touted as the worldâs largest trial using AI to assist in breast-cancer screening, the most ambitious of several efforts to deepen the use of the technology to improve care. AIâs potential to accelerate health research is one of its greatest promises, with leaders in the sector forecasting that it will be used to develop a cure for cancer within a lifetime.
Progress on that front is important not just to patients, but also the tech sector, which is under increasing fire over its impact on inflation and jobs. The pharmaceutical industry is skeptical, however: Novartisâ CEO said too little was yet understood about the human body for rapid development to take place.

US stocks looked set to bounce back from a huge selloff, a pullback that prompted Asian regulators to intervene. Mondayâs slump in Asia followed on from Fridayâs rout in the US, where the Nasdaq recorded its worst week since the COVID-19 pandemic and the S&P 500 entered correction territory, down almost 20% from its October peak.
Still, analysts warned any recovery this week could be temporary, even if US earnings remain strong: Investors have become bearish on AI firms as concerns mount that they have committed to spending huge sums building infrastructure at a time of rising debt costs, with even market leadersâ bonds likely to be priced below investment grade, The Wall Street Journal reported.
